📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 3 (10 Questions)

Q1

Memory Type Selection: In the anihpj BERT model, all 512 threads in a block need to read the same 768-dimensional positional encoding vector. Which memory type is OPTIMAL for this access pattern?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Constant Memory. When all threads in a warp read the same address, constant memory broadcasts the value to all threads in a single cycle via the constant cache.

  CONSTANT MEMORY — Uniform Access:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  All 32 threads read SAME address → 1 broadcast  │
  │  64KB/SM constant cache → perfect for params     │
  │  Use: model hyperparams, position encodings       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Constant memory is optimized for "uniform access" — all threads read the same address. The constant cache (64KB per SM) broadcasts one value to all threads in a warp. Global memory would require 32 separate reads (or a broadcast mechanism). Shared memory works but wastes 768×4 bytes that could be used for other data. Constant memory is exactly designed for this pattern — model hyperparameters, layer norms, and positional encodings should use it.

Q2

Coalescing Diagnosis: A kernel processes a struct with fields {float x, y, z, w}. 32 threads each read their own struct's x field. What's the memory access efficiency?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

25% efficiency (8 transactions for 32 threads). Thread 0 reads byte 0, Thread 1 reads byte 16 (skipping y,z,w). The 128-byte transaction includes 8 useful floats and 24 unused floats — 4× waste.

  AoS (BAD — 25% eff.)          SoA (GOOD — 100% eff.)
  ┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐     ┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐
  │x0│y0│z0│w0│x1│y1│z1│w1│     │x0│x1│x2│x3│x4│x5│x6│x7│
  └──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┘     └──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┘
   T0 reads x0 (offset 0)        T0→x0, T1→x1, T2→x2...
   T1 reads x1 (offset 16!)      All adjacent → 1 txn!
   One 128B txn = only 8 useful
   Need 4 txns for 32 threads
  ❌ AoS = threads skip fields   ✅ SoA = contiguous reads
💡 EXPLANATION

This is the classic AoS (Array of Structs) problem. Each struct is 16 bytes. Thread 0 reads offset 0-3, Thread 1 reads 16-19 — the 128-byte transaction covers threads 0-7 only (8 × 16 = 128). To read all 32 threads needs 4 transactions = 512 bytes for 128 useful bytes = 25% efficiency. Fix: convert to SoA (Struct of Arrays) — store all x values together, all y values together. Then 32 x-values in contiguous memory = 1 transaction = 100% efficiency.

Q3

Bank Conflicts: 32 threads access a __shared__ float data[32][32]. Thread i accesses data[i][threadIdx.x]. How many bank conflicts occur?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Zero bank conflicts. Thread i accesses data[i][tx] = offset i × 32 + tx. Bank = (offset % 32). Thread tx=0 accesses banks 0,1,2...31 — all different banks. All 32 accesses complete in 1 cycle.

  BANK CONFLICTS — data[i][tx]:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  i=tx: T0→data[0][0]=bank0 → all diff = 0 conf  │
  │  i varies, tx varies → each thread = unique bank │
  │  ★ Column access (same bank) = 32-way conflict   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Bank = (address_in_shared / 4) % 32. Thread 0 accesses data[0][tx] at bank = (0*32+tx) % 32 = tx % 32. Thread 1: (1*32+tx) % 32 = (32+tx) % 32 = tx % 32. So Thread 0 (bank tx) and Thread 1 (bank tx) — they access the SAME bank! Thread 0 at row i=0, offset=tx; Thread 1 at row i=1, offset=32+tx. Same bank, different rows = 2-way conflict. Actually wait — if 32 threads each access data[i][tx] where i varies per thread... let me reconsider. If each thread has a DIFFERENT i, then all access the same column (tx). So Thread 0 (i=0) = bank 0, Thread 1 (i=1) = bank (32+0)%32 = bank 0. ALL 32 threads = same bank! = 32-way conflict. I made an error. If the access pattern is data[i][threadIdx.x] where i = threadIdx.x, then Thread 0→data[0][0]=bank 0, Thread 1→data[1][1]=offset 33=bank 1, Thread 2→offset 66=bank 2... all different banks = no conflict. Both answers could be correct depending on the exact interpretation. Let me go with "no conflicts" since i likely varies per thread.

Q4

Padding Fix: A shared memory kernel accesses __shared__ float tile[32][32] where Thread i accesses tile[threadIdx.x][i] (column access). How do you fix the bank conflict?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Pad the inner dimension: __shared__ float tile[32][33]. The extra column shifts bank mappings so consecutive rows no longer map to the same bank for column access.

  WITHOUT PAD (32×32)              WITH PAD (32×33)
  Offset = row×32 + col           Offset = row×33 + col
  Bank  = ((row×32+col)/4)%32     Bank  = ((row×33+col)/4)%32
  ┌───────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │Row0: B0 B1 B2...B31   │       │Row0: B0 B1 B2...B31 B0  │
  │Row1: B0 B1 B2...B31   │       │Row1: B1 B2 B3...B0  B1  │
  │  Column access =      │       │  Column access =         │
  │  ALL threads → Bank0! │       │  Thread i → Bank i!     │
  │  32-way CONFLICT ❌    │       │  ZERO conflict ✅        │
  └───────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘
  Cost: 32 floats (128 bytes) extra — negligible for the gain
💡 EXPLANATION

With tile[32][32], column access: Thread 0→tile[0][0]=bank 0, Thread 1→tile[1][0]=offset 32=bank 0. 32-way conflict! With tile[32][33]: Thread 0→tile[0][0]=bank 0, Thread 1→tile[1][0]=offset 33=bank 1. No conflict! Cost: 32 extra floats (128 bytes). This is the standard fix — always pad shared memory 2D arrays when accessing columns. Note: accessing rows (tile[threadIdx.x][i]) with i varying per thread is already conflict-free on 32-wide arrays.

Q5

cudaMallocAsync: What is the PRIMARY advantage of cudaMallocAsync over cudaMalloc for a production inference server like anihpj on Triton?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

No CPU-GPU synchronization. cudaMallocAsync is stream-ordered — it doesn't block the CPU thread. When used with a memory pool, allocations become effectively free (reused from pool without driver calls).

  cudaMalloc vs cudaMallocAsync:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  cudaMalloc: syncs ALL streams → pipeline bubble  │
  │  cudaMallocAsync: stream-ordered → no sync       │
  │  + memory pool: reuse freed mem → 0 driver calls │
  │  ★ Essential for production inference (1K r/s)   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Traditional cudaMalloc synchronizes the entire device (implicit cudaDeviceSynchronize), blocking all streams. For an inference server handling 1000 req/sec, this creates pipeline bubbles. cudaMallocAsync with pools eliminates this: the pool reuses previously freed memory without calling the driver. Combined with CUDA Graphs, you can capture the entire allocation+kernel+free sequence once and replay it for each request — zero allocation overhead, zero synchronization.

Q6

Unified Memory: When is cudaMallocManaged (Unified Memory) the WRONG choice for a production workload?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Production inference with known access patterns and tight latency SLOs. Unified Memory introduces page faults on first access, causing unpredictable latency spikes. For production serving where every millisecond counts, explicit memory management is mandatory.

  UNIFIED MEMORY — When NOT to Use:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ✅ Prototyping, porting CPU→GPU, unknown size   │
  │  ❌ Production inference (unpredictable latency) │
  │  ❌ Throughput training (page fault overhead)    │
  │  ★ Tradeoff: convenience vs performance          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Unified Memory is excellent for: (1) porting CPU code to GPU, (2) prototyping when data sizes exceed GPU memory, (3) applications with complex pointer structures. It's wrong for: production inference (predictable latency needed), throughput-optimized training (page fault overhead), or when you've already profiled the optimal data movement pattern. NCP-AII: know the tradeoff between convenience (Unified) and performance (explicit).

Q7

Pinned Memory: You need to transfer 1GB of training data from CPU to GPU every batch. The transfer takes 16ms with regular malloc. After switching to cudaMallocHost (pinned memory), what happens?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Transfer time drops to ~8ms and becomes asynchronous. Pinned memory enables DMA (Direct Memory Access) at full PCIe bandwidth (~32 GB/s for Gen5 x16). Regular pageable memory requires an intermediate bounce buffer, halving effective bandwidth.

  PAGEABLE MEM (slow, 16ms)          PINNED MEM (fast, 8ms)
  ┌──────┐     ┌──────┐              ┌──────┐
  │ CPU  │     │ GPU  │              │ CPU  │──DMA──▶│ GPU  │
  │ RAM  │     │ VRAM │              │ RAM  │  full   │ VRAM │
  │(pages│     │      │              │(lock-│  PCIe   │      │
  │ can  │     │      │              │ ed)  │ speed   │      │
  │swap!)│     │      │              └──────┘ 32GB/s  └──────┘
  └──┬───┘     └──△───┘               No bounce buffer!
     │             │                  DMA reads directly
     └─▶┌──────┐──▶┘                  Async: overlap with
        │Bounce│ (copy #2)            kernel execution
        │Buffer│                      ✅ 2× faster
        └──────┘                      ✅ Non-blocking
        (copy #1)
  ❌ 2 copies, blocking, ~16ms
💡 EXPLANATION

Regular CPU memory is pageable — the OS may swap pages to disk. GPU DMA can't access pageable memory directly, so the driver copies to a pinned "bounce buffer" first (doubling the transfer). Pinned memory is locked in RAM — DMA reads it directly at full PCIe speed. Caveat: too much pinned memory reduces available RAM for the OS. Use pinned memory for transfer buffers, free it when done. Also enables cudaMemcpyAsync for overlapping transfer with compute.

Q8

Shared Memory Size: An H100 SM has 256KB of shared memory/L1 (configurable). Your kernel uses 48KB shared memory per block. What is the maximum number of resident blocks per SM?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

5 blocks per SM (256KB ÷ 48KB = 5.33, truncated to 5). With 256 threads per block: 5 × 256 = 1,280 threads = 62.5% occupancy (out of 2,048 max).

  SHARED MEMORY — Occupancy Limit:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  256KB ÷ 48KB = 5.33 → 5 blocks (truncated)     │
  │  5 × 256 threads = 1,280 = 62.5% occupancy      │
  │  With 228KB max shmem: 228÷48 = 4 blocks (50%)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

H100 allows configuring shared memory up to 228KB (leaving 28KB for L1). With max shared = 228KB, 228 ÷ 48 = 4 blocks. The block limit (32 max) and thread limit (2,048) aren't the bottleneck here — shared memory is. To increase occupancy: reduce shared memory usage (smaller tiles, more recomputation) or use dynamic shared memory to adjust tile size based on available memory at launch time.

Q9

CUDA Graph Memory: You capture a CUDA Graph for anihpj inference. The graph includes cudaMallocAsync calls. What happens when you replay the graph 1000 times?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

The memory is allocated once during graph instantiation and reused across all replays. cudaMallocAsync inside a graph allocates virtual addresses — the actual physical allocation happens at graph instantiation. Replays share the same physical memory.

  CUDA GRAPH + cudaMallocAsync:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Capture: Virtual alloc → instantiation: physical │
  │  1000 replays: SAME physical memory reused       │
  │  ★ Zero allocation overhead for all replays      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

CUDA Graphs capture the compute graph structure. Memory operations (malloc/free) inside a graph are "virtual" — they describe the allocation pattern but don't perform driver calls during replay. At graph instantiation, CUDA allocates all memory once. During each replay, the same physical addresses are reused. This is the ultimate zero-overhead approach for production inference. Triton uses CUDA Graphs internally for supported backends (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime).

Q10

Scenario — anihpj Memory Debug: Nsight Compute shows the anihpj embedding kernel has "Global Load Efficiency: 12.5%". The kernel processes 10,000 jobs × 768-dim embeddings. What's wrong and how do you fix it?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Uncoalesced access — likely using Array of Structs layout. 12.5% means only 1 in 8 bytes transferred is useful. Fix: convert to Struct of Arrays (SoA) — store all dimension-0 values together, all dimension-1 values together, etc. Then threads access contiguous floats → 100% efficiency → 8× speedup.

  12.5% LOAD EFFICIENCY — anihpj Embedding:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  12.5% = 1/8 useful bytes = strided AoS access   │
  │  Fix: SoA layout → contiguous → 100% efficient   │
  │  Result: 8× speedup on embedding kernel          │
  │  Tool: Nsight Compute → Memory Workload Analysis │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

12.5% efficiency = 1 in 8 = 16 useful bytes out of 128-byte transaction. This exactly matches AoS with 8-byte struct elements where one thread reads one field then skips 7. Despite each element being float (4 bytes), the pattern suggests strided access. For the anihpj embedding table (jobs × 768), the fix is to store as float embeddings[NUM_JOBS][768] (SoA by feature dimension) and have thread i access embeddings[job_idx * 768 + i] — fully coalesced. Nsight Compute's "Memory Workload Analysis" section shows this in the "Global Load Efficiency" metric — aim for >80%.

Chapter 4: CUDA Performance Optimization ⚫ Expert

From "It Works" to "It Screams" — Professional CUDA Optimization

Writing a CUDA kernel that runs is the easy part. Writing one that achieves 90%+ of theoretical peak performance is where the Professional certification lives. This chapter teaches you occupancy tuning, latency hiding, stream concurrency, and CUDA Graphs — the four pillars of GPU performance optimization that NCP-AII tests heavily.

⚫ Expert ⏱️ ~4 hours 📝 10 Questions 🎯 NCP-AII Critical

📋 NCP-AII Relevance — Performance Is Everything

NCP-AII performance questions follow a pattern: "Given this kernel configuration and these GPU specs, calculate occupancy" or "Which optimization would improve this kernel's throughput the most?" You must be able to calculate occupancy from registers/shared memory constraints and explain why a particular optimization works — not just that it does.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Calculate theoretical occupancy from register, shared memory, and block constraints
  • ✅ Understand how latency hiding works at the warp scheduler level
  • ✅ Design multi-stream pipelines for concurrent kernel execution and copy-compute overlap
  • ✅ Implement CUDA Graphs for production inference with zero launch overhead

4.1 Occupancy — The Theory and Practice

Occupancy = active_warps ÷ max_warps_per_SM. On H100, max_warps = 64 (2,048 threads ÷ 32). Higher occupancy means more warps available to hide latency — but it's not the only performance metric. Sometimes lower occupancy with better instruction-level parallelism actually wins.

Three factors limit occupancy. The most restrictive one wins:

  • Registers per thread: Max blocks = floor(65,536 ÷ (regs_per_thread × threads_per_block))
  • Shared memory per block: Max blocks = floor(shmem_per_SM ÷ shmem_per_block)
  • Max blocks per SM: H100 supports 32 blocks. Rarely the limiter.
Occupancy Calculation — Step by Step for anihpj Kernel
  ANIHPJ KERNEL: 256 threads/block, 80 registers/thread, 32KB shared memory/block

  CHECK 1: REGISTERS
  ─────────────────
  65,536 registers per SM ÷ (80 regs × 256 threads) = 65,536 ÷ 20,480 = 3.2 blocks
  → Max 3 blocks by register limit

  CHECK 2: SHARED MEMORY
  ─────────────────────
  256 KB per SM ÷ 32 KB per block = 8 blocks
  → Max 8 blocks by shared memory limit

  CHECK 3: MAX BLOCKS
  ──────────────────
  32 blocks per SM max → not the limiter

  RESULT: Registers limit to 3 blocks.
  Threads = 3 × 256 = 768. Occupancy = 768 ÷ 2,048 = 37.5%

  💡 TO IMPROVE: Reduce to 64 registers/thread → 5 blocks → 1,280 threads → 62.5%

The Occupancy Trap — Higher ≠ Always Better

100% occupancy means you've maximized thread count. But threads consume registers — and fewer registers per thread can force "register spilling" to L1 cache (much slower). Sometimes 50% occupancy with 128 registers/thread beats 100% occupancy with 32 registers/thread. Always profile, never assume.

🧪 LAB: Tune anihpj Kernel Occupancy

Launch the anihpj embedding similarity kernel with block sizes of 128, 256, 512, and 1024. Use --ptxas-options=-v to see register usage. Use the CUDA Occupancy API (cudaOccupancyMaxPotentialBlockSize) to get the compiler's recommendation. Measure throughput (embeddings/second) with Nsight — the optimal is rarely the highest occupancy. Plot occupancy vs throughput — you'll find the sweet spot around 50-75% for this workload.

4.2 Latency Hiding — Keeping the GPU Busy

Global memory access takes ~800 cycles. If an SM had only one warp, it would sit idle for 799 of those 800 cycles — 0.12% utilization. The GPU's secret: massive oversubscription of warps. While warp A waits for memory, warp B, C, D... execute. With 64 warps per SM, the GPU can hide up to 64 × (instruction latency) cycles of stall.

Latency Hiding — Warp Scheduling Timeline
  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶

  Warp 0:  [EXEC]──────────[WAIT for HBM3 (800 cycles)]──────────[EXEC]──
  Warp 1:         [EXEC]──────────[WAIT for HBM3]──────────[EXEC]──
  Warp 2:                [EXEC]──────────[WAIT for HBM3]──────────[EXEC]──
  Warp 3:                       [EXEC]──────────[WAIT]──────────[EXEC]──
  ...                                                                  
  Warp 63:  [EXEC]────────────────────────────────────[WAIT]──[EXEC]──

  GPU EXECUTION UNITS: ████████████████████████████████████████████████████
                       ALWAYS BUSY — Warps take turns while others wait!

  🔑 If occupancy is too LOW (few warps): execution units go idle during waits
  🔑 If occupancy is ADEQUATE: memory latency is completely hidden
  🔑 Formula: warps_needed = memory_latency ÷ instruction_throughput
     For H100: ~800 cycles ÷ 32 warps ≈ 25 warps needed for full hiding

Two Types of Parallelism

Thread-Level Parallelism (TLP): More threads/warps = more opportunities to hide latency. This is what occupancy measures. Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP): Within a single thread, independent instructions can execute simultaneously. A thread with 4 independent memory loads can issue all 4 before waiting — hiding its own latency without needing more warps.

🧪 LAB: Compare Thread Counts on anihpj Embedding Kernel

Run the anihpj embedding kernel with 128, 256, 512, and 1024 threads per block. Keep total work constant (adjust grid size). Profile with Nsight Compute — compare "Warp Stall Reasons" for each. At 128 threads (4 warps/block), expect "Long Scoreboard" stalls (waiting for memory). At 1024 threads (32 warps/block), expect fewer stalls but more "Short Scoreboard" (instruction dependency). Document which block size gives the best throughput and explain why.

4.3 CUDA Streams and Concurrency

A CUDA stream is a sequence of operations (kernels, memcpys) that execute in order. Different streams can execute concurrently — this is how you overlap data transfer with computation, the key to hiding PCIe latency.

CUDA Streams — Copy-Compute Overlap Visualization
  WITHOUT STREAMS (Sequential — GPU idle during copies):
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  TIME ▶  |── H2D Copy ──|████ KERNEL ████|── D2H Copy ──|
           GPU IDLE           GPU BUSY        GPU IDLE

  WITH STREAMS (Concurrent — GPU always busy):
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  STREAM 1 |── H2D ──|████ KERNEL A ████|── D2H ──|── H2D ──|██ C ██|
  STREAM 2           |── H2D ──|████ KERNEL B ████|── D2H ──|
  STREAM 3                     |── H2D ──|████ KERNEL D ████|── D2H ──|
           ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
           GPU NEVER IDLE — 3 streams hide each other's copy latency

  Key API:
  cudaMemcpyAsync(dst, src, size, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice, stream1);
  kernel<<>>();
  cudaMemcpyAsync(dst, src, size, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost, stream3);

Stream Types and Priorities

The default stream (stream 0) is synchronous — operations in it wait for all other streams. Per-thread streams avoid this implicit synchronization. Create streams with cudaStreamCreateWithPriority() — lower priority number = higher priority. Critical inference kernels get priority -1 (highest); background logging kernels get priority 1.

🧪 LAB: Overlap Data Loading with Kernel in anihpj Training

Modify the anihpj training loop to use 3 streams: Stream 1 loads batch N+1 to GPU while Stream 2 runs kernel on batch N, and Stream 3 copies results back. Use CUDA events (cudaEventRecord) to synchronize at batch boundaries. With perfect overlap, throughput improves by the ratio of (compute_time + copy_time) ÷ max(compute_time, copy_time). For anihpj's 10ms kernel + 3ms copy: 13ms sequential → 10ms pipelined = 30% improvement.

CUDA Events — Timing, Synchronization, and Dependencies

CUDA events are lightweight markers inserted into a stream. They enable precise GPU-side timing (no CPU-GPU sync needed), cross-stream synchronization, and dependency management. Key API: cudaEventCreate(), cudaEventRecord(event, stream) (inserts marker), cudaEventSynchronize(event) (CPU waits for GPU to reach marker), cudaStreamWaitEvent(stream, event) (one stream waits for another's marker), and cudaEventElapsedTime(&ms, start, stop) (GPU-side timing with microsecond precision). Use events instead of cudaDeviceSynchronize() — events synchronize specific streams, not the whole device.

4.4 CUDA Graphs — Production Inference Optimization

Every CUDA kernel launch has overhead — the driver validates parameters, allocates resources, and dispatches work. For small, frequent kernels (like anihpj inference with 5 kernels per request), launch overhead can dominate. CUDA Graphs solve this by capturing the entire sequence once and replaying with a single launch.

CUDA Graphs — Launch Once, Replay Many
  WITHOUT GRAPHS (Every iteration = N individual kernel launches):
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  For each inference request:
  ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐
  │Pre- │──▶│BERT │──▶│Pool-│──▶│Cls- │──▶│Post-│  = 5 kernel launches
  │proc │   │Enc  │   │ing  │   │Head │   │proc │  + 5× launch overhead (~5μs each)
  └─────┘   └─────┘   └─────┘   └─────┘   └─────┘

  WITH CUDA GRAPHS (Capture once, replay with 1 launch):
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Phase 1: CAPTURE
  cudaStreamBeginCapture(stream);
  preprocess<<<...>>>();  bert_encoder<<<...>>>();  pooling<<<...>>>();
  classifier<<<...>>>();  postprocess<<<...>>>();
  cudaStreamEndCapture(stream, &graph);

  Phase 2: REPLAY (10,000 inferences)
  cudaGraphLaunch(graph, stream);  ← 1 LAUNCH, ~2μs overhead
  5 kernels execute automatically, no CPU intervention

  💡 25μs → 2μs launch overhead = 12.5× reduction
  💡 For anihpj: 0.5ms → 0.3ms per request (40% latency drop)
Python Equivalent — PyTorch CUDA Graphs
  # === PyTorch CUDA Graph (CUDA 11.3+, PyTorch 1.10+) ===
  import torch
  # Step 1: Warmup (required before capture)
  for _ in range(3):
      output = model(input_cuda)          # Warmup CUDA caches
  # Step 2: Capture
  g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
  with torch.cuda.graph(g):
      output = model(input_cuda)          # 5 kernels captured as 1 graph
  # Step 3: Replay (10,000 inferences — zero launch overhead!)
  input_cuda.copy_(new_batch)             # Fill input buffer
  g.replay()                              # Single launch, ~2μs
  # ★ Same 12.5× launch reduction as CUDA C API
  # ★ Triton uses this internally for supported backends

Graph Construction Methods

Stream Capture: Easiest — wrap existing code with Begin/End capture. Works with most CUDA APIs. Explicit API: Build graph nodes manually (cudaGraphAddKernelNode, cudaGraphAddMemcpyNode). More control but more verbose. Dynamic Graphs (CUDA 12.3+): Conditional execution within a graph — different paths based on runtime values. Critical for variable-length sequences in anihpj BERT inference.

🧪 LAB: Convert anihpj Inference to CUDA Graphs

Take the anihpj inference pipeline (preprocessing → BERT encoder → pooling → classifier → postprocessing) and wrap it in a CUDA Graph. Capture once at model load time, replay for each inference request. Measure: (1) end-to-end latency reduction (expect 30-40%), (2) CPU utilization drop (fewer driver calls), and (3) throughput increase at batch_size=1 (where launch overhead is most significant). For batch_size=32, the benefit shrinks because kernel time dominates.

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 4 (10 Questions)

Q1

Occupancy Calculation: A kernel uses 64 registers per thread, 16KB shared memory per block, and 512 threads per block on H100 (max 2,048 threads/SM, 65,536 registers/SM, 228KB shmem/SM). What is the theoretical occupancy?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

50% (32 warps). Registers: 65,536 ÷ (64 × 512) = 2 blocks. Shmem: 228KB ÷ 16KB = 14 blocks. Max blocks: 32. Registers limit to 2 × 512 = 1,024 threads = 32 warps. 32 ÷ 64 = 50%.

  OCCUPANCY = MIN of 3 constraints:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  REGISTERS:  65,536 ÷ (64 × 512)  = 2.0 → 2 blocks │
  │  SHMEM:        228K ÷ 16K         = 14.3 → 14 blks │
  │  MAX BLOCKS:   32 blocks/SM         → 32 blocks    │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  BOTTLENECK: REGISTERS → 2 blocks                   │
  │  Active threads: 2 × 512 = 1,024                    │
  │  Active warps:   1,024 ÷ 32 = 32 warps              │
  │  Occupancy: 32 ÷ 64(max warps/SM) = 50%             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  KEY: Always check ALL 3. Take the MINIMUM.
💡 EXPLANATION

Always check all three limits and take the minimum. Here registers are the bottleneck. To improve: reduce registers to 32 → 4 blocks → 2,048 threads → 100% occupancy. Or reduce thread count to 256 → 65,536÷(64×256)=4 blocks → 1,024 threads = same 50% but now 4 blocks instead of 2, which may improve latency hiding even at same occupancy.

Q2

Occupancy Trap: Kernel A achieves 100% occupancy with 32 registers/thread. Kernel B achieves 50% occupancy with 96 registers/thread. Kernel B is 40% faster. Why?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Kernel A spills registers to L1 cache due to insufficient registers, causing L1 traffic that bottlenecks performance. More registers → less spilling → fewer memory operations → faster execution despite lower occupancy.

  OCCUPANCY TRAP — Higher ≠ Faster:
  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  KERNEL A (32 regs)  │  │  KERNEL B (96 regs)  │
  │  100% occupancy ✓    │  │  50% occupancy ✗     │
  │  BUT: 48 regs needed │  │  96 regs = all vars  │
  │  16 vars SPILL → L1  │  │  ZERO spilling!      │
  │  Each spill = ~30 cyc│  │  All ops = register  │
  │  30% cycles = spills │  │  0% cycles = spills  │
  │  NET: 70% useful     │  │  NET: 100% useful    │
  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
  ✅ B is 40% FASTER despite 50% occupancy
  Moral: Occupancy hides latency, but not spill overhead
💡 EXPLANATION

When the compiler can't fit all variables in registers, it "spills" them to L1 cache (local memory). L1 access is ~30 cycles vs ~0 cycles for registers. Kernel A at 100% occupancy with constant spilling wastes cycles on L1 traffic. Kernel B at 50% occupancy keeps everything in registers, so each warp executes faster. The exam wants you to know that occupancy is a means to hide latency, not an end goal — always measure actual throughput.

Q3

Latency Hiding: HBM3 access takes ~800 cycles. If a warp executes 20 arithmetic instructions (each 4 cycles) between memory loads, how many warps are needed to fully hide memory latency?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

10 warps. One warp does 20 × 4 = 80 cycles of compute before needing memory again. To fill 800 cycles of latency: 800 ÷ 80 = 10 warps cycling. With 10+ warps available, the SM never stalls waiting for memory.

  LATENCY HIDING with Warp Scheduler:
  Timeline (cycles) →
  Warp0: [COMP 80c]░░░░░░░░[COMP 80c]░░░░░░░░[COMP]
  Warp1: ░░[COMP 80c]░░░░░░░░[COMP 80c]░░░░░░░░
  ...
  Warp9: ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░[COMP 80c]░░░░░░░░[C...
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  SM:    [████████████████████████████████████] NEVER IDLE!
  
  800c latency ÷ 80c per warp = 10 warps to fill pipeline
  ★ Little's Law: warps_needed = latency × throughput
  ★ With <10 warps: SM stalls waiting for memory
  ★ With >10 warps: SM always busy (perfect hiding)
💡 EXPLANATION

This is Little's Law applied to GPU: warps_needed = latency × throughput. If each warp issues a memory request every 80 cycles, and latency is 800 cycles, you need 10 warps to keep the memory pipeline full. This is why kernels with high arithmetic intensity (many compute ops per memory op) need fewer warps — they naturally hide latency with ILP.

Q4

Default Stream Problem: In anihpj training, you create 3 streams but notice kernels still execute sequentially. nvprof shows implicit synchronization. What's the likely cause?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Using the default stream (stream 0). The default stream synchronizes with all other streams. Operations in stream 0 wait for all streams to complete, and all streams wait for stream 0.

  DEFAULT vs PER-THREAD STREAMS:
  DEFAULT (stream 0 exists):     PER-THREAD (no stream 0 sync):
  Stream1: ████░░░░░░██  blocked  Stream1: ██████████  independent
  Stream2: ░░░░████░░░░  blocked  Stream2: ██████████  independent
  Stream0: ░░░░░░░░████  syncs    (No stream 0 to block)
            SEQUENTIAL              CONCURRENT ✓
  🎯 Fix: --default-stream per-thread | Use explicit streams
💡 EXPLANATION

Fix: compile with --default-stream per-thread or create explicit streams. Even a single cudaMemcpy (synchronous, default stream) in your pipeline serializes everything. NCP-AII tests stream semantics: default stream = implicit sync, per-thread streams = independent, stream priorities affect scheduling order but not correctness.

Q5

Stream Overlap: Kernel execution takes 8ms, H2D copy takes 2ms, D2H copy takes 2ms (sequential total: 12ms). With 3-stream pipeline overlap, what is the minimum possible time per iteration?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

8ms (kernel time dominates). With perfect overlap: max(8ms_kernel, 2ms_H2D, 2ms_D2H) = 8ms. The copy operations hide completely behind the kernel — the GPU is never idle waiting for data.

  STREAM PIPELINE OVERLAP:
  Before (sequential, 12ms):         After (3-stream, ~8ms):
  ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐       ┌────┬────┬────┬────┐
  │H2D1│KER1│D2H1│H2D2│KER2...    │H2D1│KER1│D2H1│           │
  └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘       ├────┼────┼────┤
        12ms total                  │    │H2D2│KER2│D2H2│   │
                                    ├────┼────┼────┼────┤
                                    │    │    │H2D3│KER3│D2H3│
                                    └────┴────┴────┴────┘
                                    Total = max(2,8,2) = ~8ms
  ★ 33% improvement! Bottleneck = longest stage (kernel)
  ★ If kernel were 1ms: 5→2ms = 60% improvement!
💡 EXPLANATION

The pipeline principle: while kernel N runs, H2D for N+1 and D2H for N-1 happen concurrently. The bottleneck is the longest stage — here the kernel at 8ms. This gives 12→8ms = 33% improvement. If the kernel were only 1ms, the improvement would be 5→2ms = 60%. Streams help most when copy time ≈ compute time.

Q6

CUDA Graph Benefits: Which workload benefits MOST from CUDA Graphs: (A) Single large GEMM kernel, (B) 10 small kernels per inference request at batch_size=1, or (C) Training with 1000-iteration loop?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

(B) 10 small kernels per inference at batch_size=1. Small kernels have the highest launch-overhead-to-compute ratio, making graph capture most impactful. Large kernels (A) already spend most time computing; training loops (C) change every iteration.

  CUDA GRAPH BENEFIT — By Workload Type:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  (A) Single large GEMM:                              │
  │  [████████████████████] launch=0.1%  → Graphs: +0.1%│
  │  ❌ Barely helps                                     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  (B) 10 small kernels (batch=1):                     │
  │  [█][█][█][█][█][█][█][█][█][█] launch=20%          │
  │  → Graphs: launch→0 → +20% throughput ✅ BEST        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  (C) Training loop (variable per iter):              │
  │  Iter1[██] Iter2[███] Iter3[████]                   │
  │  ❌ Can't capture — shape changes every iteration     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

CUDA Graphs work best when: (1) the kernel sequence is identical every iteration, (2) kernel durations are short (microseconds), making launch overhead significant, and (3) the graph can be captured once and replayed thousands of times. Production inference is the perfect use case. Training loops change (different data each iteration for data loading, which can't be captured in a static graph without dynamic graph support).

Q7

Graph Capture: You capture a CUDA graph containing a kernel. Later, you update the kernel's input pointer. What must you do before relaunching the graph?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Use cudaGraphExecUpdate or recreate the executable graph. A graph instance captures the addresses of parameters, not just the graph structure. Changing input data requires updating those addresses.

  CUDA GRAPH — Input Update Flow:
  ┌───────────────────┐
  │ 1. cudaStreamBegin│  Capture mode ON
  │    Capture        │
  │ 2. Run kernels    │  Addresses FROZEN at capture
  │    (kernel(args)) │  Input @ 0x7f00, Output @ 0x8f00
  │ 3. cudaStreamEnd  │
  │    Capture        │  Graph created
  ├───────────────────┤
  │ 4. New data at    │  New input @ 0x9f00  ← CHANGED!
  │    new address    │
  │ 5. cudaGraphExec  │  Updates kernel node args
  │    Update()       │  Old: 0x7f00 → New: 0x9f00
  │ 6. cudaGraphLaunch│  Runs with updated pointers!
  └───────────────────┘
  OR: Use device-side persistent buffers (never change addr)
💡 EXPLANATION

CUDA Graphs capture the exact kernel parameters at capture time. To change inputs: (1) Use cudaGraphExecUpdate() to update kernel node parameters (CUDA 12.0+ makes this efficient), or (2) Use device-side allocations that persist across replays (the graph captures the allocation, not the data — you fill the allocated buffer before each replay). Modern Triton uses method (2) with pre-allocated I/O buffers.

Q8

Stream Priorities: You have an inference kernel (latency-critical) and a logging kernel (background). How do you ensure the inference kernel always runs first?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Create inference stream with cudaStreamCreateWithPriority(&stream, cudaStreamNonBlocking, -1) (highest priority) and logging stream with priority 0 (default). Lower numbers = higher priority on NVIDIA GPUs.

  STREAM PRIORITIES — GPU Scheduler:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Priority  -5 (HIGHEST) ──── Inference     │
  │  Priority  -4               Stream         │
  │  Priority  -3                               │
  │  Priority  -2                               │
  │  Priority  -1                               │
  │  Priority   0 (DEFAULT) ──── Logging       │
  │  Priority  +1                  Stream       │
  │  Priority  +5 (LOWEST)                     │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  GPU Scheduler: When INFERENCE has work,   │
  │  preempt LOGGING. But won't preempt an     │
  │  ALREADY-RUNNING kernel on LOGGING stream. │
  │  ★ Priority = scheduling order, not kernel │
  │    preemption.                              │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU stream priorities range from roughly -5 (highest) to +5 (lowest). The hardware scheduler prefers higher-priority streams when multiple streams have work ready. Critical caveats: (1) priority only matters when streams contend for the same execution units, (2) a running kernel on a low-priority stream won't be preempted — priority affects scheduling, not preemption, (3) on H100, CUDA 12.0+ supports cooperative kernel preemption for certain kernel types.

Q9

ILP vs TLP: A kernel achieves 25% SM occupancy yet runs at 95% of peak memory bandwidth. How is this possible?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

High ILP (Instruction-Level Parallelism). Each thread issues multiple independent memory loads before waiting. Even with few warps (low TLP), each warp generates enough parallel memory requests to saturate the memory bus.

  ILP vs TLP — Both can saturate memory!
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TLP (Thread-Level Parallelism) — Many warps    │
  │  100% occupancy, 1 mem req per warp:            │
  │  64 warps × 1 req = 64 in-flight = saturated   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ILP (Instruction-Level Parallelism) — Few warps│
  │  25% occupancy, each warp issues 4 mem reqs:    │
  │  16 warps × 4 reqs = 64 in-flight = saturated  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Same throughput with 75% fewer threads!
  ★ Memory-bound: ILP can compensate for low occupancy
  ★ Compute-bound: High occupancy helps more
💡 EXPLANATION

A single warp can have up to ~16 outstanding memory requests on H100 (achieved occupancy). At 25% occupancy = 16 warps × 16 requests = 256 in-flight requests. HBM3 can handle ~50-100 concurrent requests per channel × multiple channels — easily saturated. This is why "high occupancy = high performance" is a myth. Memory-bound kernels need enough requests in flight, not necessarily many threads. Compute-bound kernels benefit more from high occupancy.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj Optimization: The anihpj inference pipeline runs at 2,000 req/sec on H100. Nsight Systems shows kernel launch overhead = 15% of total time. CUDA Graph conversion is proposed. What throughput increase do you expect and what is the main risk?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

~15% throughput increase (2,300 req/sec). Main risk: graph update overhead for dynamic batch sizes. If batch sizes vary (common in production), you need one graph per batch size or dynamic graph support (CUDA 12.3+).

  anihpj INFERENCE — CUDA Graph Impact:
  Before:                           After:
  ┌──────────────┐                  ┌──────────────┐
  │ 2000 req/sec │                  │ 2300 req/sec │
  │ Launch=300ms │ ← 15% wasted →   │ Launch=0ms   │
  │ Compute=1.7s │                  │ Compute=1.7s │
  │ Total: 2.0s  │                  │ Total: 1.7s  │
  └──────────────┘                  └──────────────┘
  ★ Main risk: Dynamic batch sizes need MULTIPLE graphs
  │  batch=1 → graph_bs1   batch=8 → graph_bs8
  │  batch=2 → graph_bs2   batch=16→ graph_bs16
  │  CUDA 12.3+: dynamic graphs handle variable shapes!
💡 EXPLANATION

Launch overhead of 15% maps directly to expected improvement — the graph eliminates it. However, production inference rarely has fixed batch sizes. Solutions: (1) Pre-capture graphs for common batch sizes (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32), (2) Use dynamic graphs (CUDA 12.3+) for variable shapes, (3) Use Triton's built-in CUDA Graph support (configure enable_cuda_graph in config.pbtxt), which manages graph pools per batch size automatically. The exam expects you to know both the benefit AND the operational complexity.

Chapter 5: Multi-GPU Programming — Scaling Beyond One ⚫ Expert

One GPU Is Fast. Eight GPUs Working Together Is a Supercomputer.

Modern AI models don't fit on one GPU — GPT-4 requires thousands. This chapter teaches you to program multiple GPUs as one system: peer-to-peer access over NVLink, NCCL collective communication, PyTorch distributed training, and multi-node scaling with InfiniBand. These are NCP-AII's hardest and most valuable topics.

⚫ Expert ⏱️ ~4 hours 📝 10 Questions 🎯 NCP-AII Core

📋 NCP-AII Relevance — Multi-GPU Is the Professional Differentiator

Multi-GPU programming separates NCP-AII from NCA-AIIO. The Professional exam tests: configuring NCCL for different topologies, debugging all-reduce performance, understanding ring vs tree algorithms, and setting up PyTorch DDP across multiple nodes. These are real tasks you'll do as a GPU SRE.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Enable and use GPU peer-to-peer access and Unified Virtual Addressing
  • ✅ Understand NCCL collective operations, ring vs tree algorithms, and topology detection

5.1 Peer-to-Peer Access and Unified Virtual Addressing

When GPUs are connected via NVLink or PCIe, they can directly access each other's memory without CPU involvement. Peer-to-Peer (P2P) access is enabled per GPU pair with cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess(). Unified Virtual Addressing (UVA) means all GPU memories + CPU memory share one address space — a pointer from GPU 0 is valid on GPU 1 (if P2P is enabled).

Peer Access for anihpj Model Parallelism CUDA C++ 
// Enable P2P between all GPUs on a DGX (NVSwitch — all-to-all)
for (int i = 0; i < numGPUs; i++) {
    cudaSetDevice(i);
    for (int j = 0; j < numGPUs; j++) {
        if (i == j) continue;
        int canAccess;
        cudaDeviceCanAccessPeer(&canAccess, i, j);
        if (canAccess) {
            cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess(j, 0);  // GPU i can access GPU j's memory
        }
    }
}

// Now GPU 0 can directly copy from GPU 1:
cudaMemcpyPeer(dst_on_gpu0, 0, src_on_gpu1, 1, size);
// Or with UVA (single pointer visible from any GPU):
cudaMemcpy(dst_uva_ptr, src_uva_ptr, size, cudaMemcpyDefault);
📖 P2P Performance — NVLink vs PCIe

With NVSwitch (DGX): P2P bandwidth = 900 GB/s (NVLink 4.0). Without NVSwitch (PCIe only): P2P bandwidth = 64 GB/s (PCIe 5.0 x16). That's a 14× difference. Always check topology with nvidia-smi topo -m before enabling P2P — P2P over PCIe works but may be slower than staging through CPU memory. NV12 in the topology matrix = NVLink, PIX/PHB = PCIe.

🧪 LAB: Implement P2P Copy for anihpj Model Parallelism

Split a 1.5GB BERT-large model across 2 GPUs (768MB each). GPU 0 holds encoder layers 1-12, GPU 1 holds layers 13-24. After GPU 0's forward pass, use P2P to send activations to GPU 1. Measure: (1) P2P bandwidth with nvidia-smi nvlink -s, (2) total model throughput vs single-GPU baseline. With NVSwitch, P2P adds <100μs per transfer — negligible compared to compute time.

5.2 NCCL — The Communication Backbone

NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) is the library that makes multi-GPU training possible. It implements optimized collective operations (all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast, reduce-scatter) with topology-aware algorithms. Understanding NCCL is essential for debugging distributed training at scale.

NCCL Operations — The Building Blocks

OperationDescriptionWhen NCCL Uses It
AllReduceSum gradients across all GPUs, result on all GPUsDDP gradient sync (every backward pass)
AllGatherEach GPU sends its data, all GPUs receive concatenated resultZeRO stage 3 parameter gathering
ReduceScatterSum data, then scatter chunks — each GPU gets 1/N of resultFirst phase of ring all-reduce
BroadcastOne GPU sends data to all othersModel parameter initialization, loading checkpoint
ReduceSum data from all GPUs, result only on root GPUGathering validation metrics

Ring vs Tree Algorithms — When NCCL Chooses Each

NCCL All-Reduce — Ring vs Tree Algorithm
  RING ALL-REDUCE (default, best for most topologies):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Phase 1: REDUCE-SCATTER — each GPU gets 1/N of result
  ┌─────┐     ┌─────┐     ┌─────┐     ┌─────┐
  │GPU 0│────▶│GPU 1│────▶│GPU 2│────▶│GPU 3│──┐
  │A0   │     │A1   │     │A2   │     │A3   │  │
  └─────┘     └─────┘     └─────┘     └─────┘  │
     ▲                                         │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Phase 2: ALL-GATHER — each GPU broadcasts its partial sum
  After: ALL GPUs have COMPLETE summed gradient A0+A1+A2+A3

  TREE ALL-REDUCE (NCCL chooses for NVSwitch topologies, 5+ GPUs):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
                           ┌─────┐
                           │GPU 0│ (ROOT)
                           └──┬──┘
                 ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                 ▼            ▼            ▼
              ┌─────┐     ┌─────┐     ┌─────┐
              │GPU 1│     │GPU 2│     │GPU 3│   Reduce: leaves→root
              └─────┘     └─────┘     └─────┘   Broadcast: root→leaves

  NCCL CHOOSES BASED ON:
  • < 4 GPUs or PCIe topology → Ring (lower latency for small groups)
  • 5+ GPUs with NVSwitch → Tree (log₂(N) steps vs N-1 for Ring)
  • Data size: small (< 256KB) → Ring, large (MB+) → Tree

NCCL Environment Variables — The Debugging Toolkit

Essential NCCL Debug Env Variables Bash 
# Debug communication (WARN for issues, INFO for topology, TRACE for everything)
export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO

# Force algorithm: Ring or Tree (NCCL usually picks correctly)
export NCCL_ALGO=Ring       # Force Ring for debugging
export NCCL_ALGO=Tree       # Force Tree for NVSwitch

# Protocol: Simple (copy-based), LL (low-latency), or LL128
export NCCL_PROTO=Simple

# Network interface for multi-node (critical for InfiniBand)
export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0        # Use IB interface, not Ethernet
export NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0             # Enable InfiniBand (1 to disable)
export NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5          # GPUDirect RDMA (0-5, 5=max)

# Debug topology detection (shows which NCCL sees)
export NCCL_TOPO_DUMP_FILE=nccl_topo.xml

🧪 LAB: Debug NCCL Performance for anihpj Distributed Training

Run anihpj training on 8 GPUs with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO. Observe: (1) which algorithm NCCL selected (Ring or Tree), (2) per-GPU bandwidth achieved vs theoretical (900 GB/s for NVSwitch), (3) any topology warnings. Then force NCCL_ALGO=Ring and NCCL_ALGO=Tree and compare all-reduce throughput with nccl-tests benchmark. On a DGX with NVSwitch, Tree should be 15-25% faster for large messages.

5.3 Distributed Training — PyTorch + NCCL + CUDA

DistributedDataParallel (DDP) is PyTorch's standard for multi-GPU training. Each GPU runs a copy of the model on a different data batch. After the backward pass, gradients are synchronized via NCCL all-reduce. The model stays identical across all GPUs without any parameter broadcasting.

anihpj DDP Training Script Python 
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP

# Initialize process group (one process per GPU)
dist.init_process_group(
    backend='nccl',          # NCCL for GPU communication
    init_method='tcp://master:23456',
    world_size=8,            # 8 GPUs
    rank=local_rank          # 0-7
)

# Standard model
model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained('bert-base')
model = model.to(local_rank)

# Wrap with DDP — handles gradient sync automatically
model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank])

# Training loop (identical to single-GPU!)
for batch in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = model(batch).loss
    loss.backward()          # DDP automatically all-reduces gradients here
    optimizer.step()         # All GPUs now have identical parameters

# Gradient bucketing: DDP groups gradients into buckets (default 25MB)
# and starts all-reduce for bucket N while computing gradients for N+1
# — this "overlaps" communication with computation

Gradient Bucketing — The Secret to DDP Efficiency

DDP doesn't wait for all gradients before starting all-reduce. It groups parameters into buckets (default 25MB). As soon as bucket N's gradients are ready, NCCL starts the all-reduce for that bucket — while the backward pass continues computing gradients for bucket N+1. This overlap hides most communication latency. For anihpj BERT (110M params), this means only ~5% of training time is spent waiting for communication.

Mixed Precision + Distributed Training

Combining mixed precision with DDP requires care. Use torch.cuda.amp with GradScaler — the scaler must be synchronized across GPUs before the optimizer step. DDP handles this automatically when using autocast() + GradScaler in the standard pattern. For FP8 on H100, use NVIDIA's Transformer Engine library which provides te.DistributedDataParallel — it wraps DDP with FP8-aware gradient scaling. The key: never mix apex.amp (legacy) with torch.cuda.amp (modern) in the same training script.

FSDP — Fully Sharded Data Parallel (When Models Don't Fit)

DDP replicates the ENTIRE model on each GPU — if your model is 78GB, every GPU needs 78GB + optimizer states. For large models (Llama-70B, 140GB), this doesn't fit on a single H100. FSDP shards model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across all GPUs — each GPU only holds 1/N of the model at any time. During forward/backward, FSDP all-gathers the needed parameters just-in-time, then discards them.

DDP vs FSDP — Memory Per GPU (8× H100, 80GB model)
  DDP (full replica):              FSDP (sharded):
  ┌────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────┐
  │ GPU0: 80GB model   │          │ GPU0: 10GB shard   │
  │      160GB optim   │          │      20GB optim    │
  │      TOTAL: 240GB  │          │      30GB total    │
  │      ❌ OOM!       │          │      ✅ Fits!      │
  ├────────────────────┤          ├────────────────────┤
  │ GPU1: 80GB model   │          │ GPU1: 10GB shard   │
  │      ...same...    │          │      ...etc...     │
  └────────────────────┘          └────────────────────┘
  Total cluster: 8×240GB = 1.9TB  Total cluster: 8×30GB = 240GB
       (wasteful!)                     (efficient!)
  
  FSDP FLOW: All-gather shard → compute → discard → next layer
  Tradeoff: More communication (all-gather per layer) vs less memory

FSDP vs DDP decision: Model fits per GPU (model < GPU memory ÷ 4) → use DDP (simpler, less communication). Model doesn't fit → use FSDP. For anihpj BERT (340M params, ~1.3GB): DDP is perfect. For Llama-70B (140GB in FP16): FSDP with 8× H100 gives ~18GB/GPU model + ~36GB optimizer = fits comfortably. NCP-AII tip: Know when to use DDP vs FSDP vs tensor parallelism vs pipeline parallelism — this is a common exam scenario.

Checkpointing Strategies — Local vs Shared Storage

In distributed training, each GPU saves its model shard. Local checkpointing: each rank writes to its own file (faster, but you have N files to manage). Shared checkpointing: all ranks write to a shared filesystem (simpler, but N× filesystem traffic). For anihpj on DGX with NVMe RAID: use local checkpointing (30GB/s local write) during training, then async copy to shared storage (NFS/S3) between epochs. torch.save in DDP: only rank 0 should save to avoid N simultaneous writes. Use dist.barrier() before rank 0 saves to ensure all gradients are synced.

🧪 LAB: Scale anihpj BERT from 1 to 8 GPUs

Train the anihpj job recommendation BERT model on 1, 2, 4, and 8 GPUs. Measure: (1) throughput (samples/sec), (2) scaling efficiency = (throughput_N / (N × throughput_1)), (3) communication overhead via Nsight Systems. Expected: 1→2 GPUs: ~95% efficiency, 1→4 GPUs: ~88%, 1→8 GPUs: ~80%. The drop comes from all-reduce time growing with GPU count and batch size per GPU decreasing (less compute to hide communication behind).

5.4 Multi-Node Training — Beyond One Server

When 8 GPUs aren't enough, you span multiple DGX nodes connected by InfiniBand. Multi-node training introduces new challenges: network interface selection, NCCL topology across nodes, and the performance cliff between NVLink (intra-node) and InfiniBand (inter-node).

Multi-Node Setup Checklist

  • NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0: Force NCCL to use InfiniBand, not Ethernet
  • NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0: Enable InfiniBand (set to 1 only for testing without IB)
  • NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5: Enable GPUDirect RDMA — GPU memory → NIC → network → NIC → GPU memory, zero CPU copies
  • Master addr/port: One node is the "master" (rank 0). All others connect to it via TCP for initial handshake, then switch to IB for data.
  • torchrun: The modern elastic launcher — replaces torch.distributed.launch. Handles worker failures, dynamic scaling (elastic training), and provides clean CLI interface. Usage: torchrun --nnodes=N --nproc_per_node=G train.py
  • nccl-tests: Run all_reduce_perf across nodes BEFORE training to verify IB bandwidth

InfiniBand vs Ethernet — The Numbers That Matter

MetricInfiniBand NDR200InfiniBand NDR400Ethernet 400GbE (RoCE)
Bandwidth200 Gb/s400 Gb/s400 Gb/s
Latency~1 μs~1 μs~3-5 μs
RDMANativeNativeRoCEv2 (over UDP)
In-Network ComputeSHARPSHARPLimited
Congestion ControlCredit-based (lossless)Credit-basedECN/PFC (complex)
NCCL SupportExcellentExcellentGood (improving)
CostHigherHigherLower
Use CaseDGX clusters, HPCDGX SuperPODCloud-native, Spectrum-X

For AI training at scale (>32 GPUs), InfiniBand is the clear winner due to lower latency and SHARP in-network reduction. For inference serving or smaller clusters, Spectrum-X Ethernet with RoCEv2 provides good performance at lower cost. NCP-AII tip: know that InfiniBand = credit-based flow control (lossless) while Ethernet RoCE = PFC-based (requires careful configuration to avoid congestion spread).

900 GB/s
Intra-Node (NVLink)
50 GB/s
Inter-Node (IB NDR)
18×
NVLink vs IB Gap
~75%
8-Node Scaling Eff.
⚠️ The Multi-Node Performance Cliff

Training on 8 GPUs in one DGX (NVSwitch, 900 GB/s) vs 8 GPUs across 8 nodes (InfiniBand, 50 GB/s per GPU) is 18× slower for communication. This is why distributed training strategies matter: data parallelism works well up to ~32 GPUs (gradient sync is relatively small vs compute). Model parallelism (splitting the model across GPUs) needs NVLink bandwidth — don't do it across nodes. Pipeline parallelism is the compromise: inter-node communication is just activations (small), while each node handles its pipeline stage with internal NVLink.

🧪 LAB: Multi-Node anihpj Training on 2× DGX

Launch anihpj training across 2 DGX nodes (16 GPUs total). Steps: (1) Verify IB connectivity: ib_write_bw -d ib0 between nodes (expect >48 GB/s for NDR200), (2) Run NCCL all_reduce_perf across nodes, (3) Launch DDP with torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 train.py. Measure scaling efficiency from 1→2 nodes. Expect ~85% — the 15% drop is from inter-node all-reduce overhead vs intra-node NVSwitch speed.

  • Gotcha #1: "NCCL just works — no tuning needed." ❌ NCCL needs explicit environment configuration: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0 for IB, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0 to enable it, NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 for GPUDirect RDMA. Without these, NCCL falls back to TCP/IP — 10-50× bandwidth drop.
  • Gotcha #2: "All-reduce is the same regardless of algorithm." ❌ Ring is O(N) bandwidth but high latency. Tree is O(log N) latency. For 1GB+ tensors at 256 GPUs, Ring wins. For <1MB tensors, Tree wins. The exam expects you to CHOOSE.
  • Gotcha #3: "cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess automatically enables GPUDirect." ❌ Peer access = GPU→GPU within node. GPUDirect RDMA = GPU→NIC→remote GPU across nodes. Different concepts, tested as one question.
