📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 5 (10 Questions)

Q1

P2P Topology: nvidia-smi topo -m shows NV12 between GPU 0 and GPU 1, and PIX between GPU 0 and GPU 2. What does this mean for P2P bandwidth?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU 0→1: 900 GB/s (NVLink via NVSwitch). GPU 0→2: 64 GB/s (PCIe). P2P works in both cases but NV12 is 14× faster. Enable P2P for all pairs but be aware of the bandwidth asymmetry.

  DGX GPU TOPOLOGY — NV12 vs PIX:
  
  ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │       NVSwitch          │◄── All-to-all @ 900 GB/s
  │   (non-blocking xbar)   │
  └──┬──────┬──────┬──────┬─┘
     │NV12  │NV12  │NV12  │NV12
     ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐      ┌────┐
  │GPU0│◄│GPU1│ │GPU2│ │GPU3│  ... │GPU7│
  └──┬─┘ └────┘ └────┘ └────┘      └────┘
     │PIX (if NVSwitch fabric mgr down)
     ▼
  ┌────┐
  │GPU2│ ← 64 GB/s max (PCIe 5.0 x16)
  └────┘
  
  🎯 NV12 = 900 GB/s (NVSwitch up)   PIX = 64 GB/s (NVSwitch down)
  🎯 Check: systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager
💡 EXPLANATION

NV12 = NVLink 12 connections (each ~75 GB/s × 12 = 900 GB/s). PIX = PCIe crossing a PCIe bridge (max PCIe 5.0 x16 = 64 GB/s). On a properly configured DGX, ALL GPU pairs should show NV12 (NVSwitch enables all-to-all). If some show PIX, NVSwitch fabric manager may not be running (systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager).

Q2

NCCL Algorithm: You're training on 4 GPUs connected via NVSwitch. NCCL_DEBUG shows "Algo:0" (Tree). You force NCCL_ALGO=Ring. What happens to all-reduce performance?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Ring becomes slightly slower (~10-15%) for 4 GPUs on NVSwitch. Tree needs log₂(4)=2 steps. Ring needs 2×(4-1)=6 steps. But for only 4 GPUs, the ring's simplicity sometimes wins for small messages. NCCL's auto-selection is usually optimal — forcing algorithms is for debugging, not production.

  RING vs TREE — All-Reduce on 4 GPUs:
  RING (N=4, steps=2(N-1)=6):      TREE (N=4, steps=2log₂N=4):
  Step1: G0→G1                   Step1: G0+G1→Sw, G2+G3→Sw
  Step2: G1→G2                   Step2: Sw sums & broadcasts
  Step3: G2→G3                   Step3: Sw→All (result)
  Step4: G3→G2
  Step5: G2→G1                   Tree = fewer steps, but
  Step6: G1→G0                   larger per-step data
  ★ Ring: O(N) latency           ★ Tree: O(log N) latency
  ★ On NVSwitch: Tree wins       ★ Without NVSwitch: Ring wins
💡 EXPLANATION

Ring algorithm steps: 2(N-1) = 6 for N=4. Tree algorithm steps: 2×log₂(N) = 4 for N=4. But each ring step transfers 1/N of data while tree transfers full data at each level. For large messages on NVSwitch (all-to-all BW > point-to-point), tree wins because it leverages the switch's broadcast capability. NCCL auto-tunes based on message size and topology — trust it unless profiling shows otherwise.

Q3

NCCL Debug: Multi-node training hangs at init_process_group(). NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows "Connected to peer X" for all local GPUs but nothing for remote GPUs. What's wrong?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NCCL is using the wrong network interface. It's likely using Ethernet (eth0) which may have a firewall or different subnet. Set NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0 to force InfiniBand, or verify the interface name with ibstat.

  NCCL DEBUG — Multi-node Hang Diagnosis:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SYMPTOM: init_process_group() hangs forever    │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  1. Check: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO                      │
  │     ❌ "Using [0]eth0:192.168.1.10<0>"           │
  │     → NCCL picked Ethernet! Firewall blocks it. │
  │     ✅ "Using [0]ib0:10.0.0.10<0>"               │
  │     → NCCL picked InfiniBand = correct!         │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  2. Fix: export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0          │
  │  3. Verify: ip addr show ib0 (must have IP)     │
  │  4. Test: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO python -c "import     │
  │     torch.distributed as dist; dist.init_proc..." │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NCCL auto-detects the fastest interface, but it may pick Ethernet if InfiniBand isn't configured as an IP interface (IPoIB not enabled). Check: ip addr show ib0 — if no IP, run sudo ip addr add 192.168.100.X/24 dev ib0. Also ensure NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0. Common gotcha: Docker containers may not see IB interfaces without --network=host or proper --device=/dev/infiniband.

Q4

DDP Gradient Sync: In PyTorch DDP, when exactly do gradients get synchronized across GPUs during training?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

During loss.backward(), as each gradient bucket fills. DDP registers hooks on parameters. As the backward pass computes gradients bucket-by-bucket, DDP launches NCCL all-reduce for each full bucket — overlapping communication with the remaining backward computation.

  DDP GRADIENT SYNC — Overlapped Communication:
  Timeline (backward pass):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Layer N: [COMPUTE▕GRADIENTS]                         │
  │ Layer N-1:     [COMPUTE▕GRADIENTS]                   │
  │ ...                ...                               │
  │ Layer 1:                      [COMPUTE▕GRADIENTS]    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ NCCL:    ░░░░░░░[ALL-REDUCE BUCKET 1]░░░[BUCKET 2]  │
  │              ▲ When bucket 1 is full                  │
  │              │ (all grads in bucket ready)            │
  │              │ Communication OVERLAPS with compute!   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Key: backward() still running while NCCL syncs!
  ★ 25MB buckets = default. Tune bucket_cap_mb for model.
💡 EXPLANATION

DDP creates parameter buckets (default 25MB). Each parameter gets a "post-accumulate" hook. When all gradients in a bucket are ready, the hook triggers NCCL all-reduce on that bucket. This means communication starts BEFORE backward() completes — this is the key to DDP's efficiency. The bucket_cap_mb parameter controls bucket size: larger = fewer all-reduce calls but less overlap.

Q5

Scaling Efficiency: anihpj BERT training achieves 1,000 samples/sec on 1 GPU and 7,200 samples/sec on 8 GPUs. What is the scaling efficiency?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

90%. Ideal scaling: 8 × 1,000 = 8,000. Actual: 7,200. Efficiency = 7,200 ÷ 8,000 = 0.90 = 90%. The 10% loss comes from NCCL all-reduce time and imperfect load balancing.

  SCALING EFFICIENCY — anihpj BERT:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1 GPU:  1,000 samples/sec                      │
  │  8 GPUs: 7,200 samples/sec                      │
  │  Ideal:  8,000 samples/sec (8× line)            │
  │  Efficiency: 7,200 ÷ 8,000 = 90%                │
  │  Lost:     800 samples/sec = all-reduce overhead│
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Rating: █████████░ 90% — EXCELLENT             │
  │  >95%: Near-perfect (very large model)          │
  │  85-95%: Good (typical for NCCL-optimized)      │
  │  70-85%: Acceptable (small model, many GPUs)    │
  │  <70%: Investigate (network or load issue)      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Scaling efficiency = T_N ÷ (N × T_1). 90% is excellent for 8 GPUs — it means communication overhead is only ~10% of training time. Factors that reduce scaling: (1) per-GPU batch size too small (less compute to hide communication), (2) model is communication-bound (many small parameters = many all-reduce calls), (3) NCCL not using optimal algorithm for the topology. Gradient accumulation can help by increasing effective batch size without reducing per-GPU batch.

Q6

NCCL Environment: What does NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 enable that NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=0 does not?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPUDirect RDMA — GPU memory → NIC → InfiniBand → NIC → GPU memory, with ZERO CPU memory involvement. Level 0 copies GPU→CPU→NIC→CPU→GPU. Level 5 copies GPU→NIC→GPU directly.

  NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL — Data Path:
  Level 0 (disabled):          Level 5 (full GPUDirect):
  ┌────┐   ┌────┐   ┌────┐    ┌────┐          ┌────┐
  │GPU │→CP│RAM │→NI│C │→IB→  │GPU │───DMA───▶│NIC │→IB→
  │VRAM│  │BUF │  │   │        │VRAM│ (PCIe)   │    │
  └────┘   └────┘   └────┘    └────┘          └────┘
    4 copies, ~100μs           2 copies, ~45μs
    50% PCIe BW wasted         100% PCIe BW utilized
  ★ Requires: nvidia_peermem + ConnectX-5+
  ★ Set: NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 (production default)
💡 EXPLANATION

GDR levels: 0=disabled (all data goes through CPU bounce buffers), 1-4=increasing levels of GPU-NIC direct access, 5=full GPUDirect RDMA (NIC reads/writes GPU memory via PCIe). Benefits: (1) eliminates CPU memory bandwidth bottleneck, (2) reduces latency by ~50%, (3) frees CPU for data loading. Requires: GPU and NIC on same PCIe root complex, supported NIC (ConnectX-5+), and nvidia_peermem kernel module loaded.

Q7

PyTorch Launch: What is the correct command to launch anihpj training on 2 nodes, 8 GPUs each (16 total), with node rank 0 as master?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Node 0: torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 --node_rank=0 --master_addr=192.168.1.10 --master_port=29500 train.py
Node 1: torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 --node_rank=1 --master_addr=192.168.1.10 --master_port=29500 train.py

  MULTI-NODE TRAINING LAUNCH (anihpj, 2×DGX):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DGX-0 (master, node_rank=0)                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8   │   │
  │  │ --node_rank=0 --master_addr=10.0.0.10    │   │
  │  │ --master_port=29500 train.py              │   │
  │  │ → Spawns 8 processes (GPU 0-7)           │   │
  │  │ → Rank 0-7 (global ranks)                │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  DGX-1 (worker, node_rank=1)                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8   │   │
  │  │ --node_rank=1 --master_addr=10.0.0.10    │   │
  │  │ --master_port=29500 train.py              │   │
  │  │ → Spawns 8 processes (GPU 0-7)           │   │
  │  │ → Rank 8-15 (global ranks)               │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  ★ master_addr = InfiniBand IP (ib0), not eth0  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

torchrun (torch.distributed.run) replaces the older torch.distributed.launch. Key parameters: nnodes (total nodes), nproc_per_node (GPUs per node), node_rank (0 for master, 1+ for workers), master_addr (IP of rank 0 node), master_port (any free port, default 29500). All nodes must use identical nnodes and nproc_per_node. The master_addr must be reachable from all nodes — use the InfiniBand IP for best performance.

Q8

Model vs Data Parallelism: Your model uses 78GB of an 80GB H100. You need to train on 8 GPUs. Which parallelism strategy should you use and why?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Model parallelism (pipeline or tensor parallelism), not data parallelism. Data parallelism requires a full model copy on each GPU — 78GB won't fit with optimizer states (Adam adds 2× model size = 156GB). Model parallelism splits the model across GPUs, reducing per-GPU memory.

  PARALLELISM STRATEGY — Memory Comparison:
  Model: 78GB | Adam optimizer: 156GB (2× model)
  Total per GPU: 78 + 156 = 234GB (with data parallel)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Data Parallel (DP):  Each GPU = 234GB → ❌ OOM   │
  │ [GPU0:Full] [GPU1:Full] ... [GPU7:Full]          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Pipeline Parallel (PP): Split layers → ✅         │
  │ [GPU0:L1-6]→[GPU1:L7-12]→[GPU2:L13-18]→...→     │
  │ Per GPU: ~30GB model + 60GB optim = 90GB ✓       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Tensor Parallel (TP): Split within layers → ✅    │
  │ Each GPU: 78/N GB model + 156/N GB optim          │
  │ N=8: ~10GB model + 20GB optim = 30GB ✓           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Data parallelism: each GPU has full model + optimizer states = ~234GB per GPU (78GB model + 156GB Adam). Doesn't fit. Pipeline parallelism: split layers across GPUs (GPU 0: layers 1-6, GPU 1: layers 7-12...). Per-GPU memory drops to ~30GB model + optimizer. Tensor parallelism: split individual layers across GPUs. NVIDIA's recommendation: < 1B params → data parallel, 1-10B → pipeline parallel, 10B+ → tensor + pipeline + data (3D parallelism).

Q9

NCCL Topology: On a DGX H100, NCCL detects the NVSwitch topology and configures a specific number of "rings" for communication. How many NVLink rings does NCCL create per GPU on an 8-GPU DGX with NVSwitch?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NCCL doesn't create rings on NVSwitch — it uses a TREE topology. NVSwitch provides all-to-all connectivity at full bandwidth without needing rings. Each GPU can communicate with every other GPU simultaneously via the switch crossbar.

  NVSwitch — Non-Blocking Crossbar:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              NVSwitch Crossbar                  │
  │  GPU0→GPU3 simultaneously with GPU1→GPU2       │
  │  ┌──────┐   ┌──────┐   ┌──────┐               │
  │  │ GPU0 │──▶│ NVSw │──▶│ GPU3 │ 900 GB/s      │
  │  └──────┘   │      │   └──────┘               │
  │  ┌──────┐   │      │   ┌──────┐               │
  │  │ GPU1 │──▶│      │──▶│ GPU2 │ 900 GB/s      │
  │  └──────┘   └──────┘   └──────┘               │
  │  ALL pairs can communicate at full bandwidth!  │
  │  No rings needed → NCCL uses TREE (w/SHARP)    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Rings are for systems WITHOUT NVSwitch!
💡 EXPLANATION

This is a key concept: NVSwitch is a non-blocking crossbar — GPU 0→GPU 3 doesn't affect GPU 1→GPU 2. NCCL exploits this by building tree topologies where the switch itself acts as the root, performing reductions in-network (SHARP). Ring topologies are for systems WITHOUT NVSwitch (PCIe-only or older NVLink mesh). The exam may trick you by asking about rings on a DGX — there are none for NCCL collective operations.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj Debug: anihpj training on 8 GPUs across 2 DGX nodes. GPU-Util is 100% on node 0 but only 40% on node 1. NCCL all-reduce tests show 48 GB/s between nodes (expected for NDR200). What's the likely issue?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Uneven data distribution or straggler effect. Node 1's GPUs finish their forward/backward faster (40% util means they're waiting) while Node 0 is still computing (100% util). The all-reduce at the end of each iteration forces Node 1's GPUs to wait for Node 0's GPUs.

  STRAGGLER EFFECT — 2-node anihpj Training:
  Timeline:
  DGX-0: [████████████████████] NCCL ░░░░[████████]
         100% util, slow compute    WAIT    Next iter
  DGX-1: [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░] NCCL ░░░░[████████]
         40% util, finishes early   WAIT    Next iter
         ────────────────────────
           DGX-1 waits HERE for DGX-0 to finish!
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ROOT CAUSES:                                    │
  │ 1. DGX-0 thermal throttle → lower clock         │
  │ 2. DGX-0 CPU maxed → slower data loading        │
  │ 3. Uneven batch sizes (data loader bug)         │
  │ CHECK: nvidia-smi -q -d CLOCK on DGX-0          │
  │ CHECK: htop on DGX-0 (data loader bottleneck?)  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ NCCL bandwidth test passing ≠ compute balanced
💡 EXPLANATION

Causes: (1) Different CPU performance on nodes (data loading bottleneck), (2) Different GPU clocks (thermal throttling on one node), (3) Uneven batch distribution. Fix: check nvidia-smi -q -d CLOCK on Node 0 — if it shows throttling, check cooling. Check CPU utilization on Node 0 — if data loader is maxed, increase num_workers. Use torch.distributed.get_world_size() and verify all ranks receive equal-sized batches. The NCCL bandwidth test passing doesn't rule out compute asymmetry.

Chapter 6: GPU Cluster Design — From Rack to SuperPOD 🔴 Advanced

Designing the AI Factory — Where Silicon Meets Infrastructure

Buying a DGX is easy. Designing the cluster around it — the network fabric, storage hierarchy, power distribution, and cooling system — is where NCP-AII professionals earn their value. This chapter teaches you to design GPU clusters from a single rack to a SuperPOD with thousands of GPUs, using anihpj's 32-GPU cluster as the hands-on case study.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~4 hours 📝 10 Questions 🎯 NCP-AII Core

📋 NCP-AII Relevance — Cluster Design on the Exam

NCP-AII tests your ability to design GPU infrastructure, not just operate it. Expect questions like: "Given X GPUs and Y budget, which network topology?" or "Calculate cooling capacity for Z kW." You must know oversubscription ratios, power density calculations, and storage tiering — these are real decisions you'll make as a GPU infrastructure engineer.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Size GPU clusters based on workload analysis: training vs inference vs development
  • ✅ Design network topologies: fat-tree, rail-optimized, DragonFly+ with correct oversubscription
  • ✅ Architect tiered storage for AI workloads including GPUDirect Storage
  • ✅ Calculate power, cooling, and PUE for GPU clusters at scale
  • ✅ Evaluate NVIDIA reference architectures and know when to customize

6.1 Cluster Sizing — How Many GPUs Do You Actually Need?

Cluster sizing isn't guesswork — it's math. The three questions you must answer: (1) What workloads run on this cluster? (2) How many GPU-hours does each workload consume? (3) What headroom do you need for growth and failures?

The GPU-Hour Calculation

FactorTrainingInferenceDevelopment
GPU-hours per runmodel_params × dataset × epochs ÷ GPU_TFLOPSrequests × model_size ÷ GPU_throughputVariable (interactive)
anihpj exampleBERT 110M × 1M samples × 3 epochs = ~24 GPU-hrs (H100)10M req/day × 2ms each = ~5.5 GPU-hrs/day4 GPUs × 8 hrs/day = 32 GPU-hrs/day
FrequencyDaily retrainingContinuous (24/7)Business hours
Target Utilization80-90%60-80% (headroom for spikes)30-50% (interactive)
anihpj Cluster Sizing — From Requirements to GPU Count
  ANIHPJ CLUSTER SIZING — 50M Users, Daily Retraining

  INPUTS:
  ───────
  Training:  BERT 110M params, 1M samples/day, 3 epochs = 24 GPU-hrs/day
  Inference: 10M requests/day × 2ms avg latency = 20,000 GPU-sec = 5.5 GPU-hrs/day
  Dev/Test:  4 dev teams × 2 GPUs × 8 hrs = 64 GPU-hrs/day
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  TOTAL:     ~94 GPU-hrs/day required

  GPU COUNT:
  ─────────
  94 GPU-hrs ÷ 24 hrs = 3.9 GPUs (at 100% utilization)
  + 30% headroom (growth) = 5.1 GPUs
  + 10% failure buffer = 5.6 GPUs
  + GPU granularity (8 GPUs per DGX) = 8 GPUs minimum

  RECOMMENDATION: 2× DGX H100 (16 GPUs)
  • 8 GPUs for production (training + inference)
  • 8 GPUs for dev/staging + future growth
  • 16 GPUs = ~3× current needs → 3-year runway

  BUDGET: ~$600K hardware + ~$72K/yr NVAIE + ~$18K/yr power/cooling

6.2 Network Topology — Fat-Tree, Rail-Optimized, DragonFly+

GPU clusters live and die by their network. An all-reduce across 32 GPUs sends gigabytes of gradient data every training step. The network must provide full bisection bandwidth — every GPU must talk to every other GPU at line rate simultaneously.

Three Topologies for AI Clusters

TopologyBest ForHopsBisection BWCost
Fat-Tree32-256 GPUs (most common)3 (Leaf→Spine→Leaf)Full (1:1)Medium
Rail-Optimized256-2048 GPUs (SuperPOD)2 (GPU-rail direct)Full (1:1)Higher
DragonFly+1000+ GPUs (hyper-scale)1-2 (high-radix)Near-full (~0.9:1)Lower (fewer switches)
Fat-Tree Network — anihpj 32-GPU Cluster Design
                        SPINE LAYER (Core)
     ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
     │Quantum-2 │  │Quantum-2 │  │Quantum-2 │  │Quantum-2 │
     │Spine 1   │  │Spine 2   │  │Spine 3   │  │Spine 4   │
     │400Gb/s×64│  │400Gb/s×64│  │400Gb/s×64│  │400Gb/s×64│
     └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘
          │             │             │             │
          └─────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────┘
                        │             │
                        ▼             ▼
                        LEAF LAYER (Edge)
     ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
     │Quantum-2 │  │Quantum-2 │  │Quantum-2 │  │Quantum-2 │
     │Leaf 1    │  │Leaf 2    │  │Leaf 3    │  │Leaf 4    │
     │400Gb/s×64│  │400Gb/s×64│  │400Gb/s×64│  │400Gb/s×64│
     └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘
          │             │             │             │
          ▼             ▼             ▼             ▼
     ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
     │ DGX H100 │ │ DGX H100 │ │ DGX H100 │ │ DGX H100 │
     │    #1    │ │    #2    │ │    #3    │ │    #4    │
     │ 8× H100  │ │ 8× H100  │ │ 8× H100  │ │ 8× H100  │
     │ 8× CX-7  │ │ 8× CX-7  │ │ 8× CX-7  │ │ 8× CX-7  │
     └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘

     🎯 8 uplinks per leaf to 4 spines = full bisection bandwidth
     🎯 Any GPU→Any GPU = 400 Gb/s (no oversubscription)
     🎯 SHARP tree: in-network all-reduce, switches do the math

Oversubscription Ratios — When Full BW Isn't Needed

1:1 (AI Training): Every GPU gets full bandwidth to every other GPU. Required for distributed training where all-reduce dominates. 3:1 (Inference): Inference servers don't communicate much — you can oversubscribe 3:1 to save on switch ports. 10:1 (Development): Dev GPUs are often idle or running single-GPU jobs — aggressive oversubscription is fine.

Rail-Optimized Topology — The SuperPOD Secret

In a rail-optimized design, GPU 0 from every DGX connects to the same leaf switch. During all-reduce, all GPU 0s communicate locally (within the same leaf) while GPU 1s do the same on another leaf. This creates N parallel "rails" that perfectly match all-reduce's communication pattern — reducing cross-switch traffic by up to 8× compared to fat-tree.

6.3 Storage Architecture for AI Workloads

AI workloads have unique storage patterns: massive sequential reads (dataset loading), burst writes (checkpointing), and random access (embedding lookups). A single-tier storage system can't satisfy all three efficiently.

Tiered Storage Architecture

TierTechnologyBandwidthCapacityUse Case
Hot (Tier 0)NVMe RAID (local)30 GB/s per DGX30 TB per DGXActive datasets, checkpoints
Warm (Tier 1)Parallel FS (Lustre/Weka)100+ GB/s aggregate500 TB - 2 PBShared datasets, model registry
Cold (Tier 2)Object Storage (S3/MinIO)10 GB/sPB-scaleArchived models, logs, backups

GPUDirect Storage — GPU Reads Directly from NVMe

GPUDirect Storage (GDS) enables the GPU to read data directly from NVMe drives via PCIe — bypassing the CPU and system memory entirely. Traditional path: NVMe → CPU → RAM → GPU (3 copies). GDS path: NVMe → GPU (1 copy). For anihpj dataset loading (30GB per epoch), GDS reduces loading time from ~1 second to ~100ms — a 10× improvement that directly reduces GPU idle time between training batches.

Checkpoint Strategies

Training jobs checkpoint model weights periodically. Frequency: Every N steps or at epoch boundaries. Too frequent = I/O bottleneck. Too rare = lost work on failure. Format: Use sharded checkpoints (one file per GPU rank) for parallel writes. Compression: FP32→FP16 checkpoint compression saves 50% storage at minimal quality loss. Replication: Keep 2 copies — one local (NVMe, fast restore) and one remote (S3, disaster recovery).

Parallel File Systems — Lustre, WEKA, VAST

Parallel file systems are the backbone of AI storage. Lustre: Open-source, battle-tested at scale (100+ GB/s), but complex to manage. WEKA: Software-defined, NVMe-optimized, cloud-native — the standard for DGX SuperPOD. VAST: Universal storage with S3/NFS/SMB protocols, good for mixed workloads. Key tuning: stripe size (match to I/O pattern), OST count (more = more parallelism), and metadata server placement (separate from data path). For anihpj: WEKA on 4 DGX nodes provides 120+ GB/s aggregate — enough to saturate all 32 H100 GPUs reading datasets simultaneously.

🧪 LAB: Benchmark GPUDirect Storage for anihpj Dataset Loading

Compare dd if=/mnt/nvme/dataset of=/dev/null bs=1M (standard) vs gdsio -f /mnt/nvme/dataset (GPUDirect). Expected: Standard = ~7 GB/s (CPU-limited), GDS = ~25 GB/s (NVMe-limited). Run with Nsight Systems to see the elimination of CPU-GPU memory copies in the timeline.

6.4 Power and Cooling — The Physics of GPU Clusters

A single DGX H100 draws 10.2 kW. Four in a rack = 40.8 kW — equivalent to 4 typical home central air conditioners running at full blast. Managing this heat is a core infrastructure skill.

Power and Cooling — anihpj 4-DGX Rack
  ANIHPJ 4-DGX RACK — POWER & COOLING CALCULATION

  INPUT POWER:
  ────────────
  4× DGX H100:       4 × 10.2 kW = 40.8 kW
  8× Quantum-2 switches: 8 × 0.5 kW = 4.0 kW
  Management/ToR:                   1.0 kW
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  TOTAL IT LOAD:                   45.8 kW

  COOLING REQUIREMENT (Air):
  ─────────────────────────
  45.8 kW × 3,412 BTU/kW = 156,270 BTU/hr
  = 13 tons of cooling (1 ton = 12,000 BTU/hr)
  ❌ THIS EXCEEDS typical air cooling limits (~25 kW/rack)
  ✅ REQUIRES liquid cooling

  COOLING REQUIREMENT (Direct Liquid):
  ────────────────────────────────────
  GPU heat captured at cold plate → CDU → facility water
  Remaining heat (~10%) handled by rear-door heat exchanger
  PUE target: 1.05-1.10

  PUE CALCULATION:
  ────────────────
  PUE = Total Facility Power ÷ IT Equipment Power
  Good (air): 1.4  |  Great (liquid): 1.1  |  World-class: 1.05
  anihpj target: 45.8 kW × 1.1 = 50.4 kW total facility draw

  ANNUAL ENERGY COST:
  ──────────────────
  50.4 kW × 24 hrs × 365 days × $0.10/kWh = $44,150/year
  (Compare: same compute on CPU = ~$440,000/year — 10× savings!)

Cooling Technologies Compared

MethodMax Rack DensityPUEComplexityBest For
Air Cooling~25 kW1.4-1.6LowEdge, small clusters
Rear-Door HX~35 kW1.2-1.3MediumRetrofit existing DCs
Direct Liquid (Cold Plate)50+ kW1.05-1.15HighDGX clusters (standard)
Immersion Cooling100+ kW1.02-1.05HighestHyper-scale, experimental
⚠️ The Power Budget Trap

Always budget power AT THE RACK, not at the GPU. A DGX H100 is rated 10.2 kW, but add 15-20% for power supply inefficiency, cooling overhead, and switch power. Real rack draw for 4 DGX: closer to 50 kW than 40 kW. Also: check your facility's 3-phase power. A 50 kW rack at 208V draws 139A — requiring a 175A circuit. At 415V (3-phase), it draws 70A — much more manageable. Always design for 415V 3-phase for GPU clusters.

CDU — Coolant Distribution Unit (Primary/Secondary Loop Design)

The CDU is the bridge between GPU cold plates and facility water. Primary loop (facility side): Warm water returns to the facility chiller or cooling tower, gets cooled, and flows back. Secondary loop (GPU side): Cooled water circulates through GPU cold plates, absorbing heat directly from the silicon. The CDU contains a heat exchanger (plate or shell-and-tube) that transfers heat from the secondary loop to the primary loop without mixing the water. Key specs: Flow rate (typically 40-60 L/min per DGX), approach temperature (ΔT between loops, ideally <5°C), and redundancy (N+1 CDU for production clusters). For anihpj's 4-DGX: 1 CDU per rack, 200 L/min capacity, N+1 pumps.

🧪 LAB: Calculate TCO for anihpj's 4-DGX Cluster

Build a 3-year TCO model: Hardware ($1.2M depreciated over 3 years), NVAIE licensing ($144K/yr), power ($44K/yr), cooling maintenance ($12K/yr), colocation ($24K/yr for half rack), and staffing (0.5 FTE GPU SRE = $75K/yr). Compare against equivalent cloud: AWS p5.48xlarge at $98/hr for 24/7 training + $12/hr inference = ~$1.0M/yr. Result: On-prem breaks even at ~15 months, saves ~$1.7M over 3 years. Present your analysis with the formulas used — this is exactly the kind of task NCP-AII performance-based items test.

6.5 Reference Architectures — NVIDIA-Certified Designs

NVIDIA publishes validated Reference Architectures (RAs) — battle-tested designs for GPU clusters at every scale. Using an RA reduces design risk, accelerates deployment, and ensures NVIDIA Enterprise Support coverage.

🏗️
DGX SuperPOD RA

Scale: 32-127 DGX nodes (256-1,016 GPUs). Network: Fat-tree or rail-optimized Quantum-2 IB. Storage: DDN A3i or WEKA parallel FS. Use: Large-scale AI training (foundation models). anihpj: Overkill for 32 GPUs — use DGX BasePOD instead.

☸️
NVIDIA AI Enterprise RA

Stack: K8s + GPU Operator + Network Operator + NVAIE. Hardware: Any NVIDIA-Certified System. Software: Pre-tested NGC containers, validated driver/CUDA combos. Use: Production AI platform on any infra. anihpj: This is our target architecture.

☁️
Cloud RAs

AWS: p5.48xlarge (8× H100). Azure: ND96isr_H100_v5 (8× H100). GCP: a3-highgpu-8g (8× H100). Pre-validated for NVAIE deployment. Use: Hybrid cloud, burst capacity, DR site.

⚠️
Custom Designs — Know the Risks

When to deviate from RAs: (1) specialized networking requirements, (2) existing data center constraints, (3) unique storage integrations. Risks: validation burden shifts to you, support may be limited, undocumented failure modes. Rule of thumb: If you're customizing, document EVERY deviation and its justification.

DGX BasePOD — The Right RA for anihpj

For anihpj's 32-GPU cluster, the DGX BasePOD RA is the correct choice: 4× DGX H100, 8× Quantum-2 switches (4 leaf, 4 spine), WEKA or DDN storage, and NVAIE software stack. This RA is validated for 16-64 GPUs — the sweet spot between a single DGX (no networking needed) and a full SuperPOD (overkill for our scale).

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 6 (10 Questions)

Q1

Cluster Sizing: You need 200 GPU-hours of training daily, 24 GPU-hours of inference, and 80 GPU-hours of development. With 80% target utilization and 20% headroom, how many H100 GPUs do you need?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

19 GPUs → 24 (3× DGX H100). Total: 304 GPU-hrs/day. At 80% util: 304÷0.8=380 capacity needed. 380÷24hrs=15.8 GPUs. +20% headroom = 19. Round to DGX granularity: 3× DGX = 24 GPUs.

  GPU SIZING CALCULATION:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Training:   200 GPU-hrs/day                      │
  │ Inference:   24 GPU-hrs/day                      │
  │ Dev:         80 GPU-hrs/day                      │
  │ TOTAL:      304 GPU-hrs/day                      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ At 80% util: 304 ÷ 0.80 = 380 GPU-hrs capacity   │
  │ GPUs (raw):  380 ÷ 24hr   = 15.8 GPUs            │
  │ +20% buffer: 15.8 × 1.20  = 19.0 GPUs            │
  │ DGX rounding: ceil(19÷8)   = 3 DGX = 24 GPUs     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ❌ 2 DGX (16 GPUs) = undersized, 84% util needed
  ✅ 3 DGX (24 GPUs) = 53% avg util, room to grow
💡 EXPLANATION

The formula: required_GPUs = total_GPUhrs ÷ (24 × target_utilization) × (1 + headroom). Always round up to DGX granularity (8 GPUs per DGX). 2 DGX = 16 GPUs is slightly under; 3 DGX = 24 provides comfortable buffer. Consider whether dev workloads can be preempted by production — if yes, you can size closer to production needs.

Q2

Oversubscription: A cluster has 32 GPUs connected via 8 leaf switches (4 GPUs per leaf) and 2 spine switches. Each leaf has 4× 400Gb/s downlinks and 2× 400Gb/s uplinks. What is the oversubscription ratio?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

2:1 (oversubscribed). Downlink capacity: 4 × 400 = 1,600 Gb/s. Uplink capacity: 2 × 400 = 800 Gb/s. Ratio = 1,600 ÷ 800 = 2:1. Half of the downlink traffic would be blocked if all GPUs communicate simultaneously.

  LEAF-SPINE OVERSUBSCRIPTION:
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │  SPINE 1     │  │  SPINE 2     │  ◄── 2 uplinks
  │  400Gb/s     │  │  400Gb/s     │      = 800 Gb/s total
  └──┬───────┬───┘  └──┬───────┬───┘
     │       │         │       │
  ┌──▼───────▼─────────▼───────▼───┐
  │         LEAF SWITCH            │
  │  4×400Gb/s down = 1,600 Gb/s   │
  └──┬──────┬──────┬──────┬───────┘
     │      │      │      │
    GPU0   GPU1   GPU2   GPU3

  RATIO = 1,600 ÷ 800 = 2:1 ❌
  At full load: 800Gb/s of GPU traffic DROPPED
  
  FIX: Add Spine 3 + Spine 4 = 4 uplinks
  1,600 ÷ 1,600 = 1:1 ✅ (non-blocking)
💡 EXPLANATION

2:1 oversubscription is NOT sufficient for AI training (requires 1:1 for all-reduce). It IS acceptable for inference (GPUs communicate rarely). To fix: add 2 more spine switches → 4 uplinks = 1,600 Gb/s → 1:1. For anihpj's training cluster, 1:1 is mandatory. For inference-only clusters, 2:1 or even 3:1 saves significant switch cost.

Q3

Fat-Tree vs Rail-Optimized: A 128-GPU cluster (16 DGX) needs all-reduce performance. Which topology provides better all-reduce throughput and why?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Rail-optimized. All GPUs at position N (GPU 0 from all 16 DGX) connect to the same leaf switch. The all-reduce communication pattern maps perfectly: GPU 0s reduce locally within their rail, then cross-rail reduction needs minimal switch hops. Fat-tree introduces 3 hops vs rail-optimized's effectively 1-2 hops for the all-reduce pattern.

  RAIL-OPTIMIZED vs FAT-TREE:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Rail: GPU-0 of all DGX → same leaf = 1-2 hops  │
  │  Fat-tree: Random leaf placement = 3 hops        │
  │  ★ Rail-optimized = 15-25% better all-reduce    │
  │  ★ Requires careful cabling: GPU position matters│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Rail-optimized is specifically designed for the all-reduce communication pattern in AI training. NCCL's ring or tree algorithms naturally align with rail topology. However, rail-optimized requires careful DGX placement — GPU 0 from every DGX MUST connect to the same leaf. This means physical cabling is more complex than fat-tree. For 128+ GPUs, the performance gain (15-25%) justifies the complexity.

Q4

GPUDirect Storage: In a traditional data path, a model checkpoint flows: GPU → CPU RAM → NVMe. With GPUDirect Storage enabled, what is the new data path?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU → NVMe (direct via PCIe). The GPU's DMA engine writes directly to NVMe storage, bypassing CPU RAM entirely. This eliminates one memory copy and frees CPU cycles.

  GPUDirect Storage — Data Path:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Without GDS: GPU→CPU RAM→NVMe (2 PCIe hops)     │
  │  With GDS:    GPU→NVMe (DMA, 1 PCIe hop)        │
  │  ★ Saves CPU cycles + 1 PCIe hop                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GDS requires: (1) NVIDIA GPU (Ampere+), (2) NVMe drives with PCIe BAR space enabled, (3) nvidia-fs.ko kernel module loaded, (4) cuFile API or compatible library (RAPIDS cuDF, PyTorch with GDS support). Benefits are most significant for large sequential I/O — checkpoints (10s of GB), dataset loading (100s of GB). Small random I/O (embedding lookups) benefits less because the PCIe transfer overhead dominates.

Q5

PUE Calculation: A data center draws 500 kW total. IT equipment (servers, switches, storage) accounts for 350 kW. What is the PUE and is it good for a GPU cluster?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

PUE = 1.43. Acceptable for air-cooled, but NOT optimal for GPU clusters. PUE = 500 ÷ 350 = 1.43. GPU clusters target <1.15 with liquid cooling. Air cooling's 1.4-1.6 means 40-60% of power goes to cooling, not compute.

  PUE = Total ÷ IT:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  500kW ÷ 350kW = 1.43 (air cooling)              │
  │  GPU target: <1.15 (liquid cooling)               │
  │  Every 0.1 PUE on 1MW = $87K/yr saved            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

PUE breakdown: 1.0 = perfect (all power to IT), 1.2 = very good, 1.5 = average, 2.0+ = poor. For GPU clusters: every 0.1 PUE improvement on a 500 kW facility saves $43,800/year at $0.10/kWh. Liquid cooling's PUE of 1.1 vs air's 1.5 on a 1 MW GPU cluster saves $350,400/year — the liquid cooling infrastructure pays for itself in 12-18 months.

Q6

Cooling Technology: You're building a 4-DGX H100 cluster (40.8 kW IT load) in a colocation facility that only supports air cooling. What must you verify before proceeding?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

The facility's per-rack cooling capacity. 40.8 kW far exceeds typical air cooling limits (10-25 kW/rack). You'd need to spread the 4 DGX across 2-4 racks, or the facility must have high-density air cooling (rare). Verify: CFM airflow, cold aisle containment, and whether the CRAC units can handle the concentrated heat load.

  DGX COOLING — 40.8kW vs Air Limits:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Air cooling: 10-25 kW/rack max                  │
  │  4× DGX = 40.8 kW → need 2-4 racks or liquid    │
  │  ★ DGX designed for liquid cooling (PUE <1.15)   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Air cooling physics: 1 kW requires ~120-160 CFM of airflow. 40.8 kW = 4,900-6,500 CFM — the airflow of a small jet engine. Most data centers are designed for 5-10 kW/rack. Solutions: (1) spread across multiple racks (4× single DGX racks), but this wastes space and may violate DGX support requirements, (2) use rear-door heat exchangers to boost per-rack capacity to ~35 kW, (3) find a liquid-cooling capable facility. DGX is designed for liquid cooling — air cooling is possible but suboptimal.

Q7

Reference Architecture: You're designing a 16-GPU cluster for internal use with no existing infrastructure. Which NVIDIA Reference Architecture is most appropriate?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

DGX BasePOD. Designed for 2-8 DGX (16-64 GPUs). Includes validated network design (usually simplified fat-tree or rail), storage recommendations, and NVAIE software stack. SuperPOD is for 32+ DGX and overkill for 16 GPUs.

  NVIDIA REFERENCE ARCHITECTURES:
  ┌─────────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │ BasePOD     │ 16-64    │ Simplified, entry-level  │
  │ SuperPOD    │ 256+     │ Full IB fabric           │
  │ SuperPOD Max│ 1000+    │ Multi-rail, liquid cool  │
  └─────────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NVIDIA's RA hierarchy: BasePOD (16-64 GPUs, simplified networking) → SuperPOD (256+ GPUs, full IB fabric) → SuperPOD Max (1000+ GPUs). BasePOD is ideal for "first cluster" deployments — it's validated, supported, and allows gradual expansion. Key BasePOD decisions: 2× DGX with no external IB needed (NVSwitch handles intra-node), or 4+ DGX requiring Quantum-2 leaf/spine fabric. anihpj's 4-DGX cluster maps to BasePOD with 8-switch IB fabric.

Q8

Storage Tiering: anihpj training loads a 500GB dataset, writes 50GB checkpoints every 1000 steps, and archives 50TB of historical models. Which storage tier for each?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Dataset: Tier 1 (Parallel FS). Checkpoints: Tier 0 (NVMe, then copy to Tier 1). Archives: Tier 2 (Object). Datasets need high throughput for loading (parallel FS delivers 100+ GB/s). Checkpoints need speed (NVMe at 30 GB/s) with safety (copy to shared FS). Archives are cold — object storage at $0.01/GB/month.

  STORAGE TIERING — anihpj:
  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
  │ Tier 0   │ NVMe (30 GB/s)   │ Checkpoints (fast)  │
  │ Tier 1   │ Parallel FS      │ Dataset (shared)    │
  │ Tier 2   │ Object ($0.01/GB)│ Archives (cold)     │
  └──────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Tiering strategy is about matching I/O patterns to storage characteristics. NVMe (Tier 0): low latency, limited capacity, expensive → active working set. Parallel FS (Tier 1): high throughput, shared, moderate cost → shared datasets and recent checkpoints. Object (Tier 2): high latency, unlimited capacity, cheap → everything else. The exam expects you to match workload I/O pattern (sequential/random, read/write ratio, bandwidth requirement) to storage tier.

Q9

Power Design: An anihpj cluster has 4 DGX H100 (10.2kW each), 8 Quantum-2 switches (0.5kW each), and management (1kW). The facility provides 208V 3-phase. What's the minimum circuit amperage per rack?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

175A circuit minimum (200A recommended). Total IT: 45.8kW. At 208V 3-phase: I = 45,800 ÷ (208 × 1.732) = 127A. With 80% continuous load derating: 127 ÷ 0.8 = 159A → next standard size = 175A breaker. Add PUE overhead at 1.1: total facility draw 50.4kW → 140A → 175A still works.

  3-PHASE POWER — anihpj (45.8kW):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  I = 45,800 ÷ (208 × 1.732) = 127A               │
  │  + 80% derating: 159A → 175A breaker             │
  │  Better: 415V → I = 70A → 90A breaker           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

3-phase power formula: Amps = Watts ÷ (Volts × √3). NEC requires 80% continuous load derating for breakers (breakers rated for 80% of label for continuous loads >3 hrs). GPU clusters run 24/7 = continuous. Always use 415V if available: 50,400 ÷ (415 × 1.732) = 70A → 90A breaker. 415V is standard for DGX deployments — insist on it during facility planning.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj Cluster Growth: anihpj currently runs on 2 DGX (16 GPUs) and needs to scale to 8 DGX (64 GPUs). The current fat-tree uses 4 leaf + 2 spine switches. What must change in the network?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Add 2 more spine switches (4 total) and upgrade to rail-optimized topology. At 8 DGX, the current 2-spine fat-tree becomes oversubscribed. Moving to 4 spines maintains 1:1. Additionally, 8 DGX is where rail-optimized topology starts outperforming fat-tree for all-reduce — reorganize GPU-to-leaf mapping to align GPU positions across DGX.

  NETWORK SCALING THRESHOLDS:
  ┌─────────┬──────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │  DGX    │   TOPOLOGY   │       NOTES           │
  ├─────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ 2-4     │ NVSwitch     │ No external IB needed │
  │         │ only         │ NVSwitch handles all  │
  ├─────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ 4-8     │ Fat-Tree     │ 4 leaf + 4 spine      │
  │         │ 1:1          │ Standard design        │
  ├─────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ 8-16    │ Rail-Opt     │ 8 leaf + 8 spine      │
  │         │              │ ★ RECABLING needed!    │
  ├─────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ 32+     │ SuperPOD     │ Dedicated mgmt net     │
  │         │ Rail-Opt     │ Full IB fabric         │
  └─────────┴──────────────┴───────────────────────┘
  anihpj: 2→8 DGX crosses the rail-opt threshold!
💡 EXPLANATION

Network scaling checkpoint: 2-4 DGX: no external IB needed (NVSwitch handles intra-node). 4-8 DGX: fat-tree with 4 leaf + 4 spine. 8-16 DGX: rail-optimized with 8 leaf + 8 spine. 32+ DGX: SuperPOD rail-optimized with dedicated management network. Each transition requires physical recabling — plan ahead. The exam expects you to identify the scaling threshold where topology changes are needed.

Chapter 7: MIG — Multi-Instance GPU in Production 🔴 Advanced

One GPU, Seven Tenants — Hardware Partitioning at Silicon Level

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) lets you slice one physical A100 or H100 into up to 7 independent GPU instances, each with dedicated compute, memory, and fault isolation. This is hardware-level multi-tenancy — not software time-slicing. For anihpj running dev, staging, and production on shared hardware, MIG is the foundation of efficient GPU sharing.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3 hours 📝 10 Questions 🐳 K8s Integration

📋 NCP-AII Relevance

MIG is a core NCP-AII topic — you must know MIG profiles, how to configure them via GPU Operator, and when to choose MIG vs vGPU vs MPS vs time-slicing. Expect scenario-based questions about multi-tenant GPU cluster design.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Understand MIG architecture: GPU Instances, Compute Instances, physical SM allocation
  • ✅ Configure MIG profiles for mixed workloads (dev/staging/prod on one GPU)
  • ✅ Deploy MIG-sliced pods on Kubernetes with proper resource requests
  • ✅ Compare MIG vs vGPU vs MPS vs time-slicing for different anihpj scenarios

7.1 MIG Architecture Deep Dive

MIG partitions a GPU at the hardware level. Each MIG instance gets dedicated SMs, memory channels, L2 cache slices, and memory bandwidth — like having multiple smaller GPUs on one physical die. There are two levels: GPU Instances (GI) which own hardware resources, and Compute Instances (CI) which subdivide a GI for multi-process isolation.

MIG Architecture — Hardware GPU Partitioning on A100
  PHYSICAL GPU (A100 80GB)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  8 GPCs (Graphics Processing Clusters) = 108 SMs total             │
  │  ┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐│
  │  │ GPC0 ││ GPC1 ││ GPC2 ││ GPC3 ││ GPC4 ││ GPC5 ││ GPC6 ││ GPC7 ││
  │  │14 SMs││14 SMs││14 SMs││14 SMs││14 SMs││14 SMs││14 SMs││14 SMs││
  │  └──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘└──────┘│
  │                                                                    │
  │  80GB HBM2e (5 stacks × 16GB)  │  L2 Cache: 40MB                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AFTER MIG PARTITIONING (Example: 7× 1g.10gb for dev + 1× full for prod)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐   │
  │ │MIG 0 │ │MIG 1 │ │MIG 2 │ │MIG 3 │ │MIG 4 │ │MIG 5 │ │MIG 6 │   │
  │ │1g.10g│ │1g.10g│ │1g.10g│ │1g.10g│ │1g.10g│ │1g.10g│ │1g.10g│   │
  │ │14 SMs│ │14 SMs│ │14 SMs│ │14 SMs│ │14 SMs│ │14 SMs│ │14 SMs│   │
  │ │10GB  │ │10GB  │ │10GB  │ │10GB  │ │10GB  │ │10GB  │ │10GB  │   │
  │ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘   │
  │   Each instance: DEDICATED SMs, memory channels, L2 cache slices    │
  │   Each instance: OWN ECC, OWN power/thermal, FAULT ISOLATED         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ProfileSMsMemoryMax CountUse Case
1g.10gb1410 GB7Light dev/proto, anihpj dev
2g.20gb2820 GB3Fine-tuning, anihpj staging
3g.40gb4240 GB2Medium training
4g.40gb5640 GB2Inference serving
7g.80gb10880 GB1Full training, anihpj prod
📖 Key Concept: MIG = Hardware, vGPU = Software

MIG runs at the GPU hardware level — each instance has its own SMs, memory channels, and ECC. A failure in one MIG instance does NOT affect others. vGPU (virtual GPU) is software-level time-slicing — all VMs share the same hardware. vGPU is used for VDI/cloud gaming; MIG is used for production AI multi-tenancy. MIG does NOT require an NVAIE license (it's built into A100/H100). vGPU DOES require NVAIE.

H100 MIG Profiles — Different from A100

H100 has different MIG profiles than A100 due to its 132 SMs (vs A100's 108). Key differences: H100 supports up to 7 instances (same max), but each 1g profile gets ~18 SMs vs A100's 14 — giving ~30% more compute per slice. H100 MIG also supports MIG + NVLink sharing (A100 MIG instances can't use NVLink).

Profile (H100)SMsMemoryMax CountKey Difference from A100
1g.20gb~1820 GB72× memory vs A100 1g.10gb
2g.40gb~3640 GB3NVLink sharing enabled
3g.80gb~5480 GB2Full HBM3 bandwidth per slice
7g.80gb13280 GB1Full GPU

🐳 MIG Configuration CLI Cheatsheet

MIG Commands — Full Lifecycle Bash 
# ENABLE MIG
sudo nvidia-smi -mig 1              # Enable MIG mode
sudo reboot                           # REBOOT REQUIRED

# LIST AVAILABLE PROFILES
nvidia-smi mig -lgip                  # List GPU Instance Profiles
nvidia-smi mig -lgipp                 # List GPU Instance Profile Placements

# CREATE MIG INSTANCES (A100, GPU 0)
nvidia-smi mig -cgi 19,19,19,19,19,19,19 -C 0  # 7× 1g.10gb (Profile ID 19)
nvidia-smi mig -cgi 14,14,14 -C 0              # 3× 2g.20gb (Profile ID 14)
nvidia-smi mig -cgi 9,9 -C 0                    # 2× 3g.40gb (Profile ID 9)
nvidia-smi mig -cgi 0 -C 0                      # 1× 7g.80gb (Profile ID 0)

# CREATE COMPUTE INSTANCES
sudo nvidia-smi mig -gci             # Create Compute Instances for all GIs

# VERIFY
nvidia-smi mig -lgt                  # List GPU Instances
nvidia-smi                           # Shows MIG slices as separate devices

# DELETE (RESET)
sudo nvidia-smi mig -dci             # Delete Compute Instances
sudo nvidia-smi mig -dgi             # Delete GPU Instances
sudo nvidia-smi -mig 0               # Disable MIG mode (REBOOT REQUIRED)

7.2 MIG + Kubernetes — Production Multi-Tenancy 🐳

When you enable MIG on a GPU and deploy the GPU Operator, K8s sees each MIG slice as a separate schedulable resource. The device plugin exposes nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb, nvidia.com/mig-2g.20gb, etc. — pods request the specific MIG profile they need.

🐳 anihpj K8s Pod with MIG Slice YAML 
# anihpj-dev pod — uses 1 MIG slice (1g.10gb) for light development
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev-notebook
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    env: dev
spec:
  containers:
  - name: jupyter
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.01-py3
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1    # Request 1 MIG slice
  nodeSelector:
    nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB  # Only MIG-capable GPUs
🐳 anihpj K8s Deployment with 2 MIG Slices for Production Inference YAML 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-inference-prod
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-inference
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-inference
        env: production
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: triton-server
        image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/mig-2g.20gb: 1   # 2× GPU slice for each replica
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /v2/health/ready
            port: 8000

MIG Strategy for anihpj — Single vs Mixed Profiles

Single profile (recommended): All MIG instances on a GPU use the same profile (e.g., 7× 1g.10gb). Simplest management, predictable performance. Mixed profiles: Different profiles on one GPU (e.g., 1× 4g.40gb for prod + 3× 1g.10gb for dev). Maximizes utilization but complicates scheduling. For anihpj: use 2 GPUs with single profiles — GPU 0 with 7× 1g.10gb for dev teams, GPU 1 with 1× 7g.80gb for production training.

Fault IsolationYes (one instance crash doesn't affect others)PartialNo (shared context)No

🧪 LAB: Compare anihpj Inference Under MIG vs Time-Slicing

Configure one A100 with MIG (3× 2g.20gb) and another with GPU Operator time-slicing (3 pods sharing the GPU). Run 3 simultaneous anihpj inference workloads and measure: (1) P99 latency, (2) throughput consistency, (3) memory isolation (can one pod OOM and crash the others?). Expected: MIG shows consistent latency (±5% variance) with full fault isolation; time-slicing shows 2-3× latency variance with no fault isolation.

🔍 Deep Dive: vGPU Architecture — How It Differs from MIG

vGPU (Virtual GPU) is NVIDIA's software-based GPU virtualization for hypervisors (VMware vSphere, Citrix Hypervisor, KVM). Unlike MIG which partitions at the hardware level, vGPU uses a mediated passthrough model where the hypervisor schedules GPU time across VMs. Understanding this distinction is tested on NCP-AII.

vGPU Architecture — Mediated Passthrough vs MIG Hardware Partitioning
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     vGPU (SOFTWARE) vs MIG (HARDWARE)              │
  │                                                                    │
  │   vGPU ARCHITECTURE                    MIG ARCHITECTURE            │
  │   ┌────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────┐      │
  │   │  VM1  │ VM2 │ VM3  │              │  Pod1 │ Pod2 │ Pod3 │      │
  │   │ apps  │apps │apps  │              │ apps  │apps  │apps  │      │
  │   │ vGPU  │vGPU │vGPU  │              │ CUDA  │CUDA  │CUDA  │      │
  │   │ driver│driver│driver│              │ ctx   │ ctx  │ ctx   │      │
  │   └───┬───┴──┬───┴──┬───┘              └───┬───┴──┬───┴──┬───┘      │
  │       │      │      │                     │      │      │          │
  │       └──────┼──────┘                     └──────┼──────┘          │
  │              ▼                                   ▼                 │
  │   ┌────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────┐      │
  │   │   HYPERVISOR       │              │   GPU HARDWARE     │      │
  │   │  (GPU Scheduler)   │              │  ┌────┬────┬────┐  │      │
  │   │   Time-slices GPU  │              │  │GI 0│GI 1│GI 2│  │      │
  │   └─────────┬──────────┘              │  │SMs │SMs │SMs │  │      │
  │             ▼                         │  │Mem │Mem │Mem │  │      │
  │   ┌────────────────────┐              │  │L2  │L2  │L2  │  │      │
  │   │    GPU DRIVER      │              │  └────┴────┴────┘  │      │
  │   │ (Physical GPU)     │              └────────────────────┘      │
  │   └────────────────────┘                                         │
  │                                                                    │
  │   ★ vGPU: 1 GPU → many VMs via SW   ★ MIG: 1 GPU → up to 7 HW   │
  │     scheduling. Best for VDI.          partitions. Best for AI.   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

vGPU Deployment Models — vWS, vPC, vApps

vGPU TypeTargetGPU MemoryLicensingUse Case
RTX Virtual Workstation (vWS)Professional designers, data scientistsUp to 48 GBNVAIE vWSCAD, AI development, rendering
Virtual PC (vPC)Knowledge workersUp to 4 GBNVAIE vPCOffice apps, web, video
Virtual Applications (vApps)App streamingUp to 2 GBNVAIE vAppsRDSH, Citrix app streaming

vGPU Lifecycle — Production vs LTS Branches

From the official NVIDIA docs: vGPU software releases follow two branch types. Production Branches get new features and are supported for 1 year — use these in test/dev to access latest capabilities. Long-Term Support (LTS) Branches provide 3 years of support with no feature changes — use these in production for stability. Current LTS: vGPU 19 (R580 driver), supported through July 2028. Exam relevance: NCP-AII may ask which branch type to use for production GPU clusters. Answer: LTS for production (3yr support, no surprises), Production branch for dev/staging (latest features).

⚠️ Exam Distinction: vGPU requires NVAIE license; MIG does NOT

This is a classic NCP-AII trick question. vGPU is licensed per concurrent user through NVIDIA AI Enterprise (NVAIE). MIG is a free hardware feature on A100/H100 — no additional license required. Scenario: "Company has 50 data scientists. They want GPU access via VMs. What's the licensing cost?" Answer: 50 × NVAIE vWS license (~$2,000/user/yr) = $100K/yr. Alternative with MIG + containers: 0 license cost (but requires container-native workflow, not VMs). The exam tests your ability to factor licensing into architecture decisions.

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 7 (10 Questions)

Q1

MIG Profiles: You need to support 5 developers each needing 10GB GPU memory for prototyping. One A100 80GB is available. What MIG configuration do you use?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

5× 1g.10gb. Each gets 14 SMs and 10GB dedicated. A100 supports max 7 of this profile. 5 fits within budget with room for 2 more. Ports: nvidia-smi mig -cgi 19,19,19,19,19 -C 0

  MIG PROFILE 1g.10gb (ID=19 on A100):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1 GPU slice = 14 SMs + 10 GB HBM2e              │
  │  Max: 7 per A100-80GB                             │
  │  5 used here → 2 spare slots for growth          │
  │  cmd: nvidia-smi mig -cgi 19,19,19,19,19 -C 0    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Profile ID 19 = 1g.10gb on A100. The command creates 5 GPU instances of this profile on GPU 0. Remaining capacity (2 more 1g.10gb) stays unused — you can't mix leftover fragments across profiles. Always plan MIG partitioning before enabling it — changing profiles requires GPU reset (drain workloads first).

Q2

MIG vs vGPU: A company wants to run 20 VMs each with GPU access for VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure). Should they use MIG or vGPU?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

vGPU. MIG max is 7 instances per GPU — insufficient for 20 VMs. vGPU supports many more instances through software time-slicing. vGPU is designed for VDI/cloud gaming; MIG is designed for AI multi-tenancy with strict performance isolation.

  GPU SHARING — Technology Match:
  ┌──────────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │ MIG          │ AI multi │ Hardware isolation, max 7│
  │ vGPU         │ VDI      │ Software slices, many    │
  │ MPS          │ Same user│ Shared context, no isol. │
  │ Time-slicing │ Dev env  │ Best-effort, cheap       │
  └──────────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NCP-AII expects you to match the technology to the use case: MIG = AI workloads needing guaranteed performance. vGPU = many lightweight GPU users (VDI). MPS = single user running multiple GPU processes. Time-slicing = dev environments where perf variance is acceptable.

Q3

🐳 K8s MIG Pod: A pod requests nvidia.com/mig-2g.20gb: 1 on a node with A100 GPUs. There are no MIG instances configured. What happens?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Pod stays Pending indefinitely. The device plugin only advertises MIG resources when MIG is enabled and instances are created. Without MIG configuration, the node has nvidia.com/gpu: 8 (full GPUs) but no MIG resources.

  K8s MIG — Why Pod Stays Pending:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod requests: nvidia.com/mig-2g.20gb            │
  │  Node has: nvidia.com/gpu: 8 (NO MIG resources)  │
  │  Result: NO MATCH → Pod Pending FOREVER          │
  │  Fix: Enable MIG → Create instances → Retry      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU Operator workflow: (1) Enable MIG on GPU: nvidia-smi -mig 1 + reboot, (2) Create MIG instances: nvidia-smi mig -cgi ..., (3) GPU Operator's device plugin detects MIG slices and advertises them as nvidia.com/mig-Xg.Ygb. Without step 1-2, the MIG resource types don't exist in the node's allocatable resources.

Q4

MIG Fault Isolation: A kernel running on MIG instance #3 triggers a double-bit ECC error (XID 48). What happens to MIG instances #0, #1, and #2?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

They continue running unaffected. Each MIG instance has dedicated memory channels and ECC. An ECC error on one instance's memory does not affect other instances — this is the definition of hardware fault isolation.

  MIG FAULT ISOLATION:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Instance #3: XID 48 → CRASH                     │
  │  Instance #0,1,2: CONTINUE RUNNING ✅            │
  │  Without MIG: ALL workloads on GPU crash         │
  │  ★ Hardware isolation = MIG's killer feature     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

This is MIG's killer feature for production. Without MIG, a GPU memory error affects ALL workloads on that GPU. With MIG, only the affected instance needs restart (or RMA if persistent). For anihpj prod: run critical inference on a dedicated MIG instance separate from dev/testing — a dev crash never impacts production.

Q5

MPS vs MIG: You're running 4 PyTorch inference models on one GPU. They all use the same CUDA context. Which technology do you use?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

MPS (Multi-Process Service). MPS allows multiple CUDA processes to share one GPU context, enabling concurrent kernel execution. It's ideal when processes are cooperative (same user, same app) and don't need hardware isolation.

  MPS vs MIG — Decision Tree:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Same user, cooperative? → MPS (no isolation)    │
  │  Different tenants, need isolation? → MIG       │
  │  VMs needing GPU? → vGPU                         │
  │  Many users, best-effort? → Time-slicing         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Decision tree: (1) Same user, cooperative processes? → MPS. (2) Different tenants needing fault isolation? → MIG. (3) VMs needing GPU? → vGPU. (4) Best-effort sharing for many users? → Time-slicing. MPS doesn't provide memory protection — one process can write another's memory. Only MIG provides true hardware isolation between processes.

Q6

🐳 MIG + GPU Operator: Which GPU Operator CRD controls MIG configuration on a K8s cluster?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

ClusterPolicy (specifically the mig section). The mig.strategy field can be single (all same profile) or mixed (different profiles per GPU). The migManager component handles MIG lifecycle.

  ClusterPolicy CRD — MIG Config:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  mig: { strategy: "mixed" }                      │
  │  Node label: nvidia.com/mig.config=all-1g.10gb   │
  │  migManager watches labels → auto-applies        │
  │  ★ Declarative GPU partitioning in K8s           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU Operator's ClusterPolicy is the single source of truth for GPU configuration. MIG section example: mig: { strategy: "mixed" } enables the mig-manager to create instances based on GPU labels. Individual GPU MIG configurations are specified via node labels: nvidia.com/mig.config: all-1g.10gb. The operator watches these labels and (re)configures MIG accordingly.

Q7

MIG Memory: An A100 80GB is configured with 3× 2g.20gb instances (60GB total used). What happens to the remaining 20GB?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

It's unusable. Memory is allocated in fixed chunks matching the MIG profile. 3× 2g.20gb uses 60GB. The remaining 20GB can't be allocated because there are no remaining SMs to pair with it (each 2g.20gb needs 28 SMs, 3× 28 = 84 of 108 SMs used). The remaining 24 SMs and 20GB are stranded.

  MIG PARTITIONING — A100 80GB:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               A100 80GB GPU                       │
  │  108 SMs ──────────────────────────────── 80GB   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ░░░░░░░░│
  │  │ 2g.20gb  │ │ 2g.20gb  │ │ 2g.20gb  │ ░20GB ░░│
  │  │ 28 SMs   │ │ 28 SMs   │ │ 28 SMs   │ ░STRAND ░│
  │  │ 20GB     │ │ 20GB     │ │ 20GB     │ ░+ 24SM ░│
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ ░░░░░░░░│
  │  84/108 SMs used    60/80GB used     UNUSABLE!  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Optimal: 7×1g.10gb = 98 SMs, 70GB (91% util)
  ✅ Optimal: 1×7g.80gb = 108 SMs, 80GB (100% util)
💡 EXPLANATION

MIG partitioning is constrained by both SM count and memory. Stranded resources are a natural consequence of fixed profile sizes. Mitigation: choose profiles that maximize utilization. For A100 80GB: 7× 1g.10gb = 98 SMs, 70GB (best utilization). 1× 7g.80gb = 108 SMs, 80GB (full GPU). 3× 2g.20gb = 84 SMs, 60GB (suboptimal — 24 SMs + 20GB stranded).

Q8

MIG Enabling: After running nvidia-smi -mig 1, nvidia-smi still shows all GPUs as non-MIG. What's missing?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU reset (reboot or GPU reset). MIG mode change requires the GPU to be reset. nvidia-smi -mig 1 enables MIG mode, but a system reboot (or nvidia-smi -r if no processes) is needed to apply. After reboot, create instances with nvidia-smi mig -cgi ....

  MIG ENABLE SEQUENCE:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. Stop GPU workloads                            │
  │  2. nvidia-smi -mig 1 (enable MIG mode)          │
  │  3. sudo reboot (GPU reset required!)            │
  │  4. nvidia-smi mig -cgi 9,9,9 -C 0              │
  │  ★ Without reboot: GPUs still show as non-MIG    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

MIG is a fundamental GPU mode change — it requires draining all GPU processes and resetting. The full sequence: (1) Stop all GPU workloads, (2) sudo nvidia-smi -mig 1, (3) sudo reboot, (4) sudo nvidia-smi mig -cgi PROFILE_ID -C GPU_ID, (5) sudo nvidia-smi mig -gci to create compute instances. GPU Operator automates this entire sequence.

Q9

🐳 MIG Node Labeling: How does the GPU Operator know which MIG configuration to apply to which GPU?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Node labels matching the pattern nvidia.com/mig.config: <config-name>. The mig-manager component watches for these labels and applies the specified MIG configuration. Common values: all-1g.10gb, all-2g.20gb, all-balanced.

  MIG NODE LABELING:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl label node dgx-01                       │
  │    nvidia.com/mig.config=all-1g.10gb             │
  │  → migManager watches → auto-applies MIG         │
  │  → 7×1g.10gb on all GPUs of dgx-01              │
  │  ★ Declarative: label = desired state           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Example: kubectl label node dgx-01 nvidia.com/mig.config=all-1g.10gb tells GPU Operator to configure all GPUs on dgx-01 with 7× 1g.10gb each. For mixed: label individual GPUs (not nodes) via nvidia.com/mig.config-gpu0=all-1g.10gb. The operator handles the nvidia-smi mig commands automatically. This is declarative GPU management — define desired state, operator makes it happen.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj MIG Design: anihpj needs: (A) 3 dev teams with 10GB each, (B) staging with 40GB, (C) production inference with 40GB. You have 2× A100 80GB. Design the MIG layout.

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU 0: 3× 1g.10gb (dev) + 1× 4g.40gb (staging). GPU 1: 1× 7g.80gb (prod — gets full GPU for max performance). Total: 3 dev + 1 staging + 1 prod = 5 workloads on 2 GPUs.

  anihpj MIG LAYOUT (2× A100 80GB):
  ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │   GPU 0 (Shared)        │  │   GPU 1 (Dedicated)     │
  ├─────────────────────────┤  ├─────────────────────────┤
  │ ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐┌───┐│  │                         │
  │ │Dev1││Dev2││Dev3││Stg││  │   ┌─────────────────┐    │
  │ │1g  ││1g  ││1g  ││4g ││  │   │   PRODUCTION    │    │
  │ │10gb││10gb││10gb││40g││  │   │   7g.80gb       │    │
  │ └────┘└────┘└────┘└───┘│  │   │   Full GPU      │    │
  │ 42SM+30GB  56SM+40GB   │  │   │   108 SMs       │    │
  │ 98/108 SMs  70/80GB    │  │   │   80 GB HBM3    │    │
  │ ★ 91% utilization      │  │   └─────────────────┘    │
  └─────────────────────────┘  │   ★ 100% utilization     │
                                │   ★ No noisy neighbor   │
  Dev=3 teams isolated         └─────────────────────────┘
  Staging=40GB for canary
  Prod=dedicated for P99 latency
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU 0: 3× 1g.10gb = 42 SMs + 30GB. 4g.40gb = 56 SMs + 40GB. Total: 98/108 SMs, 70/80GB — 91% utilization. GPU 1: 7g.80gb = full GPU for production. Alternative: 6× 1g.10gb across both GPUs + 1× 2g.20gb for staging — but staging needs 40GB, so 4g.40gb on one GPU + 7g.80gb on the other is optimal. Production gets dedicated hardware (no noisy neighbor).

Chapter 8: GPU Operator — Production-Grade GPU Management 🔴 Advanced

Automating GPU Infrastructure on Kubernetes — The Operator Way

Manually installing NVIDIA drivers, CUDA toolkit, and device plugins on every K8s node is a recipe for drift and disaster. The GPU Operator automates the entire GPU software lifecycle on Kubernetes — from driver installation to monitoring export. This is the standard for production GPU clusters.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📝 10 Questions 🐳 K8s-Native

📋 NCP-AII Relevance

GPU Operator is tested on NCP-AII: its architecture, CRDs, driver lifecycle, and troubleshooting. You'll see scenario questions like "GPU pods stuck Pending after driver upgrade — diagnose." The operator is the bridge between GPU hardware and K8s orchestration — a critical Professional-level skill.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Understand GPU Operator architecture: driver, toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter
  • ✅ Deploy and configure GPU Operator via Helm and ClusterPolicy CRD
  • ✅ Configure MIG through GPU Operator declaratively
  • ✅ Troubleshoot common GPU Operator failures on anihpj K8s cluster

8.1 GPU Operator Architecture 🐳

The GPU Operator is a set of cooperating components deployed as a Helm chart. Each component handles one layer of the GPU software stack:

GPU Operator Architecture — 6 Components Working Together
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║                     GPU OPERATOR — LIFECYCLE LAYERS                      ║
  ║                                                                          ║
  ║  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    ║
  ║  │  1️⃣ DRIVER CONTAINER (DaemonSet)                                 │    ║
  ║  │  Installs NVIDIA kernel module. Precompiled or DKMS.             │    ║
  ║  │  Runs FIRST — all other components depend on it.                 │    ║
  ║  └────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘    ║
  ║                               │                                         ║
  ║  ┌────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┐    ║
  ║  │  2️⃣ TOOLKIT CONTAINER (DaemonSet)                                │    ║
  ║  │  Installs nvidia-container-toolkit. Configures container runtimes.│   ║
  ║  │  Enables --gpus flag and nvidia.com/gpu resource type.           │    ║
  ║  └────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘    ║
  ║                               │                                         ║
  ║       ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐                 ║
  ║       │                       │                       │                 ║
  ║       ▼                       ▼                       ▼                 ║
  ║  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                  ║
  ║  │ 3️⃣ DEVICE    │  │ 4️⃣ DCGM      │  │ 5️⃣ MIG       │                  ║
  ║  │    PLUGIN    │  │    EXPORTER  │  │    MANAGER   │                  ║
  ║  │  K8s resource │  │  Prometheus  │  │  MIG config  │                  ║
  ║  │  advertising │  │  metrics     │  │  lifecycle   │                  ║
  ║  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘                  ║

ComponentWhat It Doesanihpj Relevance
Driver ContainerInstalls NVIDIA driver (precompiled or DKMS). Runs as DaemonSet on GPU nodes.Ensures all anihpj K8s nodes have matching driver versions
Toolkit ContainerInstalls NVIDIA Container Toolkit (nvidia-container-runtime, CDI).Enables GPU passthrough to anihpj Docker containers

🐳 Deploy GPU Operator on anihpj K8s Cluster

GPU Operator Deployment on anihpj Bash 
# Add NVIDIA Helm repo
helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia
helm repo update

# Install GPU Operator with default config
helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator \
  --namespace gpu-operator \
  --create-namespace \
  --set driver.enabled=true \
  --set toolkit.enabled=true \
  --set devicePlugin.enabled=true \
  --set dcgmExporter.enabled=true

# Verify installation
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator
# Expected: driver, toolkit, device-plugin, dcgm-exporter pods Running

# Check GPU resources available to K8s
kubectl describe node dgx-01 | grep nvidia
# Expected: nvidia.com/gpu: 8 (or MIG slices if configured)

GPU Operator Helm Values — Key Configuration Options

Helm ValueDefaultDescription
driver.enabledtrueInstall NVIDIA driver via container
driver.version"" (latest)Pin to specific version (e.g., "550.54.15")
driver.useDKMSfalseUse DKMS instead of precompiled driver
toolkit.enabledtrueInstall NVIDIA Container Toolkit
devicePlugin.enabledtrueDeploy K8s device plugin
dcgmExporter.enabledtrueDeploy DCGM Prometheus exporter
mig.strategysingleMIG strategy: "single" or "mixed"
validator.enabledtrueRun GPU diagnostics on startup
gfd.enabledtrueEnable GPU Feature Discovery labels
📖 Driver Lifecycle — Precompiled vs DKMS

Precompiled: NVIDIA provides pre-built driver containers matching specific kernel versions. Faster startup, but kernel must match. DKMS (Dynamic Kernel Module Support): Driver compiles against the running kernel at startup. Works on any kernel, but slower first start. For DGX (known kernel), use precompiled. For custom Linux builds, use DKMS. GPU Operator defaults to precompiled and falls back to DKMS if no match found.

8.2 GPU Operator Advanced Configuration 🐳

Driver Version Pinning

Production clusters should pin driver versions to ensure consistency. The ClusterPolicy CRD controls this:

🐳 ClusterPolicy — Driver Pinning + MIG YAML 
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: cluster-policy
spec:
  driver:
    enabled: true
    version: "550.54.15"       # Pin to specific driver version
    repo: "nvcr.io/nvidia"
  toolkit:
    enabled: true
  devicePlugin:
    enabled: true
  mig:
    strategy: mixed             # Allow mixed MIG profiles per GPU
  gfd:                          # GPU Feature Discovery
    enabled: true
  validator:
    enabled: true
    repository: nvcr.io/nvidia/cloud-native

🐳 MIG via GPU Operator — Declarative Configuration

Instead of manual nvidia-smi MIG commands, use node labels:

🐳 Declarative MIG Configuration for anihpj Bash 
# Label GPU nodes for MIG configuration
kubectl label node dgx-01 nvidia.com/mig.config=all-1g.10gb
kubectl label node dgx-02 nvidia.com/mig.config=all-2g.20gb

# For mixed profiles on GPU 0:
kubectl label node dgx-03 nvidia.com/mig.config-gpu0.config=all-1g.10gb

# GPU Operator's mig-manager watches labels and configures MIG automatically
# Check status:
kubectl logs -n gpu-operator -l app=mig-manager
nvidia-smi mig -lgt  # List GPU instances (after operator applies config)

8.3 GPU Operator Troubleshooting 🐳

🐳 Pod Stuck Pending? Diagnose GPU Availability

GPU Operator Troubleshooting Flow Bash 
# SYMPTOM: anihpj pod stuck Pending, requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1
# STEP 1: Check node GPU capacity
kubectl describe node dgx-01 | grep -A5 "Allocatable"
# If nvidia.com/gpu = 0 → device plugin not advertising GPUs

# STEP 2: Check device plugin status
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator | grep device-plugin
kubectl logs -n gpu-operator device-plugin-xxx

# STEP 3: Verify GPU visible at OS level
ssh dgx-01
nvidia-smi                    # Do GPUs appear?
lsmod | grep nvidia           # Driver loaded?

# STEP 4: Check driver container
kubectl logs -n gpu-operator -l app=nvidia-driver-daemonset

# COMMON ISSUES:
# - Secure Boot enabled → driver can't load unsigned kernel module
#   Fix: disable Secure Boot OR sign the module
# - Wrong containerd config → toolkit not configured
#   Fix: /etc/containerd/config.toml must use nvidia-container-runtime
# - Driver version mismatch → precompiled driver doesn't match kernel
#   Fix: switch to DKMS driver OR update kernel to match

🧪 LAB: Simulate GPU Operator Failure and Recovery

Delete the device plugin pod (kubectl delete pod -n gpu-operator device-plugin-xxx). Observe: (1) nvidia.com/gpu disappears from node capacity (describe node), (2) Running GPU pods continue (they already have GPUs assigned), (3) New GPU pods stay Pending. GPU Operator recreates the device plugin within ~30 seconds. After recovery, new pods can schedule again. This simulates a real production scenario — know what breaks and how fast it recovers.

8.4 GPU Operator — Complete Component Reference (Official Docs)

From the official NVIDIA GPU Operator documentation, the operator manages 15+ software components across every GPU node. You don't need to memorize all 15, but you MUST know the core 6 and what each optional component provides. NCP-AII questions test whether you know which component handles which function.

#ComponentTypeFunctionExam?
1GPU DriverCoreInstalls NVIDIA driver (precompiled or DKMS). Version controlled by ClusterPolicy.🎯
2Container ToolkitCoreConfigures containerd/CRI-O for GPU passthrough. Mounts nvidia-container-runtime.🎯
3Device PluginCoreAdvertises nvidia.com/gpu to K8s. Enables GPU scheduling. Registers with kubelet.🎯
4DCGM + ExporterCoreGPU telemetry (50+ fields). Exports to Prometheus. Powers all GPU dashboards.🎯
5MIG ManagerCoreManages MIG partitioning strategy (single, mixed, none). Applies per-node MIG config.🎯
6Feature Discovery (GFD)CoreAuto-labels nodes with GPU model, driver version, CUDA version, memory. Enables nodeSelector.
7ValidatorSupportRuns post-install validation: GPU visible? Driver correct version? Toolkit configured?
8Driver ManagerSupportOrchestrates driver lifecycle per node. Handles precompiled vs DKMS selection.
9Kata ManagerSecurityEnables Kata Containers runtime for GPU VMs — stronger isolation than standard containers.
10Confidential Computing MgrSecurityManages GPU TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) for confidential AI workloads.🎯
11vGPU Device ManagerVirtualizationManages vGPU allocation for VMs on hypervisors (VMware, KVM). Separate from MIG.
12KubeVirt GPU PluginVirtualizationEnables GPU passthrough to KubeVirt-managed VMs on K8s.
13GDS DriverStorageGPUDirect Storage kernel module (nvidia-fs.ko). Enables GPU↔NVMe direct DMA.
14GDRCopy DriverPerformanceEnables CPU-to-GPU memory copy via BAR mapping. Used by profiling and debugging tools.
15Sandbox ValidatorSecurityValidates sandboxed container environments for GPU workloads before deployment.

🧪 LAB — Deploy GPU Operator with Custom Component Selection for anihpj

Objective: Deploy GPU Operator with only the components anihpj needs. (1) Review the 15 components above, (2) anihpj needs: driver, toolkit, device plugin, DCGM (monitoring), MIG manager (multi-tenant), GFD (node labels), validator (post-install), (3) Disable unnecessary components in ClusterPolicy: kataManager.enabled: false, vgpuDeviceManager.enabled: false, gds.enabled: false, (4) helm install with custom values, (5) Verify: kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator shows only enabled components, (6) Run validator to confirm all GPUs healthy. Benefits: reduced resource usage (each component is a pod), smaller attack surface, simpler troubleshooting.
