📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 8 (10 Questions)

Q1

GPU Operator Components: Which GPU Operator component is responsible for making GPUs visible as Kubernetes resources?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Device Plugin. It registers with kubelet and advertises nvidia.com/gpu (or MIG slices) as allocatable resources. Without it, K8s doesn't know GPUs exist.

  GPU OPERATOR — Component Architecture:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 GPU OPERATOR                      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ┌──────────┐  → Kernel module for GPU HW access  │
  │ │ DRIVER   │     (nvidia.ko, nvidia-uvm.ko)      │
  │ └──────────┘                                     │
  │ ┌──────────┐  → nvidia-container-runtime hook    │
  │ │ TOOLKIT  │     GPU passthrough to containers    │
  │ └──────────┘                                     │
  │ ┌──────────┐  → ★ Registers nvidia.com/gpu       │
  │ │ DEVICE   │     with kubelet. WITHOUT THIS =     │
  │ │ PLUGIN   │     K8s sees 0 GPUs!                │
  │ └──────────┘                                     │
  │ ┌──────────┐  → Prometheus metrics exporter      │
  │ │ DCGM EXP │     GPU util, temp, ECC, XID         │
  │ └──────────┘                                     │
  │ ┌──────────┐  → Manages MIG partition lifecycle  │
  │ │ MIG MGR  │     nvidia-smi mig -cgi automation   │
  │ └──────────┘                                     │
  │ ┌──────────┐  → GPU health validation             │
  │ │VALIDATOR │     dcgmi diag + taint on failure    │
  │ └──────────┘                                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Component responsibilities: Driver = kernel module. Toolkit = container runtime integration. Device Plugin = K8s resource advertisement. DCGM Exporter = Prometheus metrics. MIG Manager = MIG lifecycle. Validator = GPU health checks. If GPUs work at OS level (nvidia-smi) but not in K8s, the device plugin is the first thing to check.

Q2

🐳 Driver Pinning: Why would you pin a specific driver version in ClusterPolicy instead of using "latest"?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Consistency and stability. Different driver versions may have different performance characteristics or bugs. Pinning ensures all nodes run the same version — critical for reproducible training results and support from NVIDIA.

  DRIVER PINNING — Why Not "latest":
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  latest = nodes drift apart (version skew)       │
  │  pinned = all nodes identical ✅                │
  │  NVAIE certifies: driver + CUDA + framework      │
  │  anihpj: pin 550.54.15, test in staging 2 weeks │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NVIDIA certifies specific driver + CUDA + framework combinations through NVAIE. Using "latest" means nodes may auto-upgrade at different times, causing version skew across the cluster. For anihpj prod: pin to NVAIE-certified driver (e.g., 550.54.15). Test new drivers in staging for 2 weeks before rolling to production.

Q3

🐳 Device Plugin Failure: After a node reboot, nvidia-smi shows all 8 GPUs but kubectl describe node shows nvidia.com/gpu: 0. What's wrong?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Device plugin hasn't restarted or registered yet. GPUs are visible at OS level (nvidia-smi works) but the K8s device plugin pod may be Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, or still initializing. Wait 30-60 seconds for it to register, or check its logs.

  DEVICE PLUGIN DEBUG:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  nvidia-smi = 8 GPUs ✅ → OS level OK            │
  │  kubectl describe node = 0 GPUs ❌              │
  │  → Device plugin pod not registered              │
  │  Check: kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator          │
  │  Fix: Wait 2-3 min (auto-recovery) or restart    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Debug flow: (1) kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator -l app=nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset — is it Running? (2) kubectl logs -n gpu-operator <device-plugin-pod> — any errors? Common causes: driver container not yet finished on node boot (device plugin starts before driver is ready), or kubelet restart causing plugin re-registration delay. GPU Operator handles this with retry logic — wait 2-3 minutes before investigating.

Q4

🐳 Containerd Config: GPU Operator toolkit installs nvidia-container-runtime. What must containerd's config.toml have for GPU containers to work?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

default_runtime_name = "nvidia" (or nvidia configured as a named runtime). The containerd config must reference the nvidia-container-runtime binary so GPU passthrough works.

  CONTAINERD GPU CONFIG:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  /etc/containerd/config.toml:                    │
  │  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"            │
  │    .containerd.runtimes.nvidia]                  │
  │  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"          │
  │  ★ Without this: containers can't see GPUs      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU Operator's toolkit container updates containerd config automatically, but manual installations require: [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.nvidia] runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2". Without this, containers can't see GPUs even though nvidia-smi works on the host. Docker has a similar config: /etc/docker/daemon.json with "default-runtime": "nvidia".

Q5

🐳 Secure Boot: GPU Operator driver container fails with "Required key not available." What's the cause?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Secure Boot is enabled and the NVIDIA kernel module isn't signed with a key trusted by the system's UEFI. The kernel refuses to load unsigned modules when Secure Boot is active.

  SECURE BOOT + NVIDIA Driver:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Fix 1: Disable Secure Boot in BIOS (simplest)   │
  │  Fix 2: mokutil --import (sign with MOK)        │
  │  Fix 3: --set driver.useSignedDriver=true       │
  │  ★ Cloud GPU instances: SB usually disabled      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Solutions: (1) Disable Secure Boot in BIOS (simplest for on-prem DGX), (2) Sign the NVIDIA module with your own MOK (Machine Owner Key) — mokutil --import, (3) Use NVIDIA's signed driver package (available for RHEL/Ubuntu). GPU Operator can be configured to use signed drivers: --set driver.useSignedDriver=true. Cloud GPU instances typically have Secure Boot disabled by default.

Q6

MIG Manager: You label a node nvidia.com/mig.config=all-2g.20gb. The GPU Operator's MIG manager sees the label. What happens next?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

The MIG manager: (1) drains GPU workloads from the node (cordon if needed), (2) enables MIG mode (nvidia-smi -mig 1), (3) reboots if required, (4) creates MIG instances matching the profile, (5) the device plugin detects new MIG slices and advertises them to K8s.

  MIG MANAGER — Declarative GPU Partitioning Flow:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Label node:                                      │
  │    kubectl label node dgx-01                        │
  │    nvidia.com/mig.config=all-2g.20gb                │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 2. MIG Manager watches labels → detects change      │
  │    │                                                │
  │    ▼                                                │
  │ 3. Cordons node (NoSchedule)                        │
  │    │                                                │
  │    ▼                                                │
  │ 4. Drains GPU pods (SIGTERM → SIGKILL)              │
  │    │                                                │
  │    ▼                                                │
  │ 5. Enables MIG: nvidia-smi -mig 1                   │
  │    + Reboot if needed                                │
  │    │                                                │
  │    ▼                                                │
  │ 6. Creates instances: nvidia-smi mig -cgi 14 -C ... │
  │    │                                                │
  │    ▼                                                │
  │ 7. Device Plugin detects new MIG slices              │
  │    → Advertises nvidia.com/mig-2g.20gb to kubelet   │
  │    │                                                │
  │    ▼                                                │
  │ 8. Uncordon node → Pods can schedule on MIG slices  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Declarative: you label, operator does the rest!
💡 EXPLANATION

This is declarative GPU management at its core. The operator handles the entire lifecycle — you don't SSH into nodes and run nvidia-smi commands. If MIG mode is already enabled but the profile doesn't match, the operator destroys old instances and creates new ones (draining workloads first). This can cause downtime — always plan MIG changes during maintenance windows.

Q7

🐳 GPU Feature Discovery: What does GPU Feature Discovery (GFD) add to nodes that the device plugin alone doesn't?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU-specific node labels such as GPU model, memory size, CUDA compute capability, and driver version. These enable nodeSelector/affinity for GPU-specific scheduling (e.g., "only schedule this pod on H100 nodes").

  GPU FEATURE DISCOVERY LABELS:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3   │
  │  nvidia.com/gpu.memory: 81920                    │
  │  nvidia.com/cuda.compute.major: 9                │
  │  nvidia.com/gpu.family: hopper                   │
  │  → nodeSelector: train on H100, infer on L40S    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GFD labels include: nvidia.com/gpu.product (e.g., NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3), nvidia.com/gpu.memory (e.g., 81920), nvidia.com/cuda.compute.major (9 for H100), nvidia.com/gpu.family (hopper). These enable: nodeSelector: nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-H100-80GB-HBM3 — critical for anihpj where training must run on H100 but inference can run on A100 or L40S.

Q8

🐳 GPU Validator: The GPU Operator's validator runs dcgmi diag. What does it validate and what happens on failure?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

It validates GPU health (memory, NVLink, PCIe, compute). On failure, the validator marks the GPU as unhealthy. The device plugin stops advertising that GPU, preventing new pods from being scheduled on it.

  GPU VALIDATOR — Health Check:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Level 1: Quick (~5 min) — Mem, PCIe, SM test    │
  │  Level 3: Full (~30 min) — NVLink stress, ECC    │
  │  On fail: Taint node → stop advertising GPU      │
  │  Recovery: Driver reload or RMA                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Validator runs: (1) GPU memory test (detects ECC errors), (2) NVLink bandwidth test, (3) PCIe bandwidth test, (4) SM stress test. Default runs level 1 (quick, ~5 min). Level 3 is full stress test (~30+ min). If a GPU fails, the node is tainted: nvidia.com/gpu.deployment.driver=<version>:NoSchedule. The GPU Operator then attempts recovery (driver reload) or marks for RMA. This is production-grade GPU health management.

Q9

GPU Operator Upgrade: You need to upgrade GPU Operator from v23.9 to v24.3 on anihpj production. What's the safest procedure?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Helm upgrade with node draining. (1) Cordon one GPU node: kubectl cordon dgx-01. (2) Drain GPU pods: kubectl drain dgx-01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data. (3) Helm upgrade operator: helm upgrade gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator -n gpu-operator --version 24.3.0. (4) Operator components restart on dgx-01. (5) Verify: kubectl describe node dgx-01 | grep nvidia. (6) Uncordon: kubectl uncordon dgx-01. Repeat for each node.

  GPU OPERATOR UPGRADE — Rolling Node-by-Node:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Cordon → Drain → Upgrade → Verify → Uncordon    │
  │  Repeat per node. Never upgrade all at once!     │
  │  Staging first → 1 prod node → wait 24h → roll  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU Operator components run as DaemonSets — upgrading the Helm chart triggers rolling updates. However, driver upgrades may require node reboots. The safest approach: rolling node-by-node with cordon/drain/upgrade/uncordon. Never upgrade all GPU nodes simultaneously — you'll lose all GPU capacity during the upgrade window. Staging first, then one prod node, observe for 24 hours, then roll to remaining nodes.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj GPU Operator Debug: After a power outage, anihpj pods requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 stay Pending. nvidia-smi works. GPU Operator pods are all Running. ClusterPolicy shows no errors. What's the most likely issue?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NVSwitch fabric manager not running after power cycle. While individual GPUs work (nvidia-smi), the NVSwitch topology is broken. The GPU Operator's validator may have detected this and stopped advertising GPUs. Check: systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager on DGX nodes. If inactive: sudo systemctl start nvidia-fabricmanager.

  POST-POWER-OUTAGE — GPU Operator Debug:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  nvidia-smi = OK ✅ | GPU Operator = Running ✅  │
  │  Pods Pending ❌                                  │
  │  → systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager         │
  │  → If inactive: sudo systemctl start + enable    │
  │  ★ fabricmanager often doesn't auto-start!       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

This is a real-world DGX gotcha. After power loss, nvidia-fabricmanager (separate from the GPU driver) may not auto-start. Without it, NVSwitch is down, and GPU-to-GPU topology shows PCIe instead of NV12. The GPU Operator's validator detects this degraded state. Fix: sudo systemctl enable --now nvidia-fabricmanager on all DGX nodes. Add this to your post-power-outage runbook. GPU Operator v24.3+ includes fabric manager health checks in the validator.

Chapter 9: NVIDIA Nsight Tools — Professional Profiling ⚫ Expert

You Can't Optimize What You Can't Measure

nvidia-smi tells you WHAT is happening. Nsight tells you WHY. At the Professional level, you don't guess at bottlenecks — you measure them with Nsight Systems (system-wide timeline), Nsight Compute (kernel instruction analysis), and DCGM (cluster-wide metrics). This chapter teaches you to use all three like a GPU performance engineer.

⚫ Expert ⏱️ ~3 hours 📝 10 Questions 🔍 Profiling

📋 NCP-AII Relevance

Performance analysis questions on NCP-AII follow a pattern: "Nsight shows X metric. What's the bottleneck and how do you fix it?" You must interpret roofline models, identify memory vs compute bound kernels, and know which Nsight tool to use for each scenario.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Use Nsight Systems to identify CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks
  • ✅ Apply roofline analysis in Nsight Compute to classify kernels as memory-bound or compute-bound
  • ✅ Configure DCGM profiling and Prometheus alerts for GPU clusters at scale

9.1 Nsight Systems — System-Wide Profiling

Nsight Systems provides a timeline view of your entire application: CPU threads, GPU streams, CUDA API calls, NCCL operations, and memory transfers — all on one synchronized timeline. It answers: "Where is the GPU idle and why?"

Key Metrics in the Timeline

MetricWhat It ShowsBottleneck Indicated
CUDA Kernel DurationHow long each kernel runsLong kernel = optimization candidate
CPU-GPU Sync GapsGPU idle between kernel launchesCPU is the bottleneck (data loading, Python overhead)
Memcpy H2D/D2HData transfer timeUse pinned memory, streams, or GPUDirect
NCCL OperationsMulti-GPU communication timeCheck NVLink topology, IB bandwidth
CUDA API OverheadcudaLaunchKernel, cudaMemcpy callsUse CUDA Graphs to eliminate launch overhead

🧪 LAB: Profile anihpj Training Loop

Run nsys profile --stats=true python train_anihpj.py on one epoch. Open the .qdrep file in Nsight Systems GUI. Look for: (1) GPU idle gaps between batches — if >20% of timeline, your data loader is the bottleneck, (2) NCCL all-reduce time as % of step time — target <10%, (3) CUDA API calls from Python — excessive cudaStreamSynchronize calls indicate unnecessary CPU-GPU sync.

MPI/NCCL Analysis — Communication vs Computation Overlap

In multi-GPU training, Nsight Systems shows NCCL operations (AllReduce, AllGather) as colored blocks on the GPU timeline. The key metric: communication-computation overlap ratio. If NCCL AllReduce bars appear during GPU idle periods (no kernel execution), communication is NOT overlapping with computation — you're losing performance. DDP with gradient bucketing should show NCCL starting before the backward pass completes. If NCCL starts AFTER backward finishes, bucketing isn't working — check bucket_cap_mb setting or NCCL_DEBUG for topology issues.

9.2 Nsight Compute — Kernel-Level Profiling

Nsight Compute analyzes individual kernel launches at the instruction level. It tells you: "This kernel achieves only 40% of theoretical memory bandwidth. Line 127 is the bottleneck because of uncoalesced access." This is the tool for deep kernel optimization.

Roofline Analysis — Memory-Bound or Compute-Bound?

The roofline model plots your kernel's performance on a graph of TFLOPS vs Arithmetic Intensity (FLOPs/byte). Kernels below the ridge are memory-bound; those on the ridge are compute-bound:

Roofline Model — H100 GPU
  TFLOPS ▲
  989 ─┤················································┌────────────────
       │                                              ╱  COMPUTE-BOUND
       │                                           ╱    (FP16 peak)
  800 ─┤········································╱·······················
       │                                    ╱
       │                                ╱
  600 ─┤····························╱··································
       │                          ╱
       │                       ╱
  400 ─┤····················╱··········································
       │                  ╱             ┌────┐
       │               ╱                │OPT │ ← After optimization
  200 ─┤············╱···················│HERE│   (move right & up)
       │    ┌────┐╱                     └────┘
  100 ─┤····│YOUR│····················································
       │    │KERN│   MEMORY-BOUND
    0  └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────
       0    200   400   600   800  1000  1200  1400  1600  1800  2000
                        OPERATIONAL INTENSITY (FLOPs/Byte) ▶

  • X-axis = FLOPs per byte loaded
  • Kernel BELOW ridge = memory-bound → coalesce, use shared memory
  • Kernel ON ridge = compute-bound → use Tensor Cores, FP16/FP8
  • Can only move UP (better HW) or RIGHT (better algorithm)

Memory Workload Analysis

Nsight Compute's Memory Workload section tells you: Global Load/Store Efficiency (aim >80% — low = uncoalesced), L1/L2 Hit Rate (aim >80% L1, >50% L2), Shared Memory Bank Conflicts (aim 0 — any conflicts serialize access), and DRAM Throughput (% of peak 3.35 TB/s used).

🧪 LAB: Profile anihpj Embedding Kernel with Roofline

Run ncu --set full -o profile python run_embedding.py. Open in Nsight Compute GUI. Check: (1) Roofline chart — where is the kernel? (2) Memory Workload — global load efficiency (expect <50% for naive embedding — fix with shared memory tiling). (3) Occupancy — if <50%, increase block size or reduce registers. After fixes, re-profile and verify the kernel moved right (better AI) and up (closer to the ridge).

9.3 DCGM Profiling — GPU Metrics at Scale

Nisight tools profile individual applications. DCGM profiles your entire GPU fleet 24/7 — capturing utilization, temperature, ECC errors, NVLink bandwidth, and more across hundreds of GPUs simultaneously.

Key DCGM Field IDs

Field IDMetricAlert If
203GPU Utilization (%)<20% for >1hr (GPU underused)
204Memory Utilization (%)>95% (near OOM)
205GPU Temperature (°C)>85°C (thermal throttling)
1001SM Clock (MHz)<1000 (throttled)
1002Memory Clock (MHz)Drop from baseline (throttled)
252ECC Errors (count)>0 (any ECC = investigate)
310XID Errors>0 (critical — see XID decision tree)

🧪 LAB: Set Up DCGM Profiling Alerts for anihpj

Deploy DCGM exporter + Prometheus + Grafana on the anihpj cluster. Create alerts: (1) GPU temp >85°C → PagerDuty, (2) XID error count >0 → critical alert, (3) GPU util <20% for 1 hour → warning (idle GPUs = wasted money), (4) NVLink bandwidth drop >20% → investigate fabric manager. Build a Grafana dashboard showing: GPU util heatmap (all GPUs), memory per GPU, top 5 hottest GPUs, XID error timeline.

📊 Chapter 9 Summary — Nsight Tools

⏱️
Nsight SystemsSystem timeline. Finds CPU-GPU sync gaps, NCCL time, memory transfer bottlenecks.
🔬
Nsight ComputeKernel-level. Roofline analysis, memory workload, occupancy, instruction mix.
📊
DCGMCluster-wide. 24/7 metrics → Prometheus → Grafana → PagerDuty alerts.
🎯
Exam FocusInterpret roofline, choose right tool, identify bottlenecks from metrics.
  • Gotcha #1: "GPU-Util=90% means the GPU is working hard." ❌ GPU-Util only measures kernel execution time — NOT whether the GPU is stalled waiting for memory or instructions. A kernel can show 90% GPU-Util while achieving only 30% of peak FLOPs because it's memory-bound. Always check Nsight Compute metrics BEFORE concluding performance is good.
  • Gotcha #2: "nsys and ncu are interchangeable." ❌ nsys (Nsight Systems) = timeline view (WHEN). ncu (Nsight Compute) = kernel view (WHY). The exam will present a scenario and ask WHICH tool to use first — the answer is ALWAYS nsys first (find the slow kernel), then ncu (analyze that kernel).
  • Gotcha #3: "The roofline peak is the same for all data types." ❌ The H100 roofline peak varies dramatically: FP64 ~34 TFLOPS, FP32 ~67 TFLOPS, FP16 ~989 TFLOPS, FP8 ~1,979 TFLOPS. An exam question might show a kernel at 500 TFLOPS in FP16 — looks great (50% of peak). Same kernel at 500 TFLOPS in FP8 — terrible (25% of peak). Always match the roofline to the data type.
  • ✅ Can I explain the profiling workflow: nsys first → ncu second → DCGM third?
  • ✅ Can I read a roofline chart and determine if a kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound?
  • ✅ Do I know that the H100 FP16 peak is 989 TFLOPS and FP8 peak is 1,979 TFLOPS?
  • ✅ Can I calculate Arithmetic Intensity = FLOPs ÷ bytes accessed from memory?
  • ✅ Do I know ncu --section SpeedOfLight gives the roofline analysis?

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 9 (10 Questions)

Q1

Tool Selection: anihpj training is slow. nvidia-smi shows 90% GPU-Util. Which tool should you use FIRST to find the bottleneck?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Nsight Systems. GPU-Util=90% looks healthy but hides CPU-GPU sync issues. Nsight Systems shows the timeline — you may find 10ms GPU idle gaps between each 50ms kernel (hidden by the 90% average). Nsight Compute comes AFTER you identify which kernel to optimize.

  PROFILING TOOL SELECTION:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Step 1: nsys (Nsight Systems) — WHERE is time?  │
  │   Timeline view: CPU threads + GPU kernels      │
  │   Finds: idle gaps, sync issues, load imbalance │
  │   Output: "Kernel X takes 60% of time"          │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Step 2: ncu (Nsight Compute) — WHY is it slow?  │
  │   Kernel analysis: roofline, occupancy, mem BW  │
  │   Finds: memory-bound vs compute-bound          │
  │   Output: "25% load efficiency — uncoalesced"   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Step 3: DCGM — Monitor in production            │
  │   Alert: temp, XID, util anomalies               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Profiling workflow: (1) Nsight Systems first — find WHERE time is spent (which kernels, where are the gaps), (2) Nsight Compute second — once you know WHICH kernel to optimize, analyze WHY it's slow, (3) DCGM third — for ongoing production monitoring. NCP-AII expects this workflow order.

Q2

Roofline: Nsight Compute shows anihpj embedding kernel at AI=50 FLOPs/byte, achieving 100 TFLOPS on H100. Is it memory-bound or compute-bound?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Memory-bound. At AI=50, the roofline is ~200 TFLOPS (memory bandwidth limited). Achieving only 100 TFLOPS at AI=50 confirms it's below the ridge — the kernel is waiting on memory, not compute.

  H100 ROOFLINE — FP16:
  
  TFLOPS ▲
  1000 ┤                    ┌────────── H100 Peak (989 TFLOPS)
   900 ┤                   ╱
   800 ┤                  ╱
   700 ┤                 ╱
   600 ┤                ╱  ← COMPUTE-BOUND REGION
   500 ┤               ╱     (above the ridge)
   400 ┤              ╱
   300 ┤             ╱
   200 ┤    ● ←────╱──── Ridge Point (~167 TFLOPS @ AI=50)
   100 ┤   ╱ ● ← Kernel (100 TFLOPS @ AI=50)
     0 ┤──╱────────────────────────▶ AI (FLOPs/byte)
        0   50  100  200  400  800
        │                   │
  MEMORY-BOUND          COMPUTE-BOUND
  
  🎯 At AI=50: Max from memory BW = 50 × 3.35TB/s = 167.5 TFLOPS
  🎯 Kernel achieves 100 → only 60% of memory roofline → MEMORY-BOUND
  🎯 Fix: Increase AI via shared memory → shift RIGHT on roofline
💡 EXPLANATION

H100 roofline: Memory BW = 3.35 TB/s. At AI=50, max achievable = 50 × 3.35 = 167.5 TFLOPS (FP16). Embedding lookup has inherently low AI (few FLOPs per byte). Fix: use shared memory to cache embeddings, increasing effective AI by reducing global memory reads. The kernel moves RIGHT on the roofline (higher AI), allowing higher achievable TFLOPS.

Q3

DCGM Field IDs: Which DCGM field ID monitors GPU temperature?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Field ID 205 (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP). Alert at >85°C. Field 203=GPU util, 204=memory util, 1001=SM clock, 252=ECC errors, 310=XID errors.

  DCGM ESSENTIAL FIELD IDs:
  ┌──────┬──────────────────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │  ID  │  METRIC                  │  ALERT THRESHOLD │
  ├──────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ 203  │ GPU Utilization (%)      │ <50% = idle     │
  │ 204  │ Frame Buffer Usage (%)   │ >95% = near OOM │
  │ 205  │ GPU Temperature (°C)     │ >85°C = throttle│
  │ 1001 │ SM Clock (MHz)           │ 0 = investigate │
  │ 310  │ XID Errors (count)       │ >0 = SEVERE     │
  │ 155  │ Power Draw (W)           │ >TDP = throttle │
  └──────┴──────────────────────────┴─────────────────┘
  ★ NCP-AII expects you to know at least 203-205-252-310
💡 EXPLANATION

NCP-AII expects you to know the key DCGM field IDs: 203 (utilization), 204 (memory), 205 (temperature), 252 (ECC), 310 (XID). These are the "vital signs" of GPU health. In exam scenarios, you'll be given DCGM output and asked "what's wrong?" — knowing which field means what is essential.

Q4

Nsight Systems Findings: Timeline shows: Kernel(10ms) → 5ms gap → Kernel(10ms) → 5ms gap... What's the fix?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

CPU is the bottleneck. The 5ms gaps are CPU time between kernel launches — likely data loading or Python overhead. Fix: (1) increase DataLoader workers, (2) use CUDA streams to overlap data copy with compute, (3) preload next batch while current batch runs.

  NSIGHT SYSTEMS TIMELINE — GPU Idle Gaps:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ GPU:  [████KERNEL████]░░░░░[████KERNEL████]░░░░░│
  │             10ms       5ms gap    10ms    5ms    │
  │ CPU:  [load][prep][launch][load][prep][launch]  │
  │              ▲                                    │
  │         Gap = CPU data loading (PyTorch overhead) │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ GPU util: (10+10)/(10+5+10+5) = 66%  ← NOT 90%! │
  │ (nvidia-smi smooths over time, hides gaps)       │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ FIX: num_workers=16, pin_memory=True,            │
  │      non_blocking=True .cuda()                   │
  │ IDEA: Use CUDA streams — overlap H2D with kernel │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Nsight Systems makes this obvious: CUDA kernel bars are separated by empty space = GPU idle. Look at the CPU thread timeline above — you'll see Python/data loading during those gaps. The metric "GPU idle %" directly quantifies this. For anihpj: increase num_workers from 4 to 16, enable pin_memory=True, and use non_blocking=True in .cuda() calls.

Q5

Memory Workload: Nsight Compute shows Global Load Efficiency = 25% for anihpj embedding kernel. What does this mean?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Uncoalesced memory access — 75% of bytes loaded are wasted. Each 128-byte transaction has only 32 useful bytes. Fix: reorganize data layout so adjacent threads access adjacent memory addresses.

  25% LOAD EFFICIENCY — Visualization:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 128-byte Transaction:                          │
  │ [x0░░][y0░░][z0░░][w0░░][x1░░][y1░░][z1░░]...│
  │  ████                  ████                    │
  │  USED                  USED                    │
  │  4 bytes useful out of every 16 bytes          │
  │  32/128 bytes = 25% efficiency                 │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ After SoA conversion:                          │
  │ [x0][x1][x2][x3][x4][x5][x6][x7]...[x31]      │
  │  ████████████████████████████████████          │
  │  ALL 128 bytes useful = 100% efficiency!       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

25% efficiency = 1 in 4 bytes useful. Typical cause: accessing data in Array-of-Structs format where threads read scattered fields. Fix: convert to Struct-of-Arrays (SoA). For embeddings: store as [num_jobs][768] float array where threads.x read contiguous dimension values. After fix, efficiency should jump to >90% with corresponding throughput improvement.

Q6

Roofline Strategy: Kernel is memory-bound at AI=30. Which optimization would NOT help?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Switching from FP32 to FP16. For a memory-bound kernel, reducing compute precision doesn't help — the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not compute throughput.

  MEMORY-BOUND vs COMPUTE-BOUND — What Helps:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ MEMORY-BOUND (AI < ridge):                       │
  │ ✅ Shared memory tiling     ❌ Higher SM clock   │
  │ ✅ Coalesce memory access    ❌ Use Tensor Cores  │
  │ ✅ Increase AI (more FLOPs)                       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ COMPUTE-BOUND (AI > ridge):                      │
  │ ✅ FP16/FP8/FP4              ❌ More shared mem  │
  │ ✅ Tensor Cores               ❌ Coalescing      │
  │ ✅ Higher SM clock                                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Match the fix to the bottleneck type!
💡 EXPLANATION

Memory-bound kernel fixes: (1) coalesce memory access (reduce transactions), (2) use shared memory tiling (cache data on-chip), (3) increase arithmetic intensity (do more compute per byte loaded). Compute-bound kernel fixes: (1) use Tensor Cores, (2) use FP16/FP8, (3) increase occupancy. NCP-AII tests whether you match the fix to the bottleneck type.

Q7

Profiling Command: Which command profiles a CUDA application and generates a report with kernel duration, memory throughput, and occupancy?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

ncu --set full --csv -o report python app.py — Nsight Compute CLI with full metric set. For timeline: nsys profile --stats=true python app.py (Nsight Systems).

  PROFILING COMMANDS — Quick Reference:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ nsys profile -o timeline python app.py            │
  │   → System timeline (CPU+GPU). Finds gaps.        │
  │   → .nsys-rep file → open in Nsight Systems GUI  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ncu --set basic -o report python app.py           │
  │   → Kernel metrics (occupancy, mem BW, roofline) │
  │   → --set full = ALL metrics (slower!)           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ncu --target-processes all python app.py          │
  │   → Profile ALL child processes (DDP training)   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ dcgmi dmon -e 203,204,205,252 -c 10               │
  │   → Live DCGM monitoring (10 samples)            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

ncu = Nsight Compute CLI (kernel-level). nsys = Nsight Systems CLI (system timeline). Key flags: --set full (all metrics, slower), --set basic (essential metrics, faster), --csv (machine-readable output), -o (output file). For NCP-AII: know which tool to use and basic CLI syntax. The exam may show profiling output and ask you to interpret it.

Q8

DCGM Alerts: You receive a DCGM alert: "DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS > 0 on GPU 3." What XID value indicates the GPU must be RMA'd immediately?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

XID 79 (GPU fell off bus) and persistent XID 48 (double-bit ECC). XID 79 = hardware disconnect, cannot be fixed in software. Persistent XID 48 (recurring after reboot) = memory hardware failure. Single XID 48 may be transient — monitor 24h before RMA.

  XID ERROR SEVERITY — Escalation Matrix:
  ┌─────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │ XID     │ MEANING             │ ACTION           │
  ├─────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ 79 🔴   │ GPU fell off bus     │ P1 → IMMEDIATE  │
  │         │ HW disconnect        │ Check PCIe, RMA  │
  │ 48 🟠   │ Double-bit ECC       │ P2 → Monitor 24h │
  │         │ Persistent → RMA     │ If recurs → RMA  │
  │ 74 🟠   │ NVLink error         │ P2 → Check FM    │
  │         │ Fabric manager?      │ systemctl status │
  │ 62 🟡   │ ECC page retirement  │ P3 → Monitor     │
  │         │ >100 pages = replace │ Schedule window  │
  │ 43/44🟡 │ Temp warn/Crit       │ P2/P1 → Throttle │
  └─────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────┘
  ★ ALWAYS run nvidia-bug-report.sh before RMA!
💡 EXPLANATION

XID severity: 79 = Sev1 (GPU disconnected, immediate RMA). 48 = Sev2 (ECC, monitor → RMA if persistent). 74 = Sev2 (NVLink error, check fabric manager). 62 = Sev3 (ECC page retirement, monitor count). DCGM alerts should escalate based on XID type: 79→PagerDuty critical, 48→high priority, 62→warning. Always run nvidia-bug-report.sh before RMA — NVIDIA support requires it.

Q9

NCCL Profiling: Nsight Systems shows NCCL AllReduce taking 45% of training step time on 8 GPUs. What should you investigate?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NCCL should be <10% of step time. At 45%, check: (1) nvidia-smi topo -m — are all GPUs using NV12 (NVSwitch)? (2) nvidia-fabricmanager running? (3) NCCL_DEBUG=INFO to see which algorithm (Ring vs Tree). (4) Gradient accumulation to reduce all-reduce frequency.

  NCCL OVERHEAD — Diagnosis & Fix:
  Normal (NVSwitch up):          Abnormal (NVSwitch down):
  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ [COMPUTE████ 90%]    │      │ [COMPUTE███ 55%]         │
  │ [NCCL ░ 10%]         │      │ [NCCL ██████████ 45%]    │
  │ ★ Acceptable          │      │ ★ INVESTIGATE!           │
  └──────────────────────┘      └──────────────────────────┘
  Gradient Accumulation Fix:
  Before: COMP→NCCL→COMP→NCCL→COMP→NCCL→COMP→NCCL (4×)
  After:  COMP→COMP→COMP→COMP→NCCL (1×, accumulate 4)
  → NCCL overhead: 40% → 10%
💡 EXPLANATION

45% NCCL time on 8 GPUs with NVSwitch is abnormal — suggests NVSwitch is not functioning (falling back to PCIe). Fix: sudo systemctl start nvidia-fabricmanager. Also check per-GPU bandwidth: nvidia-smi nvlink -s. Each lane should show active. If bandwidth is low on specific lanes, reseat NVSwitch cables or RMA. Gradient accumulation: accumulate 4 batches before all-reduce → NCCL called 4× less often → overhead drops to ~12%.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj Profiling: Nsight Compute shows anihpj BERT kernel has Occupancy=100%, SM Utilization=40%, Memory Utilization=95%. What's the diagnosis and fix?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Memory-bound with register spilling. 100% occupancy with 40% SM utilization = SMs are full of warps but they're ALL waiting on memory. SM Utilization=40% means only 40% of cycles have active warps executing — the other 60% are stalled waiting for data. Fix: shared memory tiling for attention mechanism, reduce global memory reads.

  PROFILING TRIANGLE — Occupancy vs SM Util vs Mem Util:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 100% Occ + 40% SM Util + 95% Mem Util            │
  │                                                   │
  │       OCCUPANCY (warps available)                 │
  │           ████████████ 100%                       │
  │       SM UTILIZATION (warps executing)            │
  │           ████ 40%                                │
  │       MEMORY UTILIZATION (BW used)                │
  │           ███████████ 95%                         │
  │                                                   │
  │  DIAGNOSIS: 100% warps alive, but only 40% run   │
  │  → 60% of warps STALLED waiting on HBM3           │
  │  → Memory bus at 95% = saturated                  │
  │  → MEMORY-BOUND!                                  │
  │  FIX: Shared memory tiling (reduce global reads)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

The combination high occupancy + low SM utilization is the classic memory-bound signature. The SMs have plenty of warps to choose from (100% occ) but none are ready because they're waiting on HBM3. Memory utilization at 95% confirms the memory bus is saturated. This is common for attention patterns — each QK^T computation reads large matrices from global memory. Tiling: load Q and K tiles into shared memory once, compute multiple output tiles from them — reduces global reads by 32×.

Chapter 10: Model Optimization for Production ⚫ Expert

From Research Model to Production Inference — The Optimization Pipeline

A PyTorch model that takes 50ms per inference in research is unusable in production. This chapter covers the three-stage optimization pipeline: TensorRT for model compilation, Triton for inference serving, and NIM for enterprise LLM deployment. Together they transform a 1.6GB PyTorch model into a 400MB optimized engine serving 1000+ requests/second.

⚫ Expert ⏱️ ~4 hours 📝 10 Questions 🚀 Production

📋 NCP-AII Relevance

Production inference optimization is a core NCP-AII topic. Expect questions about TensorRT optimization phases, Triton ensemble configuration, dynamic batching, and NIM deployment patterns. The exam tests whether you can take a model from training to production with proper optimization at each stage.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Build TensorRT engines with layer fusion, FP16/INT8 calibration, and kernel auto-tuning
  • ✅ Deploy LLMs with TensorRT-LLM using in-flight batching and quantization
  • ✅ Configure Triton ensembles and Model Analyzer for optimal inference performance
  • ✅ Deploy enterprise LLM services using NVIDIA NIM

10.1 TensorRT Deep Dive — Beyond Basic Optimization

TensorRT takes a trained model and produces an optimized inference engine through three phases: export, optimization, and deployment. The result is typically 3-10× faster with 2-4× less memory.

Phase 1: Export (PyTorch → ONNX → TensorRT)

The model flows through three formats: PyTorch (.pt) → ONNX (intermediate, 800MB) → TensorRT Engine (400MB). Use trtexec for CLI conversion or the TensorRT Python API for programmatic builds. Key flags: --fp16 (half precision), --int8 (requires calibration), --workspace=4096 (memory for tuning, MB).

Phase 2: Optimization — What TensorRT Does Under the Hood

TensorRT Optimization Pipeline

  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐       ┌─────────────────────┐       ┌──────────┐

  • INT8 Calibration: 1000 samples → dynamic range                 └──────────┘
  • Kernel Auto-Tuning: 50+ impls tried, fastest wins              anihpj API

Phase 3: Deploy (TensorRT → Triton → API)

The optimized TRT engine is loaded by Triton Inference Server. Triton handles dynamic batching, model versioning, and multi-GPU inference. The Django REST API calls Triton via gRPC or HTTP — achieving <2ms P99 latency for the anihpj job recommendation pipeline with 1000+ concurrent users.

The anihpj skill embedding layer uses a custom lookup + attention fusion not supported by default TensorRT ops. Implement an IPluginV2 that fuses the embedding table lookup with dot-product scoring. Expected: 3× speedup over separate embedding + matmul layers. Profile with trtexec --plugins=libanihpj_plugin.so.

10.2 TensorRT-LLM — LLM Inference at Scale

TensorRT-LLM extends TensorRT with LLM-specific optimizations. Key innovations: in-flight batching (continuous batching — new requests join without waiting for the current batch to finish), PagedAttention (KV-cache managed in pages, like virtual memory — eliminates fragmentation), and quantization (INT4/INT8 weight-only, SmoothQuant, AWQ — 4× memory reduction with minimal quality loss).

Multi-GPU LLM Inference

Large models (Llama-70B, 140GB) exceed single GPU memory. TensorRT-LLM supports tensor parallelism — split each transformer layer's weight matrices across GPUs, all-reduce activations between layers. With NVSwitch (900 GB/s), the all-reduce overhead is <5% of total inference time. For anihpj's Llama-3-8B job description generator: fits on single H100, no tensor parallelism needed. Target: <50ms per token, <2s for a 40-token job description.

ModelSize (FP16)GPUs NeededParallelismTokens/sec
Llama-3-8B16 GB1× H100None (fits)~120 tok/s
Llama-3-70B140 GB2× H100Tensor Parallelism~35 tok/s
Mixtral 8×7B94 GB2× H100Tensor Parallelism~50 tok/s
GPT-4 scale (1.7T)~3.4 TB8× H100TP + PP~10 tok/s

Model Analyzer — Automatic Performance Tuning

Instead of manually guessing instance counts and batch sizes, Triton's Model Analyzer automatically sweeps configurations and finds the optimal setup: model-analyzer profile --model-repository=/models --profile-models anihpj_ensemble --concurrency 1,2,4,8,16,32,64. It measures latency and throughput at each concurrency level, then reports the optimal instance group count, dynamic batching parameters, and GPU allocation.

Rate Limiting and Priority Queues — Multi-Tenant Inference

In production, different anihpj tenants (free users vs premium customers) need different QoS. Triton supports rate limiting (max requests/sec per model) and priority queues (premium requests jump ahead of free-tier requests). Configure via --rate-limit=2000 (global limit) and model config priority_levels (0=highest, 255=lowest). Premium API key → priority 0 → always served first. Free tier → priority 100 → served when capacity available. Combined with K8s ResourceQuotas per namespace, this enables production-grade multi-tenant GPU inference.

10.4 NIM in Production — Enterprise LLM Deployment

NVIDIA NIM (NVIDIA Inference Microservice) packages optimized LLMs as ready-to-deploy Docker containers. Each NIM includes: the optimized TensorRT-LLM engine, OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, health checks, Prometheus metrics, and enterprise security features — all in one container.

NIM Customization — LoRA Adapters and System Prompts

NIM supports LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters — small trainable modules that customize a base LLM without modifying its weights. For anihpj: train a LoRA adapter on HR policy documents and job description templates. The base Llama-3-8B model stays frozen; the LoRA adapter (only ~50MB) specializes it for HR tasks. NIM loads base model once, then hot-swaps LoRA adapters per request: curl -H "NIM-LORA: anihpj-hr-v2" http://nim:8000/v1/completions. Custom system prompts are set via the OpenAI-compatible API: include system role in the messages array to set context. For NCP-AII: know that LoRA enables multi-tenant LLM serving on one GPU — each tenant gets their own adapter, zero model duplication.

Q1

TensorRT Pipeline: What are the three phases of TensorRT model optimization in order?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Export (PyTorch→ONNX) → Optimization (fusion+calibration+tuning) → Deploy (TRT Engine→Triton). Export converts to ONNX. Optimization applies layer fusion, precision calibration, and kernel auto-tuning. Deploy loads the engine in Triton.

  TensorRT OPTIMIZATION PIPELINE:
  
  ┌─────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌───────────┐
  │ EXPORT  │───▶│ OPTIMIZATION │───▶│  DEPLOY   │
  │ PyTorch │    │              │    │           │
  │   ↓     │    │ 1.LayerFusion│    │Triton INF │
  │ ONNX    │    │  Conv+BN+ReLU│    │ Server    │
  │         │    │  → 1 kernel  │    │           │
  │         │    │              │    │ Dynamic   │
  │         │    │ 2.Calibration│    │ Batching  │
  │         │    │  FP32→INT8   │    │ HTTP/gRPC │
  │         │    │  1000 samples│    │           │
  │         │    │              │    │ 15ms→3ms  │
  │         │    │ 3.KernelTune │    │ (FP16)    │
  │         │    │  50+ per     │    │ 3ms→1.5ms │
  │         │    │  layer       │    │ (INT8)    │
  └─────────┘    └──────────────┘    └───────────┘
  
  🎯 Export=format change, Optimize=make fast, Deploy=serve
💡 EXPLANATION

NCP-AII expects you to know the optimization pipeline stages and what happens in each. Export: model format conversion. Optimization: TensorRT's magic — layer fusion (3 ops→1 kernel), INT8 calibration (1000 samples→dynamic range), kernel tuning (50+ per layer). Deploy: Triton loads .engine file, serves via HTTP/gRPC with dynamic batching.

Q2

INT8 Calibration: Why does INT8 quantization require a calibration dataset?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

To determine the dynamic range (min/max) of each tensor. INT8 has only 256 values — without calibration, the range maps poorly to FP32, causing large accuracy loss. Calibration runs 500-1000 representative samples through the model to find optimal per-tensor scaling factors.

  INT8 CALIBRATION — Why It's Needed:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Without calibration: [0.001...999.0] → all 256   │
  │ levels crammed into wide range = poor resolution │
  │                                                  │
  │ [0][1][2]...[127]░...░░░...░░░[128]...[255]      │
  │  Most values map to level 0-10 only!             │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ With calibration (KL divergence minimization):   │
  │ [0.001...2.5] → 256 levels spread evenly         │
  │                                                  │
  │ [0][1][2][3][4][5]...[128]...[255]               │
  │  All levels used = <1% accuracy loss!            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Calibration dataset MUST match production data
💡 EXPLANATION

INT8 maps FP32 range [min, max] → [-128, 127]. Without calibration, a single outlier can stretch the range, wasting most INT8 levels. Calibration collects activation distribution statistics, then TensorRT picks scaling factors that minimize KL divergence between FP32 and INT8 distributions. Result: <1% accuracy loss for 4× speedup. The calibration dataset MUST be representative of production data — using training data for calibration gives overly optimistic results.

Q3

In-Flight Batching: How does TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching differ from Triton's dynamic batching?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Dynamic batching waits for a batch to fill, then processes all together. In-flight batching adds/removes requests mid-batch — a new request joins immediately without waiting for the current batch to finish. This is critical for LLMs where tokens are generated one-at-a-time with variable lengths.

  DYNAMIC vs IN-FLIGHT BATCHING (LLM):
  Dynamic:                          In-Flight:
  Time →                            Time →
  Batch [A B C]████████████          Batch [A B C]███████
               ALL 3 generate                A finishes early
               same # tokens        Batch [B C D]███████
  Batch [D E F]░░░░wait░█████                   D joins mid-batch!
                                      (no waiting for batch to end)
  ❌ Slowest request blocks all       ✅ Requests come & go freely
  ★ GPU util: ~40%                    ★ GPU util: ~90% (2-3× better)
💡 EXPLANATION

LLM inference is autoregressive — each request generates tokens one by one, taking different numbers of steps. Dynamic batching would hold up all requests waiting for the slowest one. In-flight batching: when a request finishes, it leaves the batch. When a new request arrives, it joins immediately. This increases GPU utilization by 2-3× for LLM serving with variable-length generation.

Q4

Triton Ensemble: What is the PRIMARY advantage of Triton ensembles over separate model servers calling each other via HTTP?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Zero network overhead and shared GPU memory. All ensemble steps run inside one Triton process — tensors pass between models via GPU memory pointers, not HTTP serialization. This eliminates network latency (0.1-1ms per hop) and CPU-GPU memory copies.

  ENSEMBLE vs SEPARATE MODELS:
  Separate (HTTP chain):              Ensemble (in-Triton):
  ┌────┐ HTTP ┌────┐ HTTP ┌────┐     ┌─────────────────┐
  │ A  │──▶──│ B  │──▶──│ C  │     │ A → B → C       │
  │GPU │     │GPU │     │GPU │     │ GPU memory ptrs │
  └────┘     └────┘     └────┘     │ Zero copy!      │
   GPU→CPU   GPU→CPU              └─────────────────┘
   serialize  serialize             Latency: ~0ms
   Latency: 3-8ms for 3 hops       Throughput: 4×
  ❌ 3× serialization overhead     ✅ Direct tensor passing
💡 EXPLANATION

Without ensembles: Model A → serialize to JSON → HTTP → deserialize → Model B. Each hop adds 0.5-2ms. With 4 models: 3-8ms overhead. With ensembles: tensor pointer passes directly from Model A's output to Model B's input in GPU memory. Zero serialization, zero network, zero CPU involvement. For anihpj's 4-step pipeline, this saves ~5ms per request — at 1000 req/sec, that's 5 seconds of latency eliminated per second.

Q6

Model Analyzer: Triton Model Analyzer tests configuration A (2 instances, batch=16) and B (4 instances, batch=8). A gives 800 req/sec at 12ms, B gives 950 req/sec at 8ms. Which do you choose for anihpj?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

B (4 instances, batch=8). Higher throughput (950 vs 800) AND lower latency (8ms vs 12ms). More instances = more parallel processing = better for both metrics. The tradeoff is GPU memory — 4 instances consume more VRAM.

  MODEL ANALYZER — Config Comparison:
  ┌──────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
  │   CONFIG     │ Instances│ Batch Sz │ Throughput│
  ├──────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ A            │ 2        │ 16       │ 800 r/s  │
  │ B (BEST) ✅  │ 4        │ 8        │ 950 r/s  │
  └──────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
  B wins: +19% throughput, -33% latency
  Tradeoff: 4× memory (more model copies in VRAM)
  ★ More instances = more parallelism = better QPS & lat
💡 EXPLANATION

Model Analyzer sweeps instance_count × max_batch_size and reports a Pareto frontier of optimal configs. General rule: more instances = better throughput (more parallelism) but more memory. Choose the config on the frontier that meets your latency SLO with maximum throughput. For anihpj with 2ms SLO: B at 8ms is still under budget and gives 19% more throughput than A.

Q7

Layer Fusion: TensorRT fuses Conv+BatchNorm+ReLU into one kernel. Why is this faster than running them separately?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Eliminates intermediate memory reads/writes and kernel launch overhead. Three separate kernels: write output to HBM3, read it back twice (BN, ReLU). Fused kernel: compute all three in registers, write once to HBM3. Saves 2× memory bandwidth and 2× launch overhead.

  LAYER FUSION — Conv+BN+ReLU:
  SEPARATE (3 kernels):               FUSED (1 kernel):
  ┌────┐   ┌────┐   ┌────┐           ┌──────────────────┐
  │Conv│→HBM│ BN │→HBM│ReLU│→HBM      │ Conv+BN+ReLU    │
  └────┘   └────┘   └────┘           │ (all in SM regs) │
  100MB    100MB    100MB             │ →HBM (1 write)   │
  Total HBM: 500MB                    └──────────────────┘
  ❌ 3× launch overhead               Total HBM: 200MB
                                      ✅ 1× launch, 2.5× less BW
💡 EXPLANATION

Separate: Conv writes 100MB → HBM3. BN reads 100MB → computes → writes 100MB. ReLU reads 100MB → computes → writes 100MB. Total: 500MB HBM3 traffic. Fused: reads input 100MB, computes all three in registers, writes 100MB. Total: 200MB traffic = 2.5× less memory bandwidth = ~2.5× faster. Plus saves 2× CUDA kernel launch overhead (~5μs each). This is TensorRT's most impactful optimization for CNN-based models.

Q8

BLS (Business Logic Scripting): When would you use Triton BLS instead of an ensemble model?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

When you need conditional routing or dynamic model selection. BLS lets you write Python that decides which model to call next based on the current result. Ensembles have a fixed DAG — BLS enables if/else, loops, and dynamic batching decisions.

  ENSEMBLE vs BLS:
  Ensemble (fixed DAG):              BLS (dynamic routing):
  ┌───┐   ┌───┐                      ┌──────────────────┐
  │ A │──▶│ B │──▶ Result            │ if conf > 0.7:   │
  └───┘   └───┘                      │   A → B → Result │
  Always: A→B                         │ else:             │
                                      │   A → Fallback   │
                                      └──────────────────┘
  ✅ Simple, predictable              ✅ Dynamic, intelligent
  ❌ No branching                      ❌ More complex to debug
💡 EXPLANATION

Use ensemble for: fixed pipeline (always A→B→C), simple data flow, no conditionals. Use BLS for: if response confidence < 0.7 → call fallback model, different preprocessing based on input type, multi-armed bandit routing, dynamic batching decisions. BLS runs inside Triton (no network overhead) and can call any model in the repository. Example: anihpj uses BLS to route simple queries to a fast BERT model and complex queries to Llama-3-8B.

Q9

NIM Security: A NIM container exposes an OpenAI-compatible API on port 8000. How do you secure it for production?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

(1) API key authentication (set NIM_API_KEY env var), (2) TLS termination via reverse proxy (NGINX/Envoy), (3) rate limiting (NIM built-in or API gateway), (4) content filtering (NIM guardrails), (5) network policy restricting access to the NIM port.

  NIM SECURITY — Defense in Depth:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  INTERNET    │  DMZ       │  K8s CLUSTER         │
  │  ┌────────┐  │  ┌──────┐  │  ┌────────────────┐ │
  │  │Client  │──▶──│NGINX │──▶──│  NIM (port 8000)│ │
  │  │+API Key│  │  │+TLS  │  │  │  +Rate Limit    │ │
  │  └────────┘  │  │+Auth │  │  │  +Guardrails    │ │
  │              │  └──────┘  │  │  +NetPolicy     │ │
  │              │            │  └────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────┘
  Layer 1: API Key   Layer 2: TLS    Layer 3: Rate Limit
  Layer 4: Content   Layer 5: K8s NetworkPolicy
💡 EXPLANATION

NIM security layers: (1) Authentication: -e NIM_API_KEY=sk-xxx, clients include in Authorization header. (2) TLS: put NIM behind NGINX with Let's Encrypt certs. (3) Rate limiting: NIM supports per-API-key rate limits. (4) Content filtering: NIM includes NeMo Guardrails for prompt injection prevention and output filtering. (5) K8s NetworkPolicy: allow ingress to port 8000 only from the Django API pod, not externally.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj Optimization: anihpj BERT inference is 15ms on PyTorch. After TensorRT FP16 optimization: 3ms. After INT8 calibration: 1.5ms. The SLO is <5ms at 2000 req/sec. Which engine and how many Triton instances on 2 GPUs?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

FP16 engine, 3 instances per GPU (6 total) with batch=8 dynamic batching. 2400 req/sec capacity > 2000 req/sec SLO with 20% headroom.

  anihpj BERT — Sizing for 2000 req/sec:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Per-instance: batch=8, latency=3ms (FP16)        │
  │  Capacity: 8 ÷ 0.003 × 0.6 = ~1600 r/s theoretical│
  │  With queuing: ~400 r/s per instance realistic    │
  │  6 instances (3/GPU × 2 GPUs) = 2400 r/s ✅       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  FP16 (3ms) vs INT8 (1.5ms): Both meet <5ms SLO  │
  │  Choose FP16: simpler, no calib maintenance       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Throughput math: instance_capacity = batch_size ÷ latency. At batch=8, latency=3ms: 8÷0.003 = 2,667 req/sec theoretical. Realistic (with queuing): ~60% = 1,600 req/sec per instance. 2 instances: ~3,200 req/sec. FP16 is sufficient. INT8 adds complexity (calibration maintenance, accuracy risk) for marginal gain. For anihpj: 2 GPU × 2 instances each, batch=8, dynamic batching with 100μs delay = meets SLO with 40% headroom for traffic spikes.

Chapter 11: InfiniBand Fabric Design & Management ⚫ Expert

The Network IS the Computer — At GPU Scale, the Fabric Matters

When training across 32+ GPUs, the network fabric determines whether you achieve 90% scaling efficiency or 40%. InfiniBand is the standard for GPU clusters because it delivers 400 Gb/s with 1μs latency and in-network computing (SHARP). This chapter teaches you to design, tune, and manage IB fabrics — the circulatory system of AI supercomputers.

⚫ Expert ⏱️ ~3 hours 📝 10 Questions 🌐 Networking

📋 NCP-AII Relevance

IB fabric design is tested on NCP-AII: subnet manager configuration, SHARP enablement, adaptive routing, and GPUDirect RDMA. Know the difference between IB and RoCE, when to use each, and how to diagnose fabric issues.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Understand InfiniBand architecture: layers, Queue Pairs, Subnet Manager
  • ✅ Tune IB performance: MTU, adaptive routing, congestion control
  • ✅ Evaluate Spectrum-X Ethernet vs InfiniBand for AI workloads
  • ✅ Configure GPUDirect RDMA, Storage, and P2P for zero-copy data paths

11.1 InfiniBand Architecture for AI

InfiniBand is fundamentally different from Ethernet. It's a lossless, credit-based fabric designed for HPC — no packet drops, no retransmissions, guaranteed delivery. The architecture has four layers: Physical (copper/optical), Link (flow control), Network (routing), and Transport (QP connections).

IB ConceptDescriptionNCP-AII Relevance
Queue Pairs (QP)Communication endpoints. RC (Reliable Connection) for NCCL, UD (Unreliable Datagram) for management.NCCL uses RC — each GPU pair creates QPs
Subnet Manager (SM)Central controller that discovers fabric topology, assigns LIDs, computes routes. Runs opensm daemon.SM failover is critical — if SM dies, fabric freezes
Partition Keys (PKeys)IB-level network isolation. Different PKeys = cannot communicate. Like VLANs but at IB layer.Isolate anihpj prod from dev at fabric level
LID (Local ID)16-bit fabric address assigned by SM. Used for routing within a subnet.Each GPU's HCA gets a unique LID

11.2 InfiniBand Performance Tuning

MTU: Default 4KB. Increase to 8KB for large message NCCL (reduces packet overhead). Adaptive Routing: Dynamically spreads traffic across multiple paths — critical for AI workloads with burst all-reduce traffic. DCQCN: Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification — IB's congestion control for RoCE (not needed on native IB which is credit-based).

SHARP (Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol): The IB switch itself performs the reduction operation during all-reduce — GPUs send data to the switch, the switch sums it in-flight, and sends back the result. This eliminates one full round of communication, reducing all-reduce time by 2× for large messages. SHARP requires InfiniBand (not available on Ethernet).

DCQCN (Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification): Used for RoCEv2 congestion control. When a switch port is congested, it marks packets with ECN bits. The receiver sends CNP (Congestion Notification Packet) back to the sender, which reduces its injection rate. DCQCN is critical for lossless RoCE — without it, PFC storms can cascade across the fabric. Native IB doesn't need DCQCN because credit-based flow control prevents congestion at the link level.

⚡ Speed Tip

Enable SHARP on all IB switches: sharp_enable=yes in opensm.conf. Verify: ibstat shows SHARP-capable HCAs. NCCL automatically uses SHARP when available. Performance gain: 15-25% all-reduce throughput improvement with zero application changes.

11.3 Spectrum-X — AI-Optimized Ethernet

Spectrum-4 switches deliver 51.2 Tb/s with 64× 800G ports. Spectrum-X adds AI-specific optimizations: adaptive routing (spray packets across all paths), congestion control (DCQCN + ECN), and lossless RoCEv2 with PFC. Compared to standard Ethernet, Spectrum-X delivers 1.7× better AI performance for all-reduce workloads. When to choose Ethernet over IB: (1) existing Ethernet infrastructure, (2) multi-tenant cloud environments, (3) smaller clusters (<16 GPUs) where IB's latency advantage is less critical.

11.4 GPUDirect RDMA — Zero-Copy Multi-Node Communication

GPUDirect — Bypassing the CPU
  WITHOUT GPUDIRECT (CPU mediates all transfers):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐
  │ GPU  │───▶│ CPU  │───▶│ RAM  │───▶│ CPU  │───▶│ NIC  │───▶ NETWORK
  │ Mem  │    │ Copy │    │ Buf  │    │ Copy │    │ Send │
  └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘
  4 CPU copies, GPU→CPU context switch latency, CPU bottleneck

  WITH GPUDIRECT RDMA (GPU talks directly to NIC):
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────┐                              ┌──────┐
  │ GPU  │────────── DMA ──────────────▶│ NIC  │───▶ NETWORK
  │ Mem  │        (PCIe direct)         │ Send │
  └──────┘                              └──────┘
  0 CPU copies, 0 context switches, MAXIMUM BANDWIDTH

  GPUDIRECT STORAGE: GPU──DMA──▶NVMe (dataset loading, no CPU)
  GPUDIRECT P2P:     GPU0──NVLink──▶GPU1 (900 GB/s, no CPU)

GPUDirect RDMA (NIC)

GPU memory → NIC DMA → wire. Requires: ConnectX-5+, GPU and NIC on same PCIe root complex, nvidia_peermem kernel module. NCCL auto-detects and uses GDR when available.

GPUDirect Storage (NVMe)

GPU → NVMe direct via PCIe. Eliminates the CPU bounce buffer during dataset loading. cuFile API enables this in RAPIDS and custom CUDA code.

GPUDirect P2P (NVLink)

GPU-to-GPU memory access without CPU. Enabled via cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess(). On DGX with NVSwitch: 900 GB/s all-to-all.

🧪 LAB: Benchmark GPUDirect RDMA for anihpj

Run ib_write_bw -d ib0 --use_cuda between two DGX nodes. Compare with and without GDR (NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 vs 0). Expected: GDR=48 GB/s (wire speed), no-GDR=20 GB/s (CPU bottleneck).

11.5 Fabric Topologies & Subnet Management — Design at Scale

🏗️ Fat-Tree Topology — The Gold Standard for GPU Clusters

The fat-tree is the dominant topology for GPU clusters because it provides full bisection bandwidth — every GPU can talk to every other GPU at full line rate simultaneously. Here's why this matters for AI:

🔧 Subnet Manager — The Brain of the IB Fabric

The Subnet Manager (SM) is the single most critical software component in an IB fabric. Without it, the fabric is dead — no routes, no LID assignments, no communication. Here's what you must know for production:

🧠
SM Responsibilities

(1) Discovers fabric topology via sweeps, (2) Assigns LIDs to every port, (3) Calculates routes (LFT — Linear Forwarding Table), (4) Distributes routes to switches, (5) Handles fabric changes (node added/removed), (6) Manages partitions (PKeys) for multi-tenancy.

⚠️
SM High Availability

The SM is a SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE. If it crashes, the fabric continues with last-known routes for a few minutes, then goes dead. Production requires: (1) Active-Standby SM pair on different physical nodes, (2) Priority-based failover (higher priority = active), (3) opensm --priority 15 --daemon. Verify: ibstat shows "Active SM" LID. Test failover quarterly.

📊
opensm vs UFM

opensm: Open-source SM. Good for clusters <256 nodes. Configuration via /etc/opensm/partitions.conf. UFM (Unified Fabric Manager): NVIDIA's enterprise SM. Telemetry, adaptive routing, cable validation, GUI. Required for >256 node clusters. Licensed per-switch. UFM integrates with DCGM for GPU↔IB correlation.

🔍
SM Health Checks

(1) ibstat — verify "State: Active" on every port, (2) ibswitches — list all switches, (3) ibhosts — list all hosts with LIDs, (4) iblinkinfo — verify all links are "Active", (5) ibdiagnet — run weekly to detect cable errors, speed mismatches, and fabric loops. Red flag: iblinkinfo showing "Down" on any link = investigate immediately.

🛤️ Rail-Optimized Design — NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD Reference

NVIDIA's reference DGX SuperPOD design uses rail-optimized topology: each DGX's 8 ConnectX-7 NICs connect to 8 separate leaf switches (one per "rail"). All NIC 0s across all DGX nodes connect to Leaf Switch 0. All NIC 1s connect to Leaf Switch 1, etc. This creates 8 independent "rails" through the fabric:

  │     │NIC0     │NIC1     │NIC2             │NIC7                    │

🧪 LAB — Design IB Fabric for anihpj Expansion (4→8 DGX)

Objective: Design the InfiniBand fabric topology for anihpj's expansion from 4 to 8 DGX nodes. (1) Choose topology: rail-optimized with 8 leaf switches (one per rail), (2) Calculate ports: 8 DGX × 8 NICs = 64 leaf ports. Add 50% headroom = 96 leaf ports → two 64-port QM2 switches per leaf (8 pairs total), (3) Spine layer: 8 leaf switches × 16 uplinks each = 128 spine ports → 4× 64-port QM2 spine switches, (4) Verify: full bisection bandwidth? 128 spine ports at 400 Gb/s = 51.2 Tb/s bisection. 64 GPUs × 400 Gb/s = 25.6 Tb/s demand. 51.2 > 25.6 ✅, (5) Cable budget: 64 × 2 (leaf+spine) = 128 cables minimum + spares, (6) SM deployment: UFM on two dedicated management nodes (active-standby), (7) Document: topology diagram, cable map, switch config, SM failover procedure.
