📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 11 (10 Questions)

Q1

Subnet Manager: What happens to an IB fabric if the Subnet Manager (opensm) crashes?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

The fabric continues operating but no new connections can be established. Existing QPs continue working. New QP connections fail. SM failover must be configured (active-standby opensm on two nodes).

  SUBNET MANAGER — Active-Standby:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Primary: opensm --priority 10                   │
  │  Standby: opensm --priority 5                    │
  │  SM down: existing QPs OK, new QPs fail          │
  │  Failover: ~30 sec. plan for it.                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

SM handles: topology discovery, LID assignment, route computation. Once routes are set, data flows without SM. But new nodes or QP creation requires SM. Configure opensm --priority 10 on primary, --priority 5 on standby. SM failover takes ~30 seconds. During that window, no new MPI ranks or NCCL communicators can initialize.

Q2

SHARP: What is the primary benefit of SHARP for distributed training?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

In-network reduction — the switch sums gradients in-flight, eliminating one round of GPU-to-GPU communication. This reduces all-reduce time by ~2× for large messages.

  ALL-REDUCE: Without SHARP vs With SHARP
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WITHOUT SHARP (2 rounds):                       │
  │ Round 1: GPU→GPU scatter-reduce (gradients)     │
  │ Round 2: GPU→GPU all-gather (results)           │
  │ Each GPU sends & receives N-1 times             │
  │                          ┌───┐                  │
  │  ┌───┐   ┌───┐   ┌───┐   │SW │                  │
  │  │G0 │──▶│G1 │──▶│G2 │──▶│   │  (dumb switch)   │
  │  └───┘   └───┘   └───┘   └───┘                  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ WITH SHARP (1 round):                           │
  │ GPUs send → Switch SUMS → Broadcasts result     │
  │                          ┌───┐                  │
  │  ┌───┐   ┌───┐   ┌───┐   │SW │ ← SUM here!      │
  │  │G0 │──▶│G1 │──▶│G2 │──▶│ΣΣΣ│──▶ all GPUs      │
  │  └───┘   └───┘   └───┘   └───┘                  │
  │ ★ Eliminates 1 full GPU→GPU round              │
  │ ★ ~2× faster all-reduce for large messages     │
  │ ★ Only on InfiniBand (not RoCE)                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

SHARP (Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol): Without SHARP, all-reduce = scatter-reduce (GPU→GPU) + all-gather (GPU→GPU). With SHARP: GPUs send to switch → switch sums → switch broadcasts result. Eliminates one full round of GPU communication. At 256 GPUs, this saves ~40% of all-reduce time. Requires: InfiniBand (not RoCE), SHARP-capable switch (Quantum-2+), NCCL configured to use SHARP. Enabled by default when available.

Q3

IB vs RoCE: Why is native InfiniBand preferred over RoCE for GPU clusters?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Credit-based flow control (lossless by design) + SHARP support + 1μs latency. RoCE requires PFC for losslessness which is complex to configure and prone to congestion spreading.

  IB vs RoCE:
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
  │ IB               │ Credit flow ctrl, SHARP, 1μs │
  │ RoCE             │ PFC (complex), no SHARP      │
  │ >32 GPUs → IB    │ <32 GPUs → RoCE OK           │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

IB vs RoCE: IB uses credit-based flow control — receiver grants credits before sender transmits. Guarantees zero packet loss at the link level. RoCE uses PFC (Priority Flow Control) which pauses entire priority lanes when buffers fill — one slow receiver can pause traffic to ALL receivers on that lane (congestion spreading). IB also supports SHARP (in-network compute) which RoCE does not. For GPU clusters >32 GPUs, IB is strongly preferred despite higher hardware cost.

Q4

GPUDirect RDMA: What kernel module enables GPUDirect RDMA?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

nvidia_peermem. It exposes GPU BAR (Base Address Register) memory to the NIC for direct DMA access. Load with modprobe nvidia_peermem.

  GPUDirect RDMA — Data Path Comparison:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WITHOUT GPUDirect RDMA (4 copies):              │
  │ GPU0 VRAM → CPU0 RAM → NIC0 → IB → NIC1 → CPU1 │
  │  → GPU1 VRAM. 2× PCIe BW wasted. ~3× latency.  │
  │                                                 │
  │ ┌────┐  PCIe   ┌────┐  IB  ┌────┐  PCIe  ┌────┐│
  │ │GPU0│──▶CPU0──│NIC0│──▶──│NIC1│──▶CPU1──│GPU1││
  │ └────┘  2x BW  └────┘      └────┘  2x BW └────┘│
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ WITH GPUDirect RDMA (2 copies):                 │
  │ GPU0 VRAM → PCIe BAR → NIC0 → IB → NIC1 →      │
  │ PCIe BAR → GPU1 VRAM. NO CPU RAM!               │
  │                                                 │
  │ ┌────┐  DMA    ┌────┐  IB  ┌────┐  DMA   ┌────┐│
  │ │GPU0│────────▶│NIC0│──▶──│NIC1│────────│GPU1││
  │ └────┘  full   └────┘      └────┘  full  └────┘│
  │         PCIe                         PCIe       │
  │ ★ 2× bandwidth, 3× lower latency               │
  │ ★ Requires: nvidia_peermem + GDR_LEVEL=5       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPUDirect RDMA data path: GPU VRAM → PCIe BAR → NIC → IB cable → remote NIC → PCIe BAR → remote GPU VRAM. No CPU RAM involvement at any step. Requires: nvidia_peermem kernel module, NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5, IB or RoCE NIC with GPUDirect support (ConnectX-6 Dx+). Without GPUDirect RDMA: GPU→CPU RAM→NIC→network→NIC→CPU RAM→GPU (2× PCIe bandwidth wasted, 2× latency). With GPUDirect: direct GPU↔NIC DMA. Bandwidth improvement: ~2×, latency improvement: ~3×.

Q5

QP Types: Which IB Queue Pair type does NCCL use and why?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

RC (Reliable Connection). NCCL requires guaranteed, in-order delivery for gradient synchronization. RC provides hardware-level reliability with zero software overhead.

  IB QP TYPES:
  ┌──────┬──────────────────────┬───────────────────┐
  │ RC   │ Reliable, in-order   │ NCCL uses this     │
  │ UC   │ Unreliable, no retry │ Rarely used        │
  │ UD   │ Datagram, no conn    │ MPI control msgs   │
  └──────┴──────────────────────┴───────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

IB QP types: RC (Reliable Connection) = guaranteed delivery, in-order, per-QP. UC (Unreliable Connection) = no retransmission. UD (Unreliable Datagram) = no connection, no guarantee. NCCL uses RC because all-reduce correctness requires every byte delivered in order. RC achieves this with hardware-level ACK/NACK and retransmission — zero CPU overhead. Downside: RC scales O(N²) for connections (each GPU needs QP to every other GPU). At 256 GPUs, that's 65K QPs per node — manageable with modern HCAs.

Q6

Adaptive Routing: Why is adaptive routing important for AI workloads?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

All-reduce creates burst traffic patterns. Static routing sends all data through one path, creating hotspots. Adaptive routing sprays packets across all available paths, maximizing total fabric throughput.

  STATIC vs ADAPTIVE ROUTING:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Static (ECMP): hash → 1 path → hotspots        │
  │  Adaptive: spray packets → all paths → +20-40%  │
  │  ★ Required for >64 GPU clusters                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

AI traffic pattern: all-reduce creates synchronized bursts — all GPUs send simultaneously, then all receive simultaneously. Static routing (ECMP/hash-based) maps each flow to ONE path — multiple flows may collide on the same link while other links sit idle. Adaptive routing (Spectrum-X, Quantum-2) distributes packets of a single flow across multiple paths, reacting to real-time congestion. Result: 20-40% higher effective fabric throughput for AI workloads. Adaptive routing is table stakes for clusters >64 GPUs.

Q7

PKeys: How do you isolate anihpj production from development at the IB fabric level?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Assign different Partition Keys (PKeys). Prod QPs use PKey 0x8001, dev QPs use PKey 0x8002. They cannot communicate even though they share the same physical fabric.

  IB FABRIC ISOLATION — PKeys:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Prod: PKey 0x8001 | Dev: PKey 0x8002            │
  │  Different PKeys → HCA blocks communication      │
  │  ★ Hardware-level isolation on shared fabric     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

IB PKeys provide hardware-level VLAN-like isolation at the fabric level. Each QP (Queue Pair) is associated with a PKey. QPs with different PKeys cannot communicate — the HCA enforces this in hardware. PKeys are configured in /etc/opensm/partitions.conf. Production pods get PKey 0x8001 (full membership), dev pods get 0x8002 (limited membership). This prevents a misconfigured dev NCCL job from interfering with production all-reduce traffic on the same physical fabric.

Q8

Spectrum-X: What Spectrum-X feature makes it 1.7× better for AI than standard Ethernet?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Adaptive routing + dynamic congestion control. Standard Ethernet uses ECMP (static hash-based routing) which creates hotspots. Spectrum-X sprays packets across all paths and adjusts in real-time based on congestion.

  SPECTRUM-X = Ethernet for AI:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Spectrum-4 switch + BF3 DPU + adaptive routing  │
  │  1.7× better than standard Ethernet for AI       │
  │  ★ Near-IB performance on Ethernet fabric        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Spectrum-X is NVIDIA's Ethernet fabric for AI: combines Spectrum-4 switch + BlueField-3 DPU + adaptive routing + congestion control. Unlike standard Ethernet (ECMP = static hash → hotspots), Spectrum-X dynamically routes around congestion in microseconds. Result: 1.7× better AI workload performance vs standard Ethernet. Key: this enables Ethernet-based GPU clusters to approach InfiniBand performance, making AI infrastructure possible without the IB premium. Spectrum-X is positioned for enterprises that want Ethernet simplicity with near-IB performance.

Q9

GPUDirect Storage: What is the data path with GDS enabled?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU → NVMe (direct PCIe DMA). No CPU, no RAM buffer. Requires cuFile API or RAPIDS/GDS-compatible library.

  GPUDirect Storage — Data Path:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Without: NVMe→CPU→GPU (2 PCIe hops)            │
  │  With GDS: NVMe→GPU (DMA, 1 hop, zero CPU)     │
  │  ★ Checkpoints 3-5× faster                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPUDirect Storage (GDS) enables GPU memory ↔ NVMe storage direct DMA over PCIe. Traditional path: NVMe → CPU RAM → GPU VRAM (2× PCIe bandwidth consumed). GDS path: NVMe → GPU VRAM (1× PCIe, zero CPU involvement). Ideal for: training data loading (petabyte-scale datasets), checkpoint save/restore (reduces checkpoint time 3-5×). Requires: cuFile library, GDS-compatible filesystem (Weka, VAST, DDN), nvidia-fs.ko kernel module. GDS is critical for training clusters where checkpoint I/O is a bottleneck.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj IB: NCCL all-reduce is 100× slower after power outage. nvidia-smi topo -m shows PIX instead of NV12. IB fabric shows all links up. What's wrong?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

nvidia-fabricmanager not running. PIX means PCIe (64 GB/s) instead of NV12/NVSwitch (900 GB/s). The IB fabric is fine — the INTRA-node NVSwitch is the problem. sudo systemctl start nvidia-fabricmanager.

  POST-POWER-OUTAGE GPU DEBUG:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  nvidia-smi topo -m shows:                       │
  │  ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐                   │
  │  │ GPU0 │ GPU1 │ GPU2 │ GPU3 │                   │
  │  ├──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤                   │
  │  │  X   │ PIX  │ PIX  │ PIX  │ ← ❌ PCIe bridge  │
  │  │ PIX  │  X   │ PIX  │ PIX  │    NOT NVSwitch!  │
  │  │ PIX  │ PIX  │  X   │ PIX  │    64 GB/s max    │
  │  │ PIX  │ PIX  │ PIX  │  X   │                   │
  │  └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘                   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  AFTER fabricmanager restart:                    │
  │  ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐                   │
  │  │  X   │ NV12 │ NV12 │ NV12 │ ← ✅ NVSwitch     │
  │  │ NV12 │  X   │ NV12 │ NV12 │    900 GB/s       │
  │  │ NV12 │ NV12 │  X   │ NV12 │    14× faster!    │
  │  │ NV12 │ NV12 │ NV12 │  X   │                   │
  │  └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ systemctl enable nvidia-fabricmanager — ALWAYS!
💡 EXPLANATION

Post-power-outage checklist: (1) Check fabric manager: systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager — often doesn't auto-start after hard power cycle. (2) Verify NVSwitch: nvidia-smi nvlink -s (all links active?). (3) Check topology: nvidia-smi topo -m (all NV12?). Without fabric manager, NVSwitch is a dumb switch — GPUs fall back to PCIe P2P at 64 GB/s vs 900 GB/s. This is why NCCL is 100× slower — not because IB is down, but because intra-node GPU communication collapsed to PCIe speeds. Always add fabric manager to auto-start: systemctl enable nvidia-fabricmanager.

Chapter 12: Network Operator & DPU Management ⚫ Expert

K8s-Native Networking and Infrastructure Offload

Managing GPU networking at scale requires automation. The Network Operator brings K8s-native management to NICs, bonds, and SR-IOV. The BlueField DPU offloads infrastructure tasks (networking, storage, security) from the host CPU — freeing cycles for AI workloads. Together they form the programmable network fabric of modern GPU clusters.

⚫ Expert ⏱️ ~2 hours 📝 10 Questions 🐳 K8s

📋 NCP-AII Relevance

Network Operator and DPU concepts appear in NCP-AII infrastructure design questions. You must know what the Network Operator manages, SR-IOV configuration for GPU pods, and DPU use cases for infrastructure offload.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • ✅ Deploy and configure Network Operator CRDs for GPU networking
  • ✅ Configure SR-IOV and NIC bonds for AI workloads
  • ✅ Understand BlueField DPU architecture and DOCA programming model

12.1 Network Operator — K8s-Native Network Management 🐳

The Network Operator manages NVIDIA networking hardware on Kubernetes. Key CRDs: NicClusterPolicy (cluster-wide NIC configuration), MacvlanNetwork (secondary networks for pods). It configures SR-IOV (splitting one physical NIC into multiple virtual functions for direct pod access), NIC bonding (active-backup for reliability, LACP for throughput), and RoCE/IB interfaces.

SR-IOV for GPU pods: Each GPU pod gets a dedicated virtual function (VF) of the ConnectX-7 NIC — direct hardware access with near-native performance. This bypasses the kernel network stack, reducing latency from ~50μs (kernel) to ~5μs (SR-IOV). For anihpj inference pods: SR-IOV ensures consistent low-latency GPU-to-GPU communication even under load.

Networking ModeLatencyBandwidthK8s Pod MobilityUse Case
Kernel (veth+bridge)~45-50μs~90% line rate✅ MigratableManagement, low BW
SR-IOV (VF passthrough)~5μs~99% line rate❌ Static to nodeNCCL, high-perf AI
Macvlan~20μs~95% line rate⚠️ LimitedMulti-VLAN isolation
Network Operator — NIC Bonding + SR-IOV Configuration
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                ConnectX-7 NIC (Physical)                 │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐      │
  │  │      Port 0         │  │      Port 1         │      │
  │  │      400 Gb/s       │  │      400 Gb/s       │      │
  │  └──────────┬──────────┘  └──────────┬──────────┘      │
  │             └─────────┬─────────────┘                   │
  │                       │ LACP Bond (800 Gb/s total)      │
  │                       ▼                                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │              SR-IOV Virtual Functions               │ │
  │  │  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐    │ │
  │  │  │ VF0  │ │ VF1  │ │ VF2  │ │ VF3  │ │ VF4  │    │ │
  │  │  │ Pod A│ │ Pod B│ │ Pod C│ │ Pod D│ │ Mgmt │    │ │
  │  │  │ NCCL │ │ NCCL │ │ Stor │ │ Infr │ │ eth0 │    │ │
  │  │  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘    │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🧪 LAB: Deploy Network Operator on anihpj

Steps: (1) helm install network-operator nvidia/network-operator -n network-operator, (2) Apply NicClusterPolicy with SR-IOV config for ConnectX-7, (3) Create MacvlanNetwork for IB VLAN, (4) Deploy test pod with SR-IOV VF: resources.limits.nvidia.com/sriov_vf: 1. Verify: ib_write_bw -d ib0 from inside the pod should show near line-rate IB bandwidth.

12.2 BlueField DPU — Infrastructure Offload in Production

The BlueField-3 DPU is a system-on-chip combining: ARM CPU cores (16× Cortex-A78), ConnectX-7 NIC (400 Gb/s), and hardware accelerators (crypto, regex, compression). It runs its own OS (DPU OS, based on Ubuntu) and offloads infrastructure tasks from the host.

Key DPU use cases: (1) OVS offload: Virtual switching runs on DPU, freeing host CPU. (2) NVMe-oF: DPU presents remote NVMe drives as local — storage virtualization. (3) IPsec/TLS: Encryption/decryption at line rate on DPU hardware. (4) Host-management vs DPU-management: Host-managed = DPU is a PCIe device. DPU-managed = DPU owns the host (runs BMC functions). For anihpj: DPU-managed model where BlueField handles storage (NVMe-oF to WEKA cluster) and security (IPsec between DGX nodes) — saving ~4 CPU cores per DGX for AI workloads.

🧪 LAB: Configure BlueField-3 DPU for anihpj Storage Offload

Enable NVMe-oF target on DPU: modprobe nvmet; nvmetcli restore /etc/nvmet/config.json. On host: verify NVMe drives appear as local with nvme list. Expected: DPU-attached WEKA storage shows as /dev/nvme0n1 with 30GB/s throughput. Measure CPU utilization on host during I/O — should be <5% (DPU handles all storage processing). Compare: without DPU offload, CPU would be 30-40% during dataset loading.

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 12 (10 Questions)

Q1

Network Operator CRD: Which CRD controls cluster-wide NIC configuration?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NicClusterPolicy. It defines NIC configuration (bonds, SR-IOV, RoCE) for all GPU nodes. Applied once, enforced everywhere.

  Network Operator CRDs — What They Manage:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ NicClusterPolicy (cluster-scoped)                │
  │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ bond.mode: lacp        (LACP vs active-bkup) │ │
  │ │ bond.miimon: 100       (link check interval) │ │
  │ │ sriov.numVFs: 8        (per NIC VFs)         │ │
  │ │ roce.enable: true      (RoCE for Ethernet)   │ │
  │ │ mtu: 9000              (jumbo frames)        │ │
  │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │ → Applied to ALL matching GPU nodes              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ MacvlanNetwork (namespace-scoped)                │
  │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ masterInterface: bond0                        │ │
  │ │ vlan: 100              (IB fabric VLAN)       │ │
  │ │ networkNamespace: gpu-workloads               │ │
  │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │ → Pod gets SECOND interface for IB traffic      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NicClusterPolicy is a cluster-scoped CRD. Define once: bond mode (LACP), SR-IOV VF count, RoCE configuration, MTU. GPU Operator applies it to all nodes with matching labels. Benefits: consistent NIC config across 100+ DGX nodes, declarative (git-ops friendly), automatically reconciles drift. If someone manually changes a NIC setting, the operator reverts it within seconds.

Q2

SR-IOV Benefit: Why use SR-IOV instead of kernel networking for GPU pods?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

10× lower latency (~5μs vs ~50μs) and near-native bandwidth. SR-IOV gives pods direct hardware access to a NIC virtual function, bypassing the kernel network stack.

  KERNEL vs SR-IOV:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Kernel: pod→veth→bridge→iptables→NIC = ~45μs   │
  │  SR-IOV: pod→VF→NIC hardware = ~5μs            │
  │  ★ 10× faster. NCCL: 1000 msgs = 45ms vs 5ms   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Kernel networking path: pod → veth → bridge → iptables → routing → qdisc → NIC driver → hardware. ~45μs overhead. SR-IOV path: pod → VF PCIe passthrough → NIC hardware. ~5μs. For GPU inference at P99<10ms, 45μs is 0.5% overhead. But for NCCL all-reduce with thousands of small messages, 45μs × 1000 messages = 45ms = 5% of a 1-second training step. SR-IOV eliminates this tax. Trade-off: SR-IOV VFs are static — cannot migrate between nodes like veth pods.

Q3

DPU Architecture: What are the three main components of a BlueField DPU?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

ARM CPU cores + ConnectX NIC + hardware accelerators (crypto, regex, compression). It's a complete SoC with its own OS.

  BlueField-3 DPU Architecture:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              BlueField-3 DPU SoC                  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ 16× ARM A78      │  │  ConnectX-7 NIC        │ │
  │ │ @ 2.5 GHz        │  │  400 Gb/s IB/Eth       │ │
  │ │ 32 GB DDR5       │  │  RDMA, RoCE, GPUDirect │ │
  │ └──────────────────┘  └────────────────────────┘ │
  │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │       HARDWARE ACCELERATORS                   │ │
  │ │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ │ │
  │ │  │ IPsec  │ │  TLS   │ │ NVMe-oF│ │Regex  │ │ │
  │ │  │ 400Gb/s│ │ 400Gb/s│ │  init  │ │engine │ │ │
  │ │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └───────┘ │ │
  │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │ Runs Ubuntu + DOCA SDK. Boots BEFORE host.       │
  │ Host sees it as: PCIe device OR management root  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

BlueField-3 DPU: 16 ARM Cortex-A78 cores, ConnectX-7 NIC (400 Gb/s), HW accelerators (IPsec, TLS, NVMe-oF, regex, compression), 32GB DDR5, runs Ubuntu/DOCA. It's a self-contained computer on a PCIe card. Key use: offload infrastructure tasks (networking, storage, security) from the host x86 CPU — freeing 15-20% CPU cycles for AI workloads. DPU boots its own OS BEFORE the host — enabling secure boot attestation and bare-metal provisioning.

Q4

NIC Bonding: Which bond mode for AI training: active-backup or LACP?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

LACP (802.3ad) for throughput. AI training needs maximum bandwidth — LACP aggregates both ports. Active-backup only uses one port at a time and is for reliability, not throughput.

  NIC BONDING — GPU Nodes:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LACP: 2 ports aggregated = 2× BW = 800 Gb/s ✅ │
  │  Active-Backup: 1 active, 1 standby = no gain   │
  │  AI training → LACP. Management → active-backup  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Bond modes for GPU: LACP bundles both NIC ports = 2× bandwidth (800 Gb/s with dual ConnectX-7). Active-backup = 1 port active, 1 standby = no bandwidth gain. For AI training: always LACP. For management network: active-backup is fine. Configure via NicClusterPolicy: bond.mode=lacp, bond.miimon=100 (link monitoring every 100ms). LACP requires switch support (port-channel on Cisco, LAG on Arista).

Q5

DPU Deployment: What's the difference between host-managed and DPU-managed deployment?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Host-managed: DPU appears as a PCIe device, host controls it. DPU-managed: DPU owns the host (BMC functions, power control), host is a peripheral. DPU boots first, then powers on the host.

  DPU DEPLOYMENT MODES:
  ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │   HOST-MANAGED          │  │   DPU-MANAGED           │
  │   (Smart NIC model)     │  │   (Control plane model) │
  ├─────────────────────────┤  ├─────────────────────────┤
  │ ┌─────┐  PCIe  ┌─────┐ │  │ ┌─────┐        ┌─────┐ │
  │ │HOST │──────▶│ DPU │ │  │ │ DPU │────────│HOST │ │
  │ │x86  │ slave │ ARM │ │  │ │ ARM │ master │x86  │ │
  │ └─────┘       └─────┘ │  │ └─────┘        └─────┘ │
  │                       │  │   ▲ Boots FIRST   │      │
  │ Host: "I see a PCIe   │  │   │ Powers on host│      │
  │  device at 04:00.0"   │  │   ▼              ▼      │
  │ Host controls DPU     │  │ DPU: "I own this server"│
  │ Simple, no arch.      │  │ DPU = BMC + NIC + Sec  │
  │ changes needed        │  │ Zero-trust foundation  │
  └─────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Current standard       ✅ Future direction
💡 EXPLANATION

Host-managed: DPU is a smart NIC — host OS sees it as a PCIe device, loads drivers, offloads tasks to it. Simpler, no architectural changes. DPU-managed: DPU is the control plane — it boots first, runs its own OS, then powers on the host. The host's BMC functions are handled by the DPU. This enables: secure boot attestation before host power-on, bare-metal provisioning via DPU, complete host isolation (DPU filters all traffic before it reaches host). DPU-managed is the future direction for zero-trust GPU infrastructure.

Q6

NVMe-oF: How does a BlueField DPU enable NVMe-oF for GPU clusters?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

DPU presents remote NVMe drives as local block devices via NVMe-oF initiator. The host sees local NVMe drives; the DPU handles the network transport transparently.

  NVMe-oF via DPU:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Storage → RDMA → DPU → /dev/nvme0n1 (local!)   │
  │  Host: "I see local NVMe" (DPU hides network)   │
  │  ★ 90%+ local perf, zero host CPU for storage   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NVMe-oF via DPU: Storage server exports NVMe drives over RDMA (NVMe-oF target). DPU on GPU node connects as NVMe-oF initiator. DPU presents remote drives as local /dev/nvmeXnY block devices to the host. Host uses them like local NVMe — no special drivers, no CPU overhead for storage networking. Benefit: disaggregated storage (GPUs and storage scale independently), 90%+ of local NVMe performance, zero host CPU for storage I/O. Critical for AI factories where training data is petabytes and must be shared across all DGX nodes.

Q7

DOCA: What is DOCA and what does it provide?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

DOCA (Data Center Infrastructure-on-a-Chip Architecture) is the SDK for BlueField DPUs. It provides libraries (DOCA Flow for packet processing, DOCA Comms for RDMA) and runtime services.

  DOCA = CUDA for DPUs:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Flow (SDN) | Comms (RDMA) | Storage (NVMe-oF)  │
  │  Security (IPsec/TLS) | Mgmt (BMC)              │
  │  ★ ARM cores + HW accelerators = full SDK       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

DOCA = CUDA for DPUs. Just as CUDA enables GPU programming, DOCA enables DPU programming. Components: DOCA Flow (software-defined networking pipeline), DOCA Comms (RDMA, UCX), DOCA Storage (NVMe-oF, compression), DOCA Security (IPsec, TLS, stateful firewall), DOCA Management (BMC, provisioning). Developers write DOCA applications that run on the DPU's ARM cores with hardware acceleration. Key for NCP-AII: know that DOCA is the DPU SDK and what it provides.

Q8

🐳 MacvlanNetwork: What does this Network Operator CRD enable?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Secondary network interfaces for pods. Beyond the default K8s pod network, MacvlanNetwork creates additional interfaces (e.g., dedicated IB VLAN) attached directly to pods.

  MacvlanNetwork — Dual Network Pods:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  eth0 = cluster network (management, low BW)     │
  │  net1 = IB VLAN (NCCL traffic, 400 Gb/s)        │
  │  ★ Pod gets SECOND interface for high-speed AI  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

K8s pods normally have ONE network interface (eth0, cluster network). MacvlanNetwork CRD adds a SECOND interface (net1) directly to the pod — this can be on a separate VLAN (IB fabric, storage network, management). GPU pods get: eth0 = cluster network (management, low-bandwidth), net1 = IB VLAN (NCCL traffic, 400 Gb/s). Configured via Network Attachment Definition + MacvlanNetwork CRD. Pod spec requests: k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: anihpj-ib-network.

Q9

DPU Security: What security benefit does DPU offload provide?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Line-rate IPsec/TLS without host CPU usage. Encryption runs on DPU hardware accelerators — the host never sees encryption keys. This enables zero-trust networking with zero performance impact on AI workloads.

  DPU SECURITY — Zero-Trust GPU Networking:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  All traffic → DPU → encrypt → wire             │
  │  Host NEVER sees keys. Compromised host = safe.  │
  │  ★ Line-rate 400Gb/s IPsec/TLS, zero CPU cost   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

DPU security model: All network traffic passes through DPU before reaching host. DPU performs line-rate IPsec/TLS encryption in hardware — host CPU is never involved and never sees encryption keys. Even if the host is compromised, the attacker cannot: read encrypted traffic, access storage encryption keys, or bypass the DPU firewall. This enables true zero-trust: every GPU-to-GPU communication is encrypted and authenticated at the hardware level with zero performance penalty. Critical for multi-tenant and regulated GPU environments.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj: anihpj inference pods experience 50μs latency between GPU pods. Switching to SR-IOV drops it to 5μs. Why is the kernel path 10× slower?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Kernel path goes through Linux network stack (sk_buff allocation, netfilter, routing, qdisc) adding ~45μs overhead. SR-IOV bypasses the kernel — the VF talks directly to the NIC hardware.

  KERNEL vs SR-IOV LATENCY:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Kernel:  socket→TCP→netfilter→qdisc→NIC = 45μs │
  │  SR-IOV:  userspace→VF doorbell→NIC = 5μs      │
  │  NCCL 10K msgs: 450ms vs 50ms = 400ms saved!   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Kernel vs SR-IOV latency breakdown: Kernel path: app→socket (2μs)→TCP/IP stack (5μs)→netfilter (3μs)→routing (2μs)→qdisc (5μs)→driver (8μs)→DMA (5μs)→NIC→wire = ~45μs. SR-IOV path: app→userspace driver (1μs)→VF doorbell (1μs)→NIC DMA (3μs)→wire = ~5μs. For anihpj inference at 1000 req/sec, 45μs vs 5μs is negligible per-request. But for NCCL all-reduce with 10,000 small messages per step, the difference is 450ms vs 50ms — nearly half a second per training step. At 1M training steps, that's 111 hours of wall-clock time saved. SR-IOV matters at scale.

Chapter 13: GPU Cluster Lifecycle Management 🔴 Advanced

From Bare Metal to Production — The Full GPU Cluster Lifecycle

GPU clusters aren't static — they're living systems that must be provisioned, upgraded, maintained, and eventually decommissioned. This chapter covers the full lifecycle: PXE-booting DGX nodes, deploying GPU Operator, executing zero-downtime upgrades, and securely decommissioning hardware. These are the operational skills that separate GPU SREs from GPU users.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3 hours 📝 10 Questions 🐳 K8s Ops

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Provision a DGX from bare metal: PXE boot → DGX OS → BCM → GPU Operator → validation
  • ✅ Execute zero-downtime GPU driver upgrades using cordon→drain→upgrade→uncordon
  • ✅ Apply firmware updates in the correct order: BMC → NVSwitch → GPU → NIC
  • ✅ Validate provisioned hardware: dcgmi diag, NCCL bandwidth test, MLPerf submission
  • ✅ Decommission DGX nodes securely: secure erase NVMe/GPU/TPM, K8s node deletion
  • ✅ Plan GPU refresh cycles: 3-4yr training, 5-7yr inference — based on TFLOPS/watt trends

🔑 Exam Tip — Cluster Lifecycle

The NCP-AII exam tests your ability to orchestrate the full GPU cluster lifecycle. Key exam scenarios: (1) Given a blank DGX, walk through provisioning steps in order — PXE boot FIRST, then BCM registration, then GPU Operator. (2) Given a driver upgrade scenario, explain why --ignore-daemonsets is required when draining. (3) Given a decommissioning scenario, identify the three assets that must be securely erased. Expect 4-5 questions from this chapter, primarily scenario-based.

13.1 Provisioning — Bare Metal to Production 🐳

DGX provisioning workflow: (1) PXE boot DGX node with DGX OS ISO, (2) Register in Base Command Manager (BCM), (3) Deploy GPU Operator via Helm, (4) Run validation suite: dcgmi diag -r 3 (full stress test, 30+ min), NCCL all_reduce_perf across all GPUs, MLPerf submission for baseline. (5) Node joins K8s cluster: kubeadm join → GPU Operator auto-deploys drivers → device plugin registers GPUs → node is Ready with nvidia.com/gpu: 8.

🐳 anihpj cluster bootstrap: kubeadm init → install Calico CNI → helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator → helm install network-operator nvidia/network-operator → join worker nodes → verify with kubectl get nodes -o wide and kubectl describe node dgx-01 | grep nvidia.

13.2 Upgrades and Maintenance 🐳

Rolling upgrade strategy: (1) Cordon: kubectl cordon dgx-01, (2) Drain GPU pods: kubectl drain dgx-01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data, (3) Upgrade driver/firmware, (4) Reboot if required, (5) Validate: nvidia-smi + dcgmi diag -r 1 (quick check, 5 min), (6) Uncordon: kubectl uncordon dgx-01. Repeat for each node. Blue-green: Build new K8s cluster with upgraded stack, migrate workloads, decom old cluster — zero risk but requires spare hardware.

Firmware update ordering: BMC → NVSwitch → GPU → NIC. Always check NVIDIA's firmware compatibility matrix — mismatched NVSwitch/GPU firmware causes XID 74 errors. Post-upgrade: run anihpj training benchmark to verify performance hasn't regressed.

🧪 LAB — Zero-Downtime GPU Driver Upgrade on K8s

Objective: Upgrade GPU driver from 535→550 on dgx-03 without interrupting anihpj inference traffic on other nodes. (1) kubectl cordon dgx-03, (2) kubectl drain dgx-03 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data, (3) Install new driver + reboot, (4) Verify nvidia-smi and dcgmi diag -r 1, (5) kubectl uncordon dgx-03. 🐳 Bonus: Script this as a K8s Job that automates steps 1-5 with pre/post validation checks.

13.3 Decommissioning & Hardware Lifecycle

GPU end-of-life indicators: (1) Warranty expiration (3 years for DGX), (2) Performance degradation (ECC retirement >100 pages), (3) Power efficiency vs newer GPUs (H100 is 3× more TFLOPS/watt than A100). Secure erase procedure: (1) nvme format -s1 /dev/nvme0n1 (crypto erase), (2) nvidia-smi --gpu-reset (clear GPU memory), (3) TPM clear for attestation reset. Refresh cycle: Training GPUs: 3-4 years. Inference GPUs: 5-7 years. Decommissioned GPUs: repurpose for dev/CI or return via NVIDIA recycling program.

🐳 K8s decommissioning: kubectl drain dgx-old --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data → kubectl delete node dgx-old → physically remove hardware → update inventory.

13.4 Automated Lifecycle Management — IaC for GPU Clusters

🤖 Why Manual GPU Cluster Management Doesn't Scale

At 4 DGX nodes, manual provisioning works. At 40 nodes, it's error-prone. At 400 nodes, it's impossible. Every manual step — SSH, driver install, config edit — is a source of drift that accumulates silently until something breaks at 3 AM. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) eliminates this drift by making every configuration declarative and reproducible.

📈 Capacity Planning — When to Add More GPUs

📊
Utilization Trigger

>80% sustained GPU utilization over 2 weeks = order more GPUs. At 80%, you have ~2 months of growth headroom before GPUs bottleneck. Ordering takes 8-12 weeks for DGX. Don't wait until 95% — you'll be capacity-constrained for months.

⏱️
Queue Depth Trigger

Average queue wait time > 30 minutes for training jobs = add GPUs. Track via Run:ai or Slurm scheduling metrics. If data scientists routinely wait hours for GPU access, they'll buy cloud GPUs on corporate cards — defeating FinOps controls.

💰
Cost Trigger

Cloud GPU spend > 6 months of on-prem DGX TCO = buy DGX. Track cloud GPU spend monthly. If you're spending $500K/year on cloud GPUs, a $2M DGX cluster pays for itself in 4 years and provides 3× more compute.

🔮
Roadmap Trigger

Planned model 2× larger = order GPUs 6 months before. LLM scaling laws: every generation is ~10× larger. If your team plans to train a 70B model (currently fine-tuning 7B), you'll need 10× more compute. Budget and order accordingly.

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 13 (10 Questions)

Q1

Provisioning Order: What is the correct order for DGX provisioning on K8s?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

PXE boot DGX OS → BCM registration → GPU Operator → validation → join K8s. GPU Operator must deploy before the node joins K8s (or immediately after) so the device plugin registers GPUs.

  DGX PROVISIONING FLOW:
  ┌──────┐   ┌──────┐   ┌───────┐   ┌──────┐   ┌──────┐
  │ PXE  │──▶│ BCM  │──▶│  GPU  │──▶│VALID.│──▶│ JOIN │
  │ Boot │   │ Reg. │   │  Op.  │   │DCGM+ │   │ K8s  │
  │      │   │      │   │ Helm  │   │ NCCL │   │      │
  └──────┘   └──────┘   └───────┘   └──────┘   └──────┘
  Step 1      Step 2      Step 3      Step 4     Step 5
  MUST be first —        GPU Op auto-  dcgmi      kubeadm
  installs DGX OS         deploys:    diag -r 2    join
                          driver +    + NCCL      node
                          toolkit +    perf test  Ready
                          device                  with
                          plugin                  GPU:8
💡 EXPLANATION

PXE boot must come first — without an OS, nothing works. BCM registration enables fleet management. GPU Operator auto-deploys driver + toolkit + device plugin — without it, K8s doesn't know GPUs exist. Validation (dcgmi diag -r 2) catches DOA hardware. Never uncordon a node before validation passes — a node with failing GPUs in production causes cascading workload failures.

Q2

Upgrade Safety: Why cordon+drain before GPU driver upgrade?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Prevents new pods from scheduling and safely evicts running pods before the driver reload (which would crash any running GPU processes).

  GPU UPGRADE FLOW:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Cordon → Drain → Upgrade → Reboot → Validate   │
  │  → Uncordon. Without drain: all GPU pods crash!  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Cordon marks a node unschedulable (no NEW pods). Drain evicts EXISTING pods gracefully (SIGTERM → 30s → SIGKILL). A GPU driver reload requires unloading/reloading the nvidia kernel module — which instantly kills all processes with open GPU file descriptors. Without drain: every GPU pod crashes with "CUDA error: unknown error" or worse, leaves GPU memory in an inconsistent state. Always: cordon → drain → upgrade → validate → uncordon.

Q3

Validation: What does dcgmi diag -r 3 test vs -r 1?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

-r 1 (quick, 5 min): basic GPU detection, memory check, PCIe. -r 3 (full, 30+ min): comprehensive stress test including NVLink bandwidth.

  DCGM DIAG LEVELS:
  ┌──────┬──────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
  │ -r 1 │ 5 min    │ Post-upgrade, quick sanity     │
  │ -r 2 │ 10 min   │ SM stress, memory BW           │
  │ -r 3 │ 30+ min  │ NVLink, ECC, thermal (new HW)  │
  │ -r 4 │ 1+ hour  │ Exhaustive (pre-RMA)           │
  └──────┴──────────┴───────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

DCGM diagnostic levels: -r 1 = quick sanity check (PCIe link, GPU visible, basic memory). Use for post-upgrade validation. -r 2 = medium (~10 min, adds SM stress, memory bandwidth). -r 3 = full (~30 min, NVLink stress, ECC test, thermal). Use for new hardware burn-in. -r 4 = exhaustive (1+ hour, every diagnostic). Use before RMA submission. Always run -r 1 after any hardware change; -r 3 before declaring a node production-ready.

Q4

Firmware Order: What's the correct firmware update order on a DGX?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

BMC → NVSwitch → GPU → NIC. BMC first (manages everything). NVSwitch before GPU (GPU depends on NVSwitch). NIC last (independent).

  FIRMWARE UPDATE ORDER — DEPENDENCY CHAIN:
  ┌──────────┐
  │ 1. BMC   │◄── Manages power, thermals, all components
  └────┬─────┘
       │ Must be done FIRST — controls everything below
       ▼
  ┌──────────┐
  │2.NVSwitch│◄── GPU-to-GPU fabric (NVLink switch)
  └────┬─────┘
       │ GPU firmware depends on NVSwitch firmware
       ▼
  ┌──────────┐
  │ 3. GPU   │◄── GPU VBIOS/firmware
  └────┬─────┘
       │ NIC is independent of GPU firmware
       ▼
  ┌──────────┐
  │ 4. NIC   │◄── ConnectX-7/8 IB cards
  └──────────┘

  ❌ WRONG: GPU → NVSwitch → BMC  (GPU breaks NVLink!)
  ✅ RIGHT: BMC → NVSwitch → GPU → NIC
💡 EXPLANATION

Firmware update order follows the hardware dependency chain. BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) is the root — it manages power, thermals, and all other components. NVSwitch firmware must be updated before GPU firmware because the GPU's NVLink interface negotiates with the NVSwitch at boot. NIC is independent (PCIe endpoint, not on NVLink fabric) so it goes last. Wrong order = NVLink fabric mismatch = GPUs can't see each other. Always: nvfw update --type bmc → nvfw update --type nvswitch → nvfw update --type gpu → nvfw update --type nic.

Q5

K8s Drain: Why use --ignore-daemonsets when draining a GPU node?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU Operator components run as DaemonSets. Without --ignore-daemonsets, drain would try to evict driver/toolkit/device-plugin pods — which can't be evicted (must run on every GPU node).

  K8s DRAIN — GPU Nodes:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MUST: --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data│
  │  Without: drain HANGS trying to evict DS pods   │
  │  GPU Op = DaemonSet: driver, toolkit, plugin     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

DaemonSets ensure one pod per node. GPU Operator deploys: nvidia-driver-daemonset, nvidia-container-toolkit-daemonset, nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset. These MUST run on every GPU node for GPUs to be available. Without --ignore-daemonsets, kubectl drain waits forever trying to evict them (they get recreated immediately by the DaemonSet controller). Always use --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data together when draining GPU nodes.

Q6

Secure Erase: What must be erased when decommissioning a DGX?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NVMe drives (crypto erase), GPU memory (nvidia-smi --gpu-reset), TPM (clear). All three contain sensitive data — models on NVMe, intermediate computations in GPU memory, attestation keys in TPM.

  DGX SECURE DECOMMISSIONING — THREE ASSETS:
  
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               DGX H100 NODE                  │
  │                                              │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  │
  │  │  NVMe    │  │   GPU    │  │   TPM    │  │
  │  │  Drives  │  │  Memory  │  │  Chip    │  │
  │  │          │  │          │  │          │  │
  │  │ Contains:│  │ Contains:│  │ Contains:│  │
  │  │ • Models │  │ • Tensors│  │ • Attest │  │
  │  │ • Data   │  │ • Grads  │  │   Keys   │  │
  │  │ • Check- │  │ • Embed- │  │ • Secure │  │
  │  │   points │  │   dings  │  │   Boot   │  │
  │  │          │  │          │  │   State  │  │
  │  │ Erase:   │  │ Erase:   │  │ Erase:   │  │
  │  │ nvme     │  │ nvidia-  │  │ tpm2_    │  │
  │  │ format   │  │ smi --   │  │ clear    │  │
  │  │ -s1      │  │ gpu-reset│  │          │  │
  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  ❌ FORGETTING ONE = DATA BREACH = AUDIT FAILURE
💡 EXPLANATION

Secure decommissioning is a compliance requirement (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR). Three data-bearing assets: (1) NVMe drives — use crypto erase (nvme format -s1) which rotates the internal encryption key in seconds, rendering all data unrecoverable. (2) GPU memory — volatile HBM, but residual data can persist for seconds after power-off; nvidia-smi --gpu-reset clears all contexts. (3) TPM — stores attestation keys and secure boot state; tpm2_clear resets to factory state. Document decommissioning with serial numbers + timestamps for audit trail. Never decommission without clearing all three — a single missed GPU could leak model weights.

Q7

Refresh Cycle: What's the typical GPU refresh cycle for training vs inference?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Training: 3-4 years. Inference: 5-7 years. Training needs latest Tensor Cores and FP8/FP4. Inference is more tolerant of older GPUs — an A100 still serves models well.

  GPU REFRESH CYCLES:
  ┌────────────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │ Training       │ 3-4 yr   │ Needs latest TC + FP8/4 │
  │ Inference      │ 5-7 yr   │ Memory-BW still adequate│
  │ Decision: TFLOPS/watt improvement → refresh sooner │
  └────────────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Training workloads are compute-bound and benefit directly from new Tensor Core generations (FP8 on H100 gives 2× speedup over A100 FP16). Inference is often memory-bandwidth-bound — the A100's 2.0 TB/s HBM2e is still adequate for many models. Refresh decisions should be driven by TFLOPS/watt improvements: H100 is ~3× more efficient than A100. If power costs dominate, refresh sooner. If capex is constrained, keep inference GPUs longer.

Q8

MLPerf: Why run MLPerf after provisioning?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Establishes baseline performance. MLPerf results are reproducible and comparable — if your DGX scores 20% below reference, something is wrong (cooling, NVSwitch, driver).

  MLPerf POST-PROVISIONING:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Run MLPerf → compare to DGX reference scores    │
  │  20% below? → Check NVSwitch, IB BW, cooling    │
  │  ★ Catches issues nvidia-smi misses             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

MLPerf is the industry-standard AI benchmark. It tests realistic workloads (BERT, ResNet, GPT-3) under controlled conditions. Every DGX ships with MLPerf reference scores. If your cluster scores significantly below reference: (1) check NVSwitch fabric manager is running, (2) verify InfiniBand bandwidth with ib_write_bw, (3) check GPU clock speeds under load (should hit boost clocks), (4) verify cooling is adequate (thermal throttling silently degrades performance). MLPerf catches issues that simple nvidia-smi checks miss.

Q9

Driver Rollback: After a driver upgrade causes XID errors, what's the rollback procedure?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Cordon → drain → uninstall new driver → install previous version → reboot → validate → uncordon. GPU Operator supports driver rollback via ClusterPolicy version pinning.

  DRIVER ROLLBACK:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ClusterPolicy: driver.version: "535" (revert)  │
  │  If XID persists after rollback → GPU damaged   │
  │  → RMA case, not rollback case                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Driver rollback is essentially the same as upgrade but in reverse. GPU Operator's ClusterPolicy CRD specifies the driver version — change driver.version: "550" back to "535" and the Operator handles the downgrade. Key: always validate with dcgmi diag -r 1 after rollback. If XID errors persist after rollback, the GPU was physically damaged by the bad driver — it's now an RMA case, not a rollback case. Document the incident for NVIDIA support.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj: anihpj needs to expand from 4 to 8 DGX. 2 new DGX arrive. Walk through adding them to the K8s cluster.

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

(1) Rack, cable (IB + Ethernet + power), (2) PXE boot DGX OS, (3) Register in BCM, (4) kubeadm join, (5) GPU Operator auto-deploys on new node, (6) Validate with dcgmi diag -r 2, (7) Uncordon node. New GPUs appear as allocatable resources.

  anihpj EXPANSION — 4→8 DGX:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Rack→PXE→BCM→kubeadm join→GPU Op→Validate→Ready│
  │  ★ Don't uncordon until dcgmi diag passes!       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Cluster expansion tests your end-to-end provisioning knowledge. Physical steps first (rack, cable, power — if these fail, nothing works). Then OS (PXE boot). Then management (BCM for fleet monitoring). Then orchestration (kubeadm join integrates with existing control plane). GPU Operator watches for new nodes and auto-deploys. Validation is critical: don't uncordon until dcgmi diag passes. A node with failing GPUs uncordoned too early will crash production workloads.

Chapter 14: Observability — Monitoring, Logging, Alerting 🔴 Advanced

You Can't Fix What You Can't See — GPU Observability at Scale

Running 32 GPUs without monitoring is flying blind. Running 32,000 without it is negligence. This chapter covers the GPU observability stack: DCGM for metrics collection, Prometheus+Grafana for dashboards and alerting, and distributed tracing for end-to-end visibility into GPU workloads.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📝 10 Questions

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Configure custom DCGM profiles — select the right metrics at the right sampling intervals
  • ✅ Build production Grafana dashboards: GPU heatmap, memory/temp, XID timeline, NVLink bandwidth
  • ✅ Define SLOs for GPU infrastructure: 99.9% GPU availability, <1% XID error rate
  • ✅ Implement GPU RED metrics: Rate (throughput), Errors (XID/ECC), Duration (kernel time)
  • ✅ Set up distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry — trace requests from Django → Triton → GPU kernel
  • ✅ Run audit logging for multi-tenant GPU clusters: who used which GPU, when, for how long

🔑 Exam Tip — GPU Observability

The NCP-AII exam tests operational monitoring skills. Know the 5 essential DCGM field IDs: 203 (GPU util), 204 (memory), 205 (temp), 252 (ECC), 310 (XID). Know when to run nvidia-bug-report.sh (before any support ticket). Know the difference between SLO and SLA — SLO is internal target, SLA is customer-facing contract. Expect scenario-based questions like: "GPU temp >85°C — what alert severity and response?"

14.1 Advanced DCGM Configuration

DCGM exports 50+ GPU metrics. For production, create a custom DCGM profile focusing on the essential metrics: utilization (203, 204), temperature (205), clocks (1001, 1002), ECC (252), XID (310), NVLink bandwidth, PCIe throughput, and power (155). Collect at 10s intervals for dashboards, 1s for profiling. DCGM DCP (Diagnostic and Control Plane) enables GPU telemetry at scale — thousands of GPUs reporting to a central DCGM server.

Profile configuration: dcgmi profile --set 1,203,204,205,1001,252,310 --interval 10. Verify: dcgmi dmon -e 203,204,205 -c 5 shows live metrics.

Bonus: Set different intervals — 10s for dashboards, 1s for a profiling window during a canary deployment.

14.2 Prometheus + Grafana — Production Dashboards

The GPU SRE dashboard should show at a glance: GPU utilization heatmap (all GPUs, green=used, red=idle or error), Memory per GPU (bar chart, alert >95%), Temperature top-10 (alert >85°C), XID error timeline (any spike = investigate), NVLink bandwidth (drop >20% = fabric issue).

RED metrics for GPUs: Rate (GPU requests/sec, training throughput), Errors (XID count, ECC errors), Duration (kernel time, job completion time). SLOs: 99.9% GPU availability, <1% XID error rate per month, <10% P99 latency degradation. PagerDuty integration: XID 48/74/79 → critical alert → page on-call SRE immediately.

Add PagerDuty alert rules: GPU temp >85°C = P2 (30min), GPU temp >95°C = P1 (immediate), XID 48/74/79 = P1. Export the dashboard JSON — it becomes your team's production dashboard template.

14.3 Logging and Tracing

GPU job logging: Capture stdout/stderr from training/inference containers → ship to Loki/Elasticsearch. nvidia-bug-report.sh: Generates comprehensive debug bundle (driver version, GPU status, ECC counts, dmesg, kernel logs). Always run this BEFORE opening an NVIDIA support ticket. Distributed tracing: OpenTelemetry spans across Django → Triton → GPU kernel. Trace ID follows a request from HTTP ingress through inference to response — critical for debugging latency issues in production. Audit logging: Log every GPU allocation: user, namespace, GPU ID, timestamp, duration. Essential for chargeback and compliance.

This data enables showback (transparency) and chargeback (billing) for GPU resources across data science teams.

14.4 GPU SLO Design & Alerting — From Metrics to Pages

🔥 GPU Error Budget — The Professional's Decision Framework

Every GPU cluster has an error budget: the amount of acceptable downtime or degradation per month. The error budget is what separates "alert fatigue" from "actionable alerts." Here's how to design it for GPU infrastructure:

GPU SLO Error Budget Calculation — anihpj Inference Cluster
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    GPU ERROR BUDGET CALCULATOR                     │
  │                                                                    │
  │  SLO: 99.9% GPU Availability (per month = 43,200 minutes)         │
  │                                                                    │
  │  Error Budget = 0.1% × 43,200 min = 43.2 minutes/month            │
  │                                                                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  BURN RATE           │  TIME TO EXHAUST  │  RESPONSE          │ │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  1× (normal ops)     │  ~30 days          │  No action         │ │
  │  │  2× (elevated)       │  ~15 days          │  Ticket filed      │ │
  │  │  5× (warning)        │  ~6 days           │  Page on-call (P3) │ │
  │  │  10× (critical)      │  ~3 days           │  Page on-call (P2) │ │
  │  │  36× (emergency)     │  ~1 day            │  Page ALL (P1)     │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                    │
  │  ★ The 36× burn rate rule: If you'd exhaust your monthly budget   │
  │    in 24 hours, page everyone. This prevents "we didn't notice"   │
  │    outages while preventing false alarms from transient blips.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📊 PromQL Cheatsheet — GPU Queries for Production

These PromQL queries power every GPU SRE dashboard. Copy them, adapt the labels, and they'll give you 90% of what you need to monitor any GPU cluster:

MetricPromQL QueryAlert Threshold
GPU UtilizationDCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTILNone (informational). >95% sustained → investigate
GPU Memory %(DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED / DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_TOTAL) * 100>95% = P3. >98% = P2
GPU TemperatureDCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP>80°C = P3. >85°C = P2. >90°C = P1
XID Errors (rate)rate(DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS[5m])>0 for XID 48/74/79 = P1
ECC Errors (rate)rate(DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_DBE_VOL_TOTAL[5m])>0 = P2 (double-bit ECC = uncorrectable)
NVLink BW (per link)DCGM_FI_DEV_NVLINK_BANDWIDTH_TOTAL<50% of expected = P3
GPU Clock ThrottleDCGM_FI_DEV_CLOCK_THROTTLE_REASONS>0 for thermal/power = P2
GPU Power DrawDCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE / DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_MGMT_LIMIT>100% (exceeds limit) = P3
SLO Burn Rate(sum(rate(errors[1h])) / sum(rate(total[1h]))) / error_budget_rate>14.4× (1h burn) = P2. >36× = P1
GPU Availability %100 - (sum(gpu_downtime_seconds) / (count(gpus) * 3600)) * 100<99.9% over 30d = P1

GPU Alert Escalation — Priority Tiers

  │  │      │ NVLink BW < 50%     │              │                  │ │
  │  │      │ SLO burn > 14×      │              │                  │ │
  │  ├──────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────┤ │
  │  │ P3   │ GPU mem > 95%       │ Next biz day │ Ticket queue     │ │

  │  └──────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                    │
  │  ★ NEVER page on GPU-Util alone. Always correlate with SLO burn.   │

📈 The Four Golden Signals for GPU Clusters

Google's SRE book defines four golden signals. Here's how they map to GPU infrastructure specifically:

⏱️
1. Latency

GPU context: P50/P95/P99 inference latency, NCCL all-reduce time, kernel execution time. Alert when: P99 > 2× baseline for 5+ minutes. Tool: Triton metrics (nv_inference_request_duration_us) + Nsight Systems timeline.

📊
2. Traffic

GPU context: Inference requests/sec, training steps/sec, data loading throughput. Alert when: Sudden 50% drop in throughput without deployment change. Tool: DCGM GPU-Util × request counter correlation.

❌
3. Errors

GPU context: XID errors, ECC errors, NCCL timeouts, CUDA OOM, kernel launch failures. Alert when: Any XID 48/74/79 or ECC double-bit error (uncorrectable). Tool: DCGM fields 252 (ECC), 310 (XID).

📈
4. Saturation

GPU context: GPU-Util > 95% sustained, GPU memory > 95%, NVLink BW saturation, SM occupancy. Alert when: Memory > 98% (impending OOM). Tool: DCGM fields 203 (util), 204 (mem BW).

🧪 LAB — Build Complete Alerting Pipeline for anihpj

Objective: Wire up the full alerting pipeline for anihpj's 32-GPU cluster. (1) Configure Prometheus alert rules for all P1/P2/P3 tiers above, (2) Set up Alertmanager with PagerDuty integration — P1 pages immediately, P2 pages after 5 min sustained, P3 creates JIRA ticket, (3) Test: intentionally trigger XID alert by running dcgmi diag -r 1 on a healthy GPU, (4) Verify: alert fires in Prometheus → Alertmanager routes to PagerDuty → on-call phone buzzes, (5) Document: alert runbook linking each alert to the troubleshooting decision tree in Appendix C. Without runbooks, alerts cause panic. With runbooks, alerts drive action.
