📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 14 (10 Questions)

Q1

DCGM Profile: Which DCGM field IDs are essential for a production GPU dashboard?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

203 (GPU util), 204 (memory), 205 (temp), 252 (ECC), 310 (XID). These 5 metrics cover utilization, memory pressure, thermal health, and error status — everything you need for a first-responder dashboard.

  GPU OBSERVABILITY STACK — Essential Metrics Flow:
  
  ┌──────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐
  │ DCGM │──▶│Prometheus│──▶│ Grafana │──▶│ PagerDuty│
  │(GPU) │   │ (scrape) │   │ (viz)   │   │ (alert)  │
  └──────┘   └──────────┘   └─────────┘   └──────────┘
     │                                  If metric > threshold
     │ 203: GPU Util     (>80% train/>60% infer)
     │ 204: Mem BW       (>70% = mem-bound)
     │ 205: Temp         (>85°C = throttle, >95°C = shutdown)
     │ 252: ECC Errors   (>0 = investigate)
     │ 310: XID Errors   (>0 = page on-call)
     ▼
  🎯 First-responder dashboard = these 5 panels + XID timeline
💡 EXPLANATION

The 5 essential DCGM field IDs form the minimum viable monitoring set: 203 (GPU utilization) — are GPUs being used or idle? 204 (framebuffer memory) — is GPU memory saturated? 205 (temperature) — are GPUs thermal throttling? 252 (ECC errors) — is GPU memory developing correctable errors (predicts failure)? 310 (XID errors) — has the GPU experienced a fatal hardware error? These 5 metrics answer "is my GPU cluster healthy?" in seconds. All other metrics (clocks, power, NVLink, PCIe) are for deep-dive investigations, not first-responder dashboards.

Q2

SLO: What's a reasonable GPU availability SLO for a production inference cluster?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

99.9% (8.7 hours downtime/year). For critical inference (revenue-generating), target 99.95% (4.4 hours/year). Training can tolerate 99.5% (1.8 days/year) since jobs can be rescheduled.

  GPU SLOs — By Workload Type:
  ┌───────────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────┐
  │  WORKLOAD     │   SLO    │  DOWNTIME/YEAR      │
  ├───────────────┼──────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │ Critical Inf  │ 99.95%   │ 4.4 hrs (N+1 needed)│
  │ Production Inf│ 99.9%    │ 8.7 hrs (1 maint +  │
  │               │          │   1 failure)         │
  │ Training      │ 99.5%    │ 1.8 days (checkpoint│
  │               │          │   allows reschedule) │
  │ Dev/CI        │ 99%      │ 3.7 days            │
  └───────────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────┘
  ★ 99.9% = "three nines" = 8.7 hrs/yr
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU SLOs must account for: planned maintenance (driver upgrades, firmware updates = ~4hrs/quarter), unplanned failures (XID errors, NVSwitch issues), and cloud provider outages (for hybrid deployments). 99.9% = 8.7 hrs/yr = roughly one DGX node failure + one maintenance window. 99.95% requires N+1 redundancy + automated failover. Training SLOs are more relaxed because checkpointing allows job resumption with minimal data loss.

Q3

nvidia-bug-report: When should you run nvidia-bug-report.sh?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Before opening any NVIDIA Enterprise Support ticket. Support requires it. Also run it immediately after any XID error.

  nvidia-bug-report.sh — What It Captures:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 📦 bug-report.gz contents:                    │
  │ ├── dmesg (kernel logs, XID events)           │
  │ ├── nvidia-smi -q (full GPU state)            │
  │ ├── DCGM diagnostics (diag output)            │
  │ ├── PCIe topology (lspci -t)                  │
  │ ├── Driver version + CUDA version             │
  │ ├── /proc/interrupts (IRQ stats)              │
  │ └── /var/log/syslog (system logs)             │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ RUN IMMEDIATELY after XID — not after reboot! │
  │ GPU state is VOLATILE — reboot clears context │
  │ Runtime: ~2 min → produces .gz file          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

nvidia-bug-report.sh collects: kernel logs (dmesg), GPU state (nvidia-smi -q), DCGM diagnostics, PCIe topology, driver version, CUDA version, and system info. This bundle gives NVIDIA support everything they need to triage. Run it IMMEDIATELY after an XID error — GPU state can change after a reboot. The script runs in ~2 minutes and produces a .gz file. Attach this to your support ticket for fastest resolution.

Q4

DCGM Intervals: What collection interval for dashboards vs profiling?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

10s for dashboards, 1s for profiling. Higher frequency = more storage and CPU. 10s is sufficient for trends; 1s needed for detailed performance analysis.

  DCGM COLLECTION INTERVALS:
  ┌───────────┬──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐
  │ INTERVAL  │ Data/Day/GPU │ Storage/Mo/GPU│  USE CASE    │
  ├───────────┼──────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 10s ✅    │ 8,640 pts    │ ~30 MB        │ Dashboards   │
  │ 30s       │ 2,880 pts    │ ~10 MB        │ Long-term    │
  │ 1s ⚡     │ 86,400 pts   │ ~300 MB       │ Profiling    │
  ├───────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┤
  │ 1000 GPUs × 30MB = 30 GB/month at 10s (manageable)     │
  │ 1000 GPUs × 300MB = 300 GB/month at 1s (only temporary)│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

DCGM interval trade-offs: 10s = 8,640 data points/day/GPU = ~1MB/day/GPU = manageable at 1000+ GPUs. 1s = 86,400 data points/day/GPU = ~10MB/day/GPU = requires significant Prometheus storage. Use 10s for always-on monitoring. Temporarily switch to 1s during: canary deployments, performance investigations, and new hardware burn-in. Prometheus retention: 15 days at 10s, 2 days at 1s. Alert on gaps >3× the interval (missing data = monitoring failure).

Q5

Alert Severity: GPU temp >85°C — what alert level and response?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

P2 (High) → check cooling within 30 min. >95°C → P1 (Critical) → immediate throttle + investigation. Thermal throttling silently degrades performance.

  GPU TEMP ALERT ESCALATION:
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │ TEMP RANGE   │  SEVERITY   │  ACTION                 │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
  │ < 75°C       │  ✅ Normal  │  No alert               │
  │ 75-85°C      │  🟡 P3 Warn │  Email notification     │
  │ 85-95°C      │  🟠 P2 High │  Slack + page in 30min  │
  │ > 95°C       │  🔴 P1 Crit │  Page NOW + nvidia-smi  │
  │              │             │  -lgc 0,1000 (throttle) │
  └──────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
  ★ >85°C = GPU is thermal throttling (silent perf loss)
  ★ Sustained temp rise of 5-10°C → investigate before failure
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU temperature alert thresholds: <75°C = normal (no alert). 75-85°C = P3 (warning, email). 85-95°C = P2 (high, Slack/page within 30 min) — GPU is throttling. >95°C = P1 (critical, immediate page) — GPU approaching thermal shutdown. At >85°C, immediate mitigation: nvidia-smi -lgc 0,1000 to lock clocks low. Check: fan speeds, CDU pump, ambient DC temp. A sustained temp increase of 5-10°C vs baseline often precedes hardware failure — investigate proactively.

Q6

Distributed Tracing: How does OpenTelemetry help debug GPU inference latency?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Trace follows request through Django→Triton→GPU kernel. Each span shows duration. If GPU kernel span is 2ms but total is 50ms, the bottleneck is outside the GPU (queue, network, pre/post processing).

  DISTRIBUTED TRACING — anihpj Request Path:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TRACE ID: abc123                                     │
  │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ Django (2ms) → HTTP (2ms) → Triton Queue (40ms!)│ │
  │ │ → GPU Kernel (3ms) → Response (2ms)             │ │
  │ │ TOTAL: 49ms            ▲ BOTTLENECK = QUEUE!     │ │
  │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │ Without tracing: You blame GPU ("only 3ms? must be  │
  │   something else...")                                │
  │ With tracing: Queue = 40ms → increase Triton copies │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

OpenTelemetry spans for anihpj inference: Span1 (Django): 50ms total | Span2 (HTTP to Triton): 2ms | Span3 (Triton queue): 40ms ← BOTTLENECK | Span4 (GPU kernel): 3ms | Span5 (Triton response): 2ms. Without tracing, you see 50ms total and blame the GPU (3ms) — completely wrong. Tracing pinpoints the 40ms queue wait. Fix: increase Triton instances or enable dynamic batching with shorter delay. Tracing is the ONLY way to accurately attribute latency in multi-service GPU pipelines.

Q7

Audit Logging: What GPU usage data should be logged for chargeback?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

User, namespace, GPU ID, start time, end time, GPU-hours consumed. Multiply by GPU-hour rate for chargeback. DCGM can export per-process GPU utilization for granular billing.

  GPU CHARGEBACK — Audit Log Schema:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ {                                                │
  │   "user": "alice@anihpj.com",                    │
  │   "namespace": "ml-training",                     │
  │   "gpu_id": "GPU-3a1b2c",                        │
  │   "gpu_type": "H100-80GB",                       │
  │   "start": "2026-06-08T10:00:00Z",               │
  │   "end": "2026-06-08T14:30:00Z",                 │
  │   "gpu_hours": 4.5,                              │
  │   "rate": "$12/hr",                              │
  │   "cost": "$54.00"                               │
  │ }                                                │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ★ Charge ALLOCATED time, not utilized time       │
  │ ★ Log to immutable storage (S3 + WORM)           │
  │ ★ Integrate with LDAP/OIDC for user mapping      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU chargeback formula: GPU-hours × hourly rate per GPU type. H100 rate = ~$5-15/hr (internal), A100 = $3-8/hr. Log with DCGM process-level metrics (field 1008 = process utilization). Integrate with your identity provider (LDAP/OIDC) to map process to user/team. Export to billing system monthly. Key: log both ALLOCATED time (GPU reserved) and UTILIZED time (GPU actually used) — teams should be charged for allocation, not utilization, to discourage GPU hoarding.

Q8

RED Metrics: What are RED metrics for GPU workloads?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Rate (requests/sec, training throughput), Errors (XID count, ECC), Duration (kernel time, job completion). Standard SRE pattern applied to GPUs.

  GPU RED METRICS:
  ┌───────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  SIGNAL   │  GPU METRIC          │  ALERT IF...     │
  ├───────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ RATE      │ DCGM 203 (GPU Util)  │ Drop >50%        │
  │           │ Triton req count     │ Spike >2× baseline│
  ├───────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ ERRORS    │ DCGM 310 (XID)       │ ANY non-zero     │
  │           │ DCGM 252 (ECC)       │ ANY non-zero     │
  ├───────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ DURATION  │ Nsight kernel time   │ >2× baseline     │
  │           │ P99 inference latency│ > SLO threshold  │
  └───────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────┘
  ★ RED = 3 golden signals of SRE, applied to GPUs
💡 EXPLANATION

RED = Rate, Errors, Duration — the three golden signals for any service. For GPUs: Rate = DCGM 203 (GPU util) for training, Triton request count for inference. Errors = DCGM 310 (XID errors), 252 (ECC errors), plus application-level errors. Duration = kernel execution time (Nsight), job completion time, P99 inference latency. Alert on: Rate drops >50% (GPU failure), Errors >0 (XID/ECC), Duration >2× baseline (thermal throttling or queue build-up).

Q9

Grafana Dashboard: What are the 5 essential panels for a GPU SRE dashboard?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU util heatmap, memory/GPU bar, temperature top-10, XID timeline, NVLink bandwidth. These 5 give you full situational awareness at a glance.

  5-PANEL GPU SRE DASHBOARD:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ 1. GPU HEATMAP  │  │ 2. MEMORY/GPU (bar)     │ │
  │ │ Green=used      │  │ Alert >95% → near OOM   │ │
  │ │ Red=idle/error  │  │                         │ │
  │ └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘ │
  │ ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ 3. TEMP TOP-10  │  │ 4. XID TIMELINE         │ │
  │ │ Alert >85°C      │  │ Any spike → investigate │ │
  │ └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────┘ │
  │ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │ │ 5. NVLINK BW (per GPU pair)                   │ │
  │ │ Drop >20% = fabric degradation                │ │
  │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

The 5-panel GPU SRE dashboard: (1) Heatmap: all GPUs × time, color = utilization — instantly spot idle or hot GPUs. (2) Memory bar: per-GPU memory usage — detect memory leaks or OOM risks. (3) Temperature top-10: hottest GPUs — catch cooling issues before throttling. (4) XID timeline: every XID event plotted — correlate with performance drops. (5) NVLink bandwidth: per-GPU-pair BW — detect fabric degradation. At 3 AM, these 5 panels tell you everything in 10 seconds.

Q10

Scenario: anihpj P99 latency spikes from 5ms to 200ms. GPU util shows 100%. DCGM shows no throttling. What do you check?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Triton queue depth metric (nv_inference_queue_duration_us). 100% GPU util with high latency = queue backing up. Check if a new model version loaded (cold start), or request spike exceeded capacity.

  LATENCY SPIKE — Differential Diagnosis:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Symptom: P99 5ms → 200ms, GPU 100%, no throttle  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ✅ GPU is healthy → problem is BEFORE the GPU    │
  │ │                                                 │
  │ ├── 1. Check: nv_inference_queue_duration_us     │
  │ │      >5000μs = QUEUE BACKUP                   │
  │ │                                                 │
  │ ├── 2. Check: request rate vs capacity           │
  │ │      2× spike? → Scale Triton instances (HPA)  │
  │ │                                                 │
  │ ├── 3. Check: model version (cold start?)        │
  │ │      New version loaded → wait for warmup      │
  │ │                                                 │
  │ └── 4. Check: max_batch_size too large?          │
  │         Head-of-line blocking → reduce batch     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

This is the classic "GPU is working hard but users are unhappy" scenario. 100% GPU util + high latency ≠ GPU problem. It means the GPU is fully saturated and requests are queuing. Differential diagnosis: (1) Check Triton metrics: nv_inference_queue_duration_us >5000μs = queue problem. (2) Check request rate: did it spike 2×? → scale Triton replicas. (3) Check model load time: new version loaded? → cold start, wait for warmup. (4) Check batch size: dynamic batching with too-large max_batch can cause head-of-line blocking. Fix: increase Triton instances or add HPA based on queue depth.

Chapter 15: Security Hardening for GPU Infrastructure 🔴 Advanced

AI Infrastructure Is a High-Value Target — Secure It Accordingly

GPU clusters run expensive hardware and process sensitive data (models, training data, user information). A compromised GPU node could exfiltrate model weights worth millions. This chapter covers container security, confidential computing, and access control for production GPU environments.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📝 10 Questions

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Harden GPU containers: rootless, seccomp/AppArmor, NetworkPolicy isolation to IB VLAN
  • ✅ Understand H100/B200 Confidential Computing (TEE) — encrypted GPU memory enclaves
  • ✅ Verify GPU attestation: confirm firmware integrity before sending sensitive data to GPU
  • ✅ Implement K8s RBAC for GPU resources: who can request GPUs at what granularity
  • ✅ Manage NGC API keys securely: HashiCorp Vault → K8s Secrets → 90-day rotation
  • ✅ Apply compliance frameworks: SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR for AI infrastructure

🔑 Exam Tip — GPU Security

The NCP-AII exam tests whether you understand that GPU containers do NOT need root. Set runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. Know the attestation workflow: GPU generates report → signed by NVIDIA root key → client verifies before provisioning keys. Know that Confidential Computing protects against host OS, hypervisor, and cloud provider access to GPU memory. Expect questions about multi-party AI training and encryption at rest for compliance.

15.1 Container Security for GPU Workloads

Image scanning: Use Trivy or Grype to scan NGC containers before deployment. Rootless containers: Set securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 1000 — GPU pods don't need root. seccomp/AppArmor: Restrict system calls available to GPU containers. A CUDA kernel only needs ioctl, mmap, mprotect — block everything else. NetworkPolicy: Isolate GPU pods to InfiniBand VLAN only — they don't need internet access. Block all egress except to Triton and storage endpoints.

🐳 anihpj hardening: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, drop ALL capabilities, add only SYS_RAWIO (required for GPU direct I/O). Use nvidia.com/gpu resource limits to prevent GPU hoarding.

Hardened GPU Pod SecurityContext
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["SYS_RAWIO"]  # Required for GPU direct I/O
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault     # Blocks 300+ syscalls
🧪 LAB — Harden anihpj Inference Pods

Objective: Take an existing anihpj Triton inference pod running as root and harden it. (1) Add the securityContext above, (2) Run Trivy scan on the NGC container: trivy image nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3, (3) Apply NetworkPolicy blocking all egress except to Triton endpoint and S3 storage, (4) Verify the pod still works — GPU access via NVIDIA Container Toolkit does NOT require root. Document any CVEs found and their severity.

15.2 Confidential Computing on NVIDIA GPUs

H100/B200 support Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) — also called Confidential Computing. The GPU creates an encrypted enclave where model weights and data are protected even from the host OS and hypervisor. Attestation workflow: (1) GPU generates attestation report (signed by NVIDIA root key), (2) Client verifies GPU is genuine and running trusted firmware, (3) Client provisions encryption keys only to attested GPU, (4) All GPU memory is encrypted with hardware AES-GCM.

Multi-party AI training: Two organizations can jointly train a model without revealing their data to each other — each party's data stays encrypted in its own TEE, only gradients (already aggregated) are shared. This is the future of privacy-preserving AI.

🧪 LAB — Deploy Confidential Computing on anihpj H100

Objective: Enable Confidential Computing (TEE) for an anihpj model serving pod. (1) Verify H100 supports CC: nvidia-smi -q | grep "Confidential Computing", (2) Enable CC mode via GPU Operator ClusterPolicy (set confidentialComputing.enabled: true), (3) Deploy a test container requesting CC: add nvidia.com/cc: enabled to pod annotations, (4) Use NVIDIA Attestation SDK to verify GPU attestation report before sending model weights. Verify that even root on the host cannot read GPU memory contents.

15.3 Access Control and Audit

K8s RBAC for GPUs: Create roles that allow GPU resource requests only for specific namespaces. Dev team can request nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1 but not nvidia.com/gpu: 8. NGC API key management: Store in HashiCorp Vault, inject via K8s Secrets, rotate every 90 days. ResourceQuota: requests.nvidia.com/gpu: 4 per namespace prevents one team from monopolizing GPUs. Compliance: GPU clusters handling PII/health data need SOC 2, HIPAA, or GDPR compliance. Key requirements: encryption at rest (GPU memory + storage), audit trails (who accessed which GPU when), data locality (GPUs in specific geographic regions).

🧪 LAB — Least-Privilege GPU Access for anihpj Data Science Team

Objective: Create K8s RBAC policies that grant the data-science team GPU access without cluster admin. (1) Create namespace: kubectl create ns ds-team, (2) Create Role allowing nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb resource requests, (3) Set ResourceQuota: max 4 MIG slices, (4) Set LimitRange: min 1 slice, max 2 slices per pod, (5) Create NetworkPolicy: pods can only talk to Triton endpoint and storage, (6) Test: data scientist creates pod requesting 8 GPUs → REJECTED. Requests 1 MIG slice → ALLOWED. This is production-grade GPU governance.

15.4 GPU Container Supply Chain Security — From Build to Runtime

🔐 Why GPU Container Security Is Different

Regular containers run CPU code. GPU containers run CUDA kernels with direct hardware access. A compromised GPU container can: exfiltrate model weights through GPU memory, run unauthorized cryptocurrency mining undetected, or exploit GPU driver vulnerabilities for host escape. The attack surface is larger because the GPU is a separate processor with its own memory, driver stack, and DMA access to system memory.

GPU Container Supply Chain — 5 Security Gates
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            GPU CONTAINER SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY                    │
  │                                                                    │
  │  GATE 1: BASE IMAGE           GATE 2: BUILD TIME                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────┐             │
  │  │ ✅ NGC signed images│      │ ✅ No secrets in   │             │
  │  │ ✅ SHA256 digest    │─────▶│    Dockerfile       │             │
  │  │ ✅ NVIDIA container │      │ ✅ Multi-stage build│             │
  │  │    scanning         │      │ ✅ SBOM generation  │             │
  │  │ ❌ :latest tag      │      │ ❌ pip install      │             │
  │  │ ❌ DockerHub GPU    │      │    without hash     │             │
  │  └────────────────────┘       └────────┬───────────┘             │
  │                                        │                          │
  │                                        ▼                          │
  │  GATE 3: REGISTRY             GATE 4: DEPLOYMENT                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐       ┌────────────────────┐             │
  │  │ ✅ Private NGC reg │       │ ✅ Admission        │             │
  │  │ ✅ Image signing   │◀──────│    controller check │             │
  │  │    (Cosign)        │       │ ✅ PSA: restricted  │             │
  │  │ ✅ Vulnerability   │       │ ✅ K8s Secret CSI   │             │
  │  │    scanning (Trivy)│       │ ❌ runAsRoot: true  │             │
  │  └────────────────────┘       └────────┬───────────┘             │
  │                                        │                          │
  │                                        ▼                          │
  │                           GATE 5: RUNTIME                         │
  │                           ┌────────────────────┐                 │
  │                           │ ✅ readOnlyRootFS  │                 │
  │                           │ ✅ seccomp GPU     │                 │
  │                           │    profile         │                 │
  │                           │ ✅ NetworkPolicy   │                 │
  │                           │ ✅ Falco GPU rules │                 │
  │                           │ ❌ privileged:true │                 │
  │                           └────────────────────┘                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🛡️ NGC Container Scanning — Trust But Verify

NGC containers from nvcr.io are NVIDIA-signed, but you still scan them. Why? Vulnerabilities are discovered AFTER release. A container that was secure in January may have critical CVEs by March. Use Trivy or Grype integrated into your CI/CD:

Scan ToolWhat It ChecksGPU-Specific
TrivyOS packages, Python/Pip, language depsCUDA toolkit version, driver compatibility
GrypeSBOM-based vulnerability matchingcuDNN, NCCL versions against NVIDIA advisories
Docker ScoutLayer analysis, policy evaluationGPU driver CVEs in base image
CosignImage signing + verificationVerify NGC signature chain: NVIDIA→image
NVIDIA Container ScannerCVE database + NVIDIA advisoriesGPU-specific CVEs (driver, CUDA, cuDNN)

📦 GPU Pod SecurityContext — The Production Standard

Every GPU pod in production should use this hardened security context. Copy it, adapt the UID, and deploy it everywhere:

Production GPU Pod SecurityContext — Hardened Template
# Hardened GPU Pod SecurityContext for anihpj Triton
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: triton-inference-hardened
spec:
  # ★ GPU access WITHOUT root or privilege escalation
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true              # Must be non-root user
    runAsUser: 1000                 # Specific UID (not 0!)
    runAsGroup: 2000                # Specific GID
    fsGroup: 2000                   # Volume mount permissions
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault          # Block dangerous syscalls

  containers:
  - name: triton
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.06-py3@sha256:abc123...
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false   # No setuid binaries
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true      # Immutable container FS
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - ALL                            # Drop ALL capabilities
      # GPU access does NOT need: SYS_ADMIN, IPC_LOCK, NET_ADMIN

    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 2            # GPU request (no root needed!)
      requests:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 2

    env:
    - name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
      value: "0,1"                    # Only see assigned GPUs
    # ★ Never: NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all (too broad)

    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp                 # Only mount specific paths
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /cache

  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 1Gi                  # Limit temp space
  - name: cache
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 10Gi                 # Limit cache
🧪 LAB — Implement GPU Container Admission Control for anihpj

Objective: Prevent insecure GPU pods from being deployed. (1) Install OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno on the anihpj cluster, (2) Create policy: BLOCK any pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu that has runAsRoot:true OR privilegeEscalation:true OR missing seccompProfile, (3) Create policy: BLOCK any pod using :latest tag from nvcr.io (must use digest), (4) Test: try deploying an insecure GPU pod → REJECTED with clear message, (5) Test: try deploying a hardened GPU pod → ALLOWED, (6) Set up Falco with GPU-specific rules: alert on CUDA kernel launch from unexpected process, alert on GPU memory allocation from non-ML container, alert on direct nvidia-smi invocation in pod. This turns security from "hope nobody does something bad" to "the system prevents it."

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 15 (10 Questions)

Q1

Rootless GPU: Do GPU containers need root access?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

No. GPU containers can run as non-root with runAsNonRoot: true and allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. The GPU device is accessed via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, not root privileges.

  GPU CONTAINERS — Rootless:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true ✅          │
  │  Toolkit uses cgroups + device nodes, not root  │
  │  ★ GPU access NEVER needs root!                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NVIDIA Container Toolkit uses cgroups and device nodes to grant GPU access without root. The toolkit mounts /dev/nvidia* devices into the container with the correct permissions. Required: runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop ALL capabilities, add only SYS_RAWIO. GPU pods running as root is a security anti-pattern — it's never needed and exposes the host to container escapes via GPU driver interfaces.

Q2

TEE: What does H100 Confidential Computing protect against?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Host OS, hypervisor, and cloud provider access to GPU memory. Model weights and data are encrypted in hardware. Even someone with physical access to the DGX cannot read GPU memory.

  H100 CONFIDENTIAL COMPUTING — TEE Architecture:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 TEE BOUNDARY                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  ENCRYPTED (invisible to all outside)      │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐ │  │
  │  │  │  Model   │  │  Data    │  │  Results │ │  │
  │  │  │ Weights  │  │ (PHI/PII)│  │ (logits) │ │  │
  │  │  │ 🔒 AES   │  │ 🔒 AES   │  │ 🔒 AES   │ │  │
  │  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘ │  │
  │  │  GPU HBM encrypted with HW-generated keys  │  │
  │  │  PCIe link: encrypted tunnel (CXL IDE)     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                      ▲                            │
  │  ┌───────────────────┴──────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  OUTSIDE TEE: Cannot READ GPU memory         │ │
  │  │  ❌ Host OS (root)  ❌ Hypervisor            │ │
  │  │  ❌ Cloud provider  ❌ Physical attacker      │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Multi-party AI: Org A + Org B pool data, neither trusts the other
💡 EXPLANATION

H100 Confidential Computing (AMD SEV-SNP equivalent) creates a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) where: (1) GPU memory is encrypted with hardware-generated keys, (2) The CPU-GPU PCIe link is encrypted, (3) Attestation verifies the GPU is genuine and running trusted firmware. Attackers with root on the host, hypervisor access, or even physical presence cannot read model weights or inference data. Critical for multi-party AI training where different organizations contribute data without trusting each other.

Q3

GPU Audit: What should be logged for compliance?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

User, namespace, GPU ID, model/training job, timestamp, duration, data accessed. Essential for SOC 2/HIPAA compliance and internal chargeback.

  GPU AUDIT LOG — Required Fields:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  { user, namespace, gpu_id, job, timestamp,     │
  │    duration, data_accessed }                     │
  │  → Immutable storage. SOC2: 1yr, HIPAA: 6yr    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU audit log must answer: Who ran what on which GPU, when, for how long, and what data was processed? Log to immutable storage (S3 with versioning + WORM). Retain for compliance period (SOC 2: 1 year, HIPAA: 6 years). Include: process name, PID, GPU utilization, memory used, start/end timestamps, and dataset identifiers. DCGM exports per-process GPU metrics — pipe these to your SIEM (Splunk/ELK) with structured JSON format.

Q4

Image Scanning: Why scan NGC containers before deployment?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NGC images may contain CVEs in base OS packages. Scanning with Trivy/Grype identifies vulnerabilities. NVIDIA patches critical CVEs but you should verify before production deployment.

  NGC IMAGE SCANNING — CI/CD Pipeline:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pull NGC → Trivy scan → CRITICAL? block         │
  │  MEDIUM/LOW? warn + allow                        │
  │  Gate via OPA/Kyverno admission controller       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NGC containers are built on Ubuntu/CentOS base images which accumulate CVEs over time. NVIDIA releases updated containers monthly, but your deployed images may be weeks old. CI/CD pipeline should: (1) pull NGC image, (2) scan with Trivy (trivy image nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3), (3) block deployment if CRITICAL CVEs found, (4) allow with warnings for MEDIUM/LOW. Gate this in your admission controller (OPA/Kyverno). Image scanning is a SOC 2 requirement.

Q5

NetworkPolicy: Why restrict GPU pods to InfiniBand VLAN only?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU pods don't need internet. Blocking egress prevents data exfiltration and limits attack surface. Only Triton endpoint and storage should be reachable.

  GPU POD NetworkPolicy — Default Deny + Explicit Allow:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │ │          GPU POD (default deny)           │     │
  │ │                                          │     │
  │ │  ALLOWED:              BLOCKED:          │     │
  │ │  ✅ IB fabric (NCCL)   ❌ Internet        │     │
  │ │  ✅ Storage endpoint   ❌ DNS external     │     │
  │ │  ✅ Triton API         ❌ Package repos   │     │
  │ │  ✅ Monitoring (DCGM)  ❌ External APIs   │     │
  │ │  ✅ DNS (internal)     ❌ SSH outside      │     │
  │ │                        ❌ All other egress│     │
  │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │  NetworkPolicy:                                   │
  │  podSelector: app=gpu-inference                   │
  │  policyTypes: [Egress]                            │
  │  egress: [storage-endpoint, triton-api, dcgm]     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Even if container is compromised, data can't leave
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU training/inference pods need: (1) IB fabric for NCCL communication, (2) Storage endpoint for checkpoints/data, (3) Triton API for inference requests. They do NOT need: internet access, DNS, package repositories, or external APIs. A NetworkPolicy blocking all egress except to approved CIDRs prevents: data exfiltration via compromised container, cryptomining on stolen GPUs, and lateral movement in case of breach. Default-deny + explicit allow is the standard.

Q6

NGC API Keys: How should NGC API keys be managed in production?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Store in HashiCorp Vault, inject via K8s Secrets, rotate every 90 days. Never hardcode in Docker images or ConfigMaps. Use External Secrets Operator for automated rotation.

  NGC API KEY — Secure Lifecycle:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NGC Console → Vault → External Secrets → K8s   │
  │  Pod: NGC_API_KEY env var                        │
  │  Rotate every 90 days. Never in git/Dockerfile!  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

NGC API key lifecycle: (1) Generate in NVIDIA NGC console, (2) Store in Vault (path: secret/ngc/api-key), (3) External Secrets Operator syncs to K8s Secret, (4) Pod mounts as env var NGC_API_KEY, (5) Rotate every 90 days via Vault auto-rotation. Audit: key usage logged. Never: in Dockerfile, in ConfigMap, in git. A leaked NGC key allows anyone to pull NVIDIA enterprise containers on your account — potentially $100K+ in unauthorized usage.

Q7

Attestation: What does GPU attestation verify?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPU is genuine NVIDIA hardware running trusted firmware. The attestation report is signed by NVIDIA's root key — clients verify this before sending sensitive data to the GPU.

  GPU ATTESTATION WORKFLOW:
  ┌──────────┐              ┌──────────┐
  │  CLIENT  │              │   GPU    │
  │(app/user)│              │(hardware)│
  └────┬─────┘              └────┬─────┘
       │ 1. Request attestation  │
       │────────────────────────▶│
       │                         │ 2. GPU firmware generates
       │                         │    report: serial#, fw hash,
       │                         │    TEE status
       │ 3. Signed report        │
       │◀────────────────────────│
       │    (NVIDIA root key)    │
       │                         │
       │ 4. Verify signature     │
       │    against NVIDIA pubkey│
       │    ┌──────────────────┐ │
       │    │ Valid? ✅ → Trust │ │
       │    │ Invalid? ❌ → Stop│ │
       │    └──────────────────┘ │
       │ 5. Provision decryption │
       │    keys to GPU          │
       │────────────────────────▶│
  ┌────┴─────┐              ┌────┴─────┐
  │ Model +  │────secure────▶│ Decrypt  │
  │ data     │   channel     │ & run    │
  └──────────┘              └──────────┘
  ★ Prevents: GPU impersonation, firmware backdoors
💡 EXPLANATION

Attestation workflow: (1) Client requests attestation from GPU, (2) GPU firmware generates report containing: GPU serial, firmware hash, TEE status, (3) Report signed by NVIDIA's hardware root key (burned into GPU at factory), (4) Client verifies signature against NVIDIA's public key, (5) If valid: GPU is genuine + firmware untampered → provision decryption keys. Prevents: GPU impersonation, firmware backdoors, and man-in-the-middle attacks between CPU and GPU.

Q8

ResourceQuota: How do you prevent one team from monopolizing GPUs?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

K8s ResourceQuota per namespace limiting requests.nvidia.com/gpu. Example: dev-team quota=4, prod-team quota=16. Combined with LimitRange for min/max per pod.

  GPU ResourceQuota — Multi-Tenant:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  dev: 4 GPUs | prod: 16 GPUs | research: 8 GPUs │
  │  + LimitRange (min 1, max 4 per pod)            │
  │  + PriorityClass: prod > staging > dev          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU multi-tenancy resource control: (1) ResourceQuota: hard limit per namespace (dev: 4 GPUs, prod: 16 GPUs, ml-research: 8 GPUs). (2) LimitRange: min 1 GPU, max 4 GPUs per pod (prevents single pod monopolizing namespace quota). (3) PriorityClass: production > staging > dev (preemption enabled). (4) MIG: further partition GPUs within namespaces. Combined, these prevent GPU hoarding, ensure fair sharing, and enable chargeback per namespace based on GPU-hours consumed.

Q9

Compliance: Which regulations apply to GPU clusters processing health data?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

HIPAA (US), GDPR (EU), SOC 2. Requirements: encryption at rest and in transit, audit trails, access controls, data locality. Confidential Computing helps meet these.

  GPU COMPLIANCE MAP:
  ┌───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ HIPAA     │ PHI encryption + audit + BAA         │
  │ GDPR      │ Data locality + right to deletion    │
  │ SOC 2     │ Security + availability controls     │
  │ Penalty:  │ HIPAA $50K/viol, GDPR 4% revenue    │
  └───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

GPU compliance mapping: HIPAA requires PHI encryption + audit + access control + BAAs. GDPR requires data locality (EU data stays in EU) + right to deletion + DPIAs. SOC 2 requires security + availability + confidentiality controls. GPU-specific compliance: (1) GPU memory encryption (Confidential Computing), (2) GPU audit logging (who accessed what model + data), (3) Network isolation (IB fabric not routable to internet), (4) Data locality (keep training data + models in-region). Non-compliance penalties: HIPAA = $50K/violation, GDPR = 4% global revenue.

Q10

Scenario: Security scan finds anihpj Triton pod running as root. What's the fix?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false. GPU access doesn't require root — NVIDIA Container Toolkit handles device access via cgroups, not privileges.

  FIX ROOT GPU PODS:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000             │
  │  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false                 │
  │  PSA: restricted profile. Gate: OPA/Gatekeeper   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Fix steps for anihpj: (1) Update Triton deployment YAML with securityContext above, (2) Add to PodSecurityPolicy/PSA: restricted profile, (3) Test: kubectl exec into pod → whoami = uid 1000, nvidia-smi still works, (4) Deploy with rolling update, (5) Verify with OPA/Gatekeeper that no future GPU pods can run as root. If NVIDIA Container Toolkit is correctly installed, GPU access works perfectly as non-root — root was never needed, it was just the insecure default.

Chapter 16: Disaster Recovery & High Availability 🔴 Advanced

GPUs Fail — Plan for It Before It Happens at 3 AM

Hardware fails. GPUs fail. NVSwitches fail. The difference between a 5-minute blip and a 3-day outage is planning. This chapter covers HA design, backup strategies, and the XID error decision tree — your field manual for GPU incidents.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~3 hours 📝 10 Questions

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Design HA GPU clusters: N+1 redundancy, multi-AZ Triton deployment, failure domain mapping
  • ✅ Implement backup strategies: S3 cross-region checkpoint replication, etcd snapshots every 6h
  • ✅ Use IaC (Terraform/Ansible) for reproducible GPU cluster rebuilds after site loss
  • ✅ Execute the XID Error Decision Tree: classify XID 48/62/74/79/43/44 and respond appropriately
  • ✅ Run quarterly DR drills: simulate DGX failure, measure RTO/RPO, document gaps
  • ✅ Write incident runbooks and post-mortem templates for GPU failure scenarios

🔑 Exam Tip — DR & HA for GPU Clusters

The NCP-AII exam tests your ability to match XID errors to correct responses. XID 79 = Sev1 (immediate — GPU fell off bus, RMA). XID 48 single occurrence = monitor 24h (could be cosmic radiation). XID 48 persistent = Sev2 (schedule RMA). XID 74 on GPU subset = NVSwitch failure (not individual GPUs). Know RTO/RPO targets: inference <1h, training <4h. Know hot spare vs cold spare tradeoffs.

16.1 GPU Cluster HA Design

Redundancy strategies: N+1 DGX nodes — keep one spare DGX powered on and ready to accept workloads. Multi-zone inference: Deploy Triton across 3 availability zones (or racks on different PDUs). If one zone fails, the load balancer routes to the remaining two — 99.99% uptime achievable. Failure domains: Map your cluster by rack, PDU, switch, and power phase. Never place all replicas of a critical service in the same failure domain.

🧪 LAB — Design HA Architecture for anihpj Inference (99.99% Uptime)

Objective: Design and document the HA architecture for anihpj's Triton inference cluster. (1) Draw deployment diagram: 3 AZs (or racks), each with 2 DGX running Triton + 1 hot spare, (2) Configure load balancer with health checks: /v2/health/ready on each Triton, (3) Set failure thresholds: if 2/3 health checks fail, remove from LB pool, (4) Calculate: with 3 AZs, each at 99.9% availability, combined = 99.97% (5.2 min downtime/month). Identify single points of failure: if your sole InfiniBand switch is shared across AZs, it undermines AZ isolation. Document all failure domains in a spreadsheet.

16.2 Backup and Recovery

Model checkpoint backup: S3 cross-region replication — checkpoints written to local NVMe, async copied to S3 in another region. etcd backup: Critical for K8s GPU clusters — etcdctl snapshot save every 6 hours, store in S3. IaC for DR: Terraform/Ansible definitions for the entire GPU cluster — if a site is lost, you can rebuild identical infrastructure from code. DR drills: Quarterly: simulate a complete DGX node failure. Measure RTO (time to restore service) and RPO (data lost). Target: RTO <1 hour for inference, <4 hours for training. RPO <1 hour.

🧪 LAB — Execute GPU Cluster DR Drill for anihpj

Objective: Run a quarterly DR drill simulating a complete DGX node failure. (1) Pick a random DGX node at 2 PM Tuesday, (2) Simulate failure: kubectl cordon + kill GPU pods, (3) Start stopwatch, (4) Execute runbook: migrate workloads to hot spare, verify S3 checkpoint integrity, verify etcd restore from snapshot, (5) Stop stopwatch when all anihpj inference endpoints return healthy. Document: RTO (should be <1h), RPO (check last checkpoint timestamp), gaps in runbook, and any manual steps that should be automated. After-action review: what broke? what surprised you? what's the fix before next quarter?

16.3 Incident Response & XID Decision Tree

XID Error Response — Decision Tree
  GPU ERROR DETECTED (dmesg or DCGM alert)
  │
  ├── XID 48: Double-Bit ECC Error
  │   ├── Single occurrence? → Monitor 24h. If repeats → RMA
  │   └── Persistent? → RMA GPU (cannot be repaired in-field)
  │
  ├── XID 74: NVLink Error
  │   ├── Check NVLink: nvidia-smi nvlink -s
  │   ├── Check fabric manager: systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager
  │   └── Persistent? → RMA GPU or NVSwitch module
  │
  ├── XID 79: GPU Fell Off Bus
  │   ├── Check PCIe: lspci | grep nvidia
  │   ├── Reseat GPU in PCIe slot, check PSU voltages
  │   └── Still missing? → RMA (hardware failure)
  │
  ├── XID 62: ECC Page Retirement (Warning)
  │   ├── <10 pages → Normal wear, monitor
  │   └── >100 pages → Schedule GPU replacement
  │
  ├── XID 43/44: GPU Temperature Warning/Critical
  │   ├── Check DCGM temp: dcgmi dmon -e 205
  │   ├── Mitigate: nvidia-smi -lgc 0,1000 (throttle)
  │   └── Check cooling infrastructure
  │
  └── Unknown/Multiple
      └── nvidia-bug-report.sh → NVIDIA support ticket

  🎯 NEVER ignore XID errors — they ALWAYS indicate real HW degradation

XID 48/62 — ECC Errors

XID 48 = double-bit ECC (uncorrectable). One occurrence may be cosmic radiation (rare). Two in 24h = failing memory bank → RMA. XID 62 = page retirement (correctable ECC). <10 pages is normal GPU aging. >100 pages means the memory is degrading rapidly.

XID 74 — NVLink Errors

Check NVLink status with nvidia-smi nvlink -s. If lanes show "inactive", check fabric manager. Run nvidia-smi nvlink -r to reset NVLink counters. Persistent errors after reset = hardware issue — RMA the GPU or NVSwitch module based on which lanes are affected.

XID 79 — GPU Fell Off Bus

Most critical GPU error. GPU disconnected from PCIe. Check lspci | grep nvidia — if GPU is completely gone, reseat in slot. Check PSU voltages. After reboot, if still missing → immediate RMA. No software fix exists for XID 79.

XID 43/44 — Thermal Events

Temperature >85°C triggers warning (43). >95°C triggers critical (44) and GPU throttles. Check liquid cooling loop pressure, CDU status, fan speeds. Mitigate by locking clock to lower frequency while investigating cooling failure.

📋 GPU Incident Post-Mortem Template

Template for every GPU incident — fill this out within 24h of resolution:

  • Incident ID: INC-YYYY-MMDD-NNN
  • Severity: Sev1 (cluster down) / Sev2 (node down) / Sev3 (single GPU) / Sev4 (warning)
  • Timeline (UTC): Detection time → Escalation time → Diagnosis time → Mitigation time → Resolution time
  • What happened: One-paragraph summary. e.g., "XID 74 on GPUs 2,3,6,7 of dgx-03. Root cause: NVSwitch 1 failed, causing 4 GPUs to lose NVLink connectivity."
  • Impact: Number of affected users/jobs. Duration of degradation. GPU-hours lost.
  • Root cause: Deep analysis — not just "NVSwitch failed" but WHY: firmware bug? thermal? manufacturing defect?
  • Resolution: What fixed it. RMA? Firmware update? Reseat cable?
  • Prevention: What changes prevent recurrence. New monitoring alert? Firmware baseline? Spare parts inventory?
  • Action items: JIRA tickets with owners and deadlines.

🧪 LAB — Write Incident Runbook for anihpj GPU Failure Scenarios: Create runbooks for: (1) Single XID 48 at 3 AM, (2) Persistent XID 48 across multiple GPUs, (3) XID 74 on all GPUs (NVSwitch dead), (4) GPU temp >95°C on all GPUs (CDU cooling failure). Each runbook: detection (what alert fires), triage (what commands to run), mitigation (immediate actions), escalation (who to page), resolution steps, verification. Review runbooks quarterly with the team.

📝 NCP-AII Practice Questions — Chapter 16 (10 Questions)

Q1

HA Design: What's the minimum redundancy for 99.9% GPU inference uptime?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

N+1 at minimum. 2+ AZs recommended. Single DGX = no HA. 2 DGX (N+1) allows one failure. 3 AZs × 2 DGX each = 99.99% with zone-level redundancy for inference.

  GPU HA LEVELS:
  ┌────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  CONFIG        │  UPTIME  │  FAILURE TOLERANCE       │
  ├────────────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │ 1 DGX          │ ~99%     │ 0 failures = ~3.7 days   │
  │ 2 DGX (N+1)   │ 99.9%    │ 1 DGX failure = 8.7 hrs  │
  │ 3 AZs × 2 DGX │ 99.99%   │ 1 AZ failure = 52 min    │
  └────────────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────────┘
  ★ N+1 = baseline + 1 spare. Hot spare = <1 min failover.
💡 EXPLANATION

N+1 means you have one more DGX than needed for baseline capacity. If baseline = 3 DGX for inference, N+1 = 4 DGX. If one fails, the remaining 3 handle full load. Multi-AZ: place DGX in different racks/PDUs/switches — a single PDU failure shouldn't kill all replicas. 3 AZs × 2 DGX each = 6 DGX (3× redundancy). Hot spare (powered on, GPU Operator running) is preferred over cold spare (powered off, 15+ min startup).

Q2

XID Priority: Which XID requires immediate on-call response (Sev1)?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

XID 79 (GPU fell off bus). Immediate Sev1 — GPU completely disconnected, workloads on that GPU are dead. Followed by persistent XID 48 (ECC) → Sev2.

  XID SEVERITY — On-Call Response:
  ┌─────────┬──────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
  │ XID     │ SEVERITY │  ON-CALL RESPONSE             │
  ├─────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ 79      │ 🔴 Sev1  │ Page NOW. GPU disconnected.   │
  │ 48(×3+) │ 🟠 Sev1  │ Escalate from Sev2 → Sev1.   │
  │ 48(×1)  │ 🟡 Sev2  │ Log + monitor 24h.           │
  │ 74      │ 🟡 Sev2  │ Check fabric manager.         │
  │ 62      │ 🟢 Sev3  │ Scheduled maintenance.        │
  └─────────┴──────────┴───────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

XID severity ranking: 79 (fell off bus) > persistent 48 (ECC) > 74 (NVLink) > single 48 > 62 (ECC retirement). XID 79 means the GPU disappeared from PCIe — all processes using it crash immediately. Check: lspci | grep nvidia (GPU missing?), dmesg | grep "PCIe error", ipmitool sensor (power supply issue?). RMA is mandatory — GPU fell off bus is always hardware failure.

Q3

DR Metrics: What's a reasonable RTO/RPO for GPU training clusters?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

RTO <4 hours, RPO <1 hour. Training can restart from last checkpoint. Inference needs faster RTO (<1 hour) since it's user-facing.

  RTO/RPO — Training vs Inference:
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │   METRIC     │  TRAINING    │  INFERENCE            │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ RTO (recover)│ < 4 hours    │ < 1 hour              │
  │ RPO (data)   │ < 1 hour     │ 0 (real-time)         │
  │ Strategy     │ Checkpoint   │ Hot spare failover    │
  │ Cost of      │ Lost compute │ Lost revenue + users  │
  │ downtime     │ time         │                       │
  └──────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────────────┘
  ★ Training = batch (restartable). Inference = real-time.
💡 EXPLANATION

RTO (Recovery Time Objective) = how fast you restore service. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) = how much data you can lose. Training: RTO <4h (time to reprovision DGX + restore checkpoint), RPO <1h (checkpoint frequency). Inference: RTO <1h (hot spare takes over), RPO = 0 (real-time, no data loss). The exam expects different RTO/RPO targets for training vs inference — they are NOT the same because training is batch (restartable), inference is real-time (must fail over).

Q4

etcd Backup: Why is etcd backup critical for GPU K8s clusters?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

etcd stores all K8s state — pod definitions, GPU resource allocations, ClusterPolicy. Losing etcd = losing the cluster configuration. Snapshot every 6 hours.

  etcd BACKUP — Critical for GPU Clusters:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  What etcd stores (K8s "source of truth"):      │
  │  ├── Pod specs (which GPU to use)               │
  │  ├── ClusterPolicy (GPU driver, MIG config)     │
  │  ├── Node objects (nvidia.com/gpu: 8)           │
  │  ├── RBAC (who can request GPUs)                │
  │  └── Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps          │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Backup: Every 6 hrs → S3 cross-region          │
  │  Without backup: Corrupted etcd = rebuild ALL   │
  │  Test restore: Quarterly in sandbox cluster     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

etcd is the K8s "source of truth." It stores: Pod specs (which GPU to use), GPU Operator ClusterPolicy (driver version, MIG config), Node objects (nvidia.com/gpu capacity), RBAC policies. Without etcd backup: a corrupted etcd means rebuilding the ENTIRE cluster from scratch — weeks of work. Backup: etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%Y%m%d).db → copy to S3 with cross-region replication. Test restore quarterly in a sandbox cluster.

Q5

Failure Domains: What failure domains should you map in a GPU cluster?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Rack, PDU, switch, power phase. Never place all replicas in the same domain. A single PDU failure shouldn't take down your entire Triton deployment.

  GPU FAILURE DOMAINS — Spread Your Risk:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  🟦 RACK:      Physical unit (network, vibration)│
  │  🟩 PDU:       Power Distribution Unit          │
  │  🟨 SWITCH:    Top-of-Rack (ToR) switch          │
  │  🟧 PHASE:     3-phase power (L1/L2/L3)         │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  BAD:  Triton replicas all on Rack-01/PDU-A      │
  │        → PDU-A fails = ALL replicas dead         │
  │  GOOD: Triton-1 on Rack-01/PDU-A                 │
  │        Triton-2 on Rack-05/PDU-B                 │
  │        Triton-3 on Rack-09/PDU-C                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Failure domain mapping: Rack (physical rack collapse/network failure), PDU (Power Distribution Unit — one PDU feeds multiple racks), Switch (ToR switch failure kills all nodes in that rack), Power phase (three-phase power — one phase failure kills 1/3 of racks). Spread critical workloads across at least 2 failure domains. Example: Triton replicas on rack-01/PDU-A and rack-05/PDU-B. A single PDU-A failure kills rack-01 but rack-05 continues serving. Document your failure domain map and update quarterly.

Q6

IaC for DR: Why use Terraform/Ansible for GPU cluster DR?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Infrastructure as Code enables reproducible cluster rebuilds. If a site is lost, `terraform apply` rebuilds identical infrastructure. Manual rebuild = days of error-prone work.

  IaC DR — Rebuild from Code:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  terraform apply  → DGX nodes, IB fabric, S3     │
  │  ansible-playbook → GPU driver, CUDA, Operator   │
  │  helm install     → GPU Operator, Network Op     │
  │  kubectl apply    → Workloads, NetworkPolicy     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Rebuild time: ~2 hrs (mostly DGX provisioning)  │
  │  Manual rebuild: ~2 WEEKS (tribal knowledge)     │
  │  ★ IaC IS your DR plan. Test it quarterly.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

IaC for GPU DR: Terraform defines compute (DGX bare metal provisioning), networking (IB fabric, VLANs, subnets), storage (S3 buckets, EFS). Ansible defines configuration (GPU driver version, CUDA toolkit, GPU Operator Helm values). Together: `terraform apply && ansible-playbook site.yml` rebuilds an identical GPU cluster in a new region in ~2 hours (mostly waiting for DGX provisioning). Without IaC: weeks of tribal knowledge, inconsistent configs, and missed steps. IaC IS your DR plan — test it quarterly.

Q7

XID 48 Response: You get one XID 48 at 3 AM. What's your immediate action?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Log it, continue monitoring. Single XID 48 can be cosmic radiation. If it repeats within 24h → drain GPU → schedule RMA. Don't wake the team for one occurrence.

  XID 48 TRIAGE — 3AM Decision Tree:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1 occurrence:                                    │
  │  └── Log it, continue monitoring (cosmic ray?)    │
  │  2 occurrences in 24h:                           │
  │  └── Cordon GPU, schedule RMA (degrading)        │
  │  Persistent (>1/hr):                             │
  │  └── Drain NOW, urgent RMA (failing memory)      │
  │  10+ in a day:                                    │
  │  └── GPU will fail completely within weeks       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Single XID 48 ≠ panic. Pattern of XID 48 = RMA.
💡 EXPLANATION

XID 48 triage: Single occurrence = likely cosmic radiation (a high-energy particle flipped a memory bit — ECC caught it). Log in incident tracker, continue monitoring for 24h. Two occurrences in 24h = likely hardware degradation → cordon the GPU, migrate workloads, schedule RMA. Persistent (hourly) = urgent RMA — the GPU memory is failing. Never ignore repeated XID 48 — ECC errors spread as memory cells degrade. A GPU with 10+ XID 48 in a day will fail completely within weeks.

Q8

DR Drill: How often should you run GPU cluster DR drills?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Quarterly. Simulate DGX node failure, measure RTO/RPO. Document gaps. Untested DR plans fail when needed. Quarterly keeps the team practiced.

  DR DRILL CADENCE:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Quarterly: Simulate 1 DGX failure (random pick)   │
  │  Biannually: Simulate 1 AZ/rack failure            │
  │  Annually: Full site failover (production traffic) │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Post-drill:                                       │
  │  ├── RTO actual vs target (gap analysis)           │
  │  ├── RPO actual vs target (checkpoint recency)     │
  │  ├── What broke? (automation gaps)                 │
  │  └── JIRA tickets for fixes before next drill      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ★ Untested DR plans fail 100% of the time when needed.
💡 EXPLANATION

Quarterly DR drills: Pick a random DGX at 2 PM Tuesday (not a planned maintenance window). Simulate complete failure — cordon + kill all pods. Execute runbook. Measure: time to detection (alert fires?), time to mitigation (hot spare takes over?), time to resolution (workloads healthy?). Post-drill: review RTO vs target, document gaps, create JIRA tickets for fixes. Untested DR plans fail 100% of the time when needed. Drills turn theoretical plans into muscle memory.

Q9

N+1 Cold Spare: N+1 hot spare vs cold spare — which for GPU clusters?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Hot spare (powered on, ready). DGX takes ~15 min to boot + GPU Operator init. Hot spare accepts workloads immediately. Cold spare adds 30-45 min to RTO.

  HOT vs COLD SPARE — RTO Comparison:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HOT SPARE (powered on, K8s-joined):             │
  │  Failover time: < 1 minute                       │
  │  Cost: Full (power + cooling + NVAIE license)    │
  │  Use: Inference (99.9%+ SLO requires it)        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  COLD SPARE (powered off or standby):            │
  │  Power on: 2 min | POST: 5 min | OS: 3 min      │
  │  GPU Op: 5 min | K8s join: 2 min = ~18 min min  │
  │  Realistic RTO: 30-45 min                        │
  │  Cost: Minimal (no power, no license)            │
  │  Use: Training (checkpoint → restart acceptable) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 EXPLANATION

Hot spare: DGX powered on, GPU Operator running, joined to K8s cluster, schedulable. Workloads migrate in <1 min (pod reschedule). Cost: power + cooling + NVAIE license (same as active node). Cold spare: DGX powered off or in standby. Must: power on (2 min), POST (5 min), OS boot (3 min), GPU Operator init (5 min), join K8s (2 min), uncordon (1 min) = ~18 min minimum, realistically 30-45 min. For 99.9% inference SLO (8.7 hrs downtime/yr), hot spare is mandated. For training clusters, cold spare may be acceptable.

Q10

Scenario — anihpj: DGX-03 shows XID 74 (NVLink) on GPUs 2,3,6,7. What's the likely failure and response?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NVSwitch failure (not individual GPUs). XID 74 on specific GPU subset = the NVSwitch port serving those GPUs. Check fabric manager, reseat NVSwitch cables. If persistent → RMA NVSwitch module (not the GPUs).

  XID 74 DIAGNOSIS — NVSwitch Port Failure:
  
  DGX-03 NVSwitch Topology:
       ┌──────────────┐
       │   NVSwitch   │
       │  (4 ports)   │
       └──┬──┬──┬──┬──┘
        P0│P1│P2│P3│
       ┌──┘  │  │  └──┐
       ▼     ▼  ▼     ▼
     GPU0  GPU1 GPU2 GPU3
     GPU4  GPU5 GPU6 GPU7 ← XID 74 on 2,3,6,7
       ▲     ▲  ▲     ▲
       └──┬──┴──┴──┬──┘
          │        │
     PORT 2-3  PORT 6-7 = FAILED
  
  🎯 Pattern: GPUs sharing NVSwitch port = port failure
  🎯 NOT: Individual GPU failure (would affect 1 GPU only)
  🎯 Action: Reseat NVSwitch cables → restart fabric mgr → RMA
💡 EXPLANATION

XID 74 = NVLink hardware error. When it affects a SUBSET of GPUs (2,3,6,7 but not 0,1,4,5), the pattern reveals the fault: GPUs 2&3 share one NVSwitch port, GPUs 6&7 share another. If both ports fail simultaneously = NVSwitch hardware failure, not individual GPU failure. Response: (1) Check nvidia-smi nvlink -s for inactive links, (2) systemctl restart nvidia-fabricmanager, (3) If persists after restart → RMA NVSwitch module. Do NOT RMA the GPUs — they're fine, the NVSwitch is the problem. Replacing GPUs won't fix it.

17.1 GPU Cost Models — Capex vs Opex

Every GPU infrastructure decision starts with a cost model. The three models — on-prem (Capex), cloud (Opex), and hybrid — each have different cost structures, risk profiles, and break-even points. Understanding them is essential for the NCP-AII exam and your career.

On-Prem DGX — CAPEX Model

Capex (Capital Expenditure): Large upfront investment, predictable ongoing costs. Best for steady, predictable workloads running 24/7. Key cost components: hardware (depreciated over 3-5 years), NVAIE licensing, power/cooling, colocation or data center space, and staffing (GPU SREs).

anihpj on-prem calculation (32 H100 GPUs, 4× DGX):

Power (40.8kW × 24/7 × $0.10/kWh)$35,741$107,222
Cooling overhead (PUE 1.15)$5,361$16,083
Colocation (1 rack × $3K/mo)$36,000$108,000
Staffing (0.5 FTE GPU SRE)$75,000$225,000

Per GPU-Year~$21,753
📖 When On-Prem Wins
  • 24/7 workloads: GPU utilization consistently above 70% — the hardware pays for itself
  • Data sovereignty: Sensitive data (healthcare, finance) can't leave your data center
  • Predictable costs: No surprise cloud bills. Budget is fixed for 3-5 years
  • Full control: You choose drivers, firmware, security patches, maintenance windows
  • Tax benefits: Capex depreciation reduces taxable income

Cloud GPU — OPEX Model

Opex (Operational Expenditure): Pay-as-you-go, no upfront capital. Best for variable workloads, experimentation, and burst capacity. Key pricing tiers: on-demand (full price, no commitment), reserved (1-3 year commitment, 30-40% discount), and spot/preemptible (60-90% discount, can be terminated anytime).

Reserved (3yr)~40%3 yearsPay even if unusedCommitted cloud-only strategy
Spot/Preemptible60-90%NoneCan be terminated anytimeFault-tolerant training, batch jobs

⚠️ The Cloud GPU Trap

At $98/hr for 8 H100 GPUs, cloud seems reasonable for short experiments. But at 24/7 usage: $98 × 24 × 365 = $858,480/year for ONE p5 instance (8 GPUs). For 32 GPUs: $3.4M/year. On-prem breaks even at ~4 months. Cloud is excellent for burst/experimentation but financial suicide for steady 24/7 workloads. Always calculate total cost before committing.

Hybrid — Baseline + Burst

The optimal strategy for most organizations: own your baseline, rent your peaks. Buy enough on-prem DGX to cover 70-80% of your steady workload. Use cloud spot instances for burst capacity, experimentation, and disaster recovery. This gives you the cost efficiency of on-prem with the flexibility of cloud.

📖 TCO Time Horizons — Short, Medium, Long Term

1-Year Horizon: Cloud almost always wins. Hardware depreciation is too front-loaded (year 1 = ~$400K). Cloud on-demand for 25% utilization = ~$858K. The longer your commitment, the stronger the on-prem case. Most enterprise GPU clusters use a 3-year refresh cycle, aligning with DGX warranty + NVAIE term.

17.2 GPU Utilization Optimization

An idle GPU is money burning. The single biggest lever in GPU FinOps is utilization — moving from 40% to 80% utilization effectively doubles your GPU capacity for zero additional cost. Here are the techniques that professional GPU operators use:

Idle GPU Detection and Auto-Remediation

Monitor DCGM field 203 (GPU utilization). If utilization stays below 10% for more than 1 hour, trigger automated response: (1) Alert the workload owner (Slack/email), (2) If no response in 30 min, cordon the GPU, (3) Preempt lower-priority jobs and reschedule higher-priority ones onto the idle GPU, (4) If still idle after 2 hours, consider shutting down (cloud) or repurposing (on-prem).

Target Utilization by Workload Type

WorkloadTarget UtilWhyanihpj Example
Training>80%Training is compute-bound — GPUs should be saturatedBERT training on H100: target 85% GPU-Util
Inference>60%Need headroom for traffic spikes and request burstsTriton serving: target 65% with 35% burst capacity
Development30-50%Interactive — developers think between runsJupyter notebooks: 40% is normal and fine
CI/CD TestingVariableShort bursts — optimize for throughput, not utilizationGPU test suite: spike to 100% for 5 min, then idle

GPU Time-Slicing — Pack More Work onto Underutilized GPUs

When a GPU is only running at 30-50% utilization (common during interactive development or light inference), you're leaving performance on the table. GPU time-slicing allows multiple workloads to share a single GPU by rapidly switching between them. NVIDIA offers two approaches:

TechnologyHow It WorksIsolationBest ForGPU Support
MPS (Multi-Process Service)Single CUDA context shared by multiple processes; kernel-level interleavingNone (shared memory space)Cooperative processes from same user — training + eval on same GPUAll NVIDIA data center GPUs
MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)Physical GPU partitioned into isolated instances with dedicated memory, cache, and computeFull hardware isolation (like separate GPUs)Multi-tenant inference — 7 teams sharing one A100/H100 securelyA100, H100, B200 only
Time-Slicing (K8s)K8s device plugin alternates GPU access between pods on a time-share basisSoft (process-level only)Dev/CI environments — multiple Jupyter pods sharing one GPUAll NVIDIA GPUs with device plugin

anihpj time-slicing strategy: (1) On training DGX: use MPS to run training + evaluation simultaneously on the same GPU (training gets 70% of SM resources, eval gets 30%), (2) On inference DGX: use MIG to give anihpj-prod, anihpj-staging, and anihpj-dev each their own isolated GPU slice with guaranteed QoS, (3) For CI/CD: use K8s time-slicing to allow 4 CI pods to share one GPU — each pod gets ~25% of GPU time, which is fine for quick test runs. This approach increases effective GPU capacity by 2-3× for mixed workloads.

⚠️ MPS vs MIG — Don't Confuse Them

MPS is a software-level multiplexer — processes share the same CUDA context, so a crash in one process can affect others. Use MPS for cooperative workloads from the same team. MIG is hardware-level partitioning — each instance has its own dedicated memory, cache, and compute slices. Use MIG for hostile multi-tenancy where tenants shouldn't interfere with each other. MIG requires A100/H100/B200; MPS works on all GPUs.

Spot Instance Strategy — Save 60-70%

Cloud spot instances are spare capacity sold at massive discounts. The tradeoff: they can be terminated with 30-120 seconds notice. Use spot for: distributed training with checkpointing (save every N steps — on termination, resume from last checkpoint), hyperparameter sweeps (each trial is independent — losing one is acceptable), batch inference (replay failed batches on on-demand instances). Do NOT use spot for: real-time inference serving (can't tolerate termination), stateful workloads without checkpointing, or workloads with strict completion deadlines.

GPU Idle Detection Script for anihpj
#!/bin/bash
# anihpj-gpu-idle-detector.sh — Detect idle GPUs and alert
THRESHOLD=10          # % utilization — below this = idle
IDLE_MINUTES=60       # How long before alerting

for GPU in $(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index --format=csv,noheader); do
    UTIL=$(dcgmi dmon -e 203 -c 1 -i $GPU 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | awk '{print $2}')
    if [ "$UTIL" -lt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
        # Check how long GPU has been idle
        IDLE_TIME=$(check_idle_duration $GPU)
        if [ "$IDLE_TIME" -gt "$((IDLE_MINUTES * 60))" ]; then
            echo "⚠️ GPU $GPU idle for ${IDLE_MINUTES}min (util=$UTIL%)"
            # Alert via PagerDuty or Slack
            curl -X POST https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue \
                -d '{"routing_key":"'$PD_KEY'","event_action":"trigger",...}'
        fi
    fi
done

Not every workload needs an H100. Matching the GPU to the workload is the essence of cost optimization. Using an H100 ($30K) for a workload that runs fine on an L40S ($8K) wastes $22K per GPU.

⚡ Speed Tip — The Right-Sizing Rule of Thumb

Train on H100, infer on L40S, prototype on RTX 4090. This combination optimizes cost-performance across the AI lifecycle. The cost ratio is roughly: H100 ($30K) : L40S ($8K) : RTX 4090 ($1.6K) = 19:5:1. Anihpj's 4-DGX cluster uses all three: H100 for nightly retraining, L40S for 24/7 inference, RTX 4090 workstations for data scientists.

17.4 NVAIE Licensing — Professional View

NVIDIA AI Enterprise (NVAIE) is a per-GPU, per-year software license that includes: enterprise support (24/7, 1-hour response for Sev1), pre-tested and validated NGC containers, security patches with SLA, and access to NVIDIA AI workflows and reference architectures. At ~$4,500/GPU/year for training and ~$2,000/GPU/year for inference, the question is: does it pay for itself?

NVAIE vs DIY — The Engineering Time Calculus

The real cost comparison isn't NVAIE vs free open-source — it's NVAIE vs engineering time. A GPU SRE costs ~$150K/year fully loaded (~$75/hr). Tasks NVAIE eliminates: testing driver/CUDA/framework compatibility (saves ~4 hrs/month), applying security patches (saves ~2 hrs/month), debugging NGC container issues (saves ~8 hrs/month), validating new CUDA versions (saves ~8 hrs/quarter). Total: ~20 hrs/month saved = $1,500/month in engineering time per cluster. At $4,500/GPU/year × 32 GPUs = $144K/year for NVAIE. Engineering time saved: $1,500 × 12 = $18K/year per SRE. For anihpj with 0.5 FTE GPU SRE, NVAIE saves ~$9K/year in engineering time — the remaining $135K pays for: guaranteed compatibility, faster time-to-production, and enterprise support for critical issues.

NVAIE Licensing — Cost vs Value Breakdown

  Inference GPUs (16): 16 × $2,000/yr = $32,000/yr
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  NVAIE VALUE (Quantified):

  🎯 NVAIE essentially pays for itself in risk reduction alone.
  🎯 For regulated industries (healthcare, finance): NVAIE is MANDATORY.
  🎯 For startups: use NGC (free) until you have revenue-dependent workloads.

License Portability — Run Anywhere

One NVAIE license covers one GPU for one year — whether that GPU is in your DGX, an OEM server, or a cloud instance. This portability means: (1) you can move workloads between on-prem and cloud without additional licensing, (2) you're not locked into specific hardware vendors (any NVIDIA-Certified System works), (3) cloud GPU instances that include NVAIE (like DGX Cloud) bundle the license in the hourly rate — no separate purchase needed.
